Common patterns: application-dev.yml for local, application-prod.yml for production, and profile-specific beans annotated with @Profile("prod") that only instantiate in that profile. Since Spring Boot 2.4, profile groups let you activate a named group (spring.profiles.group.production=prod-db,prod-metrics) so one flag turns on multiple profiles.

Practical debugging: the Actuator /actuator/env endpoint (when exposed) lists every property with its source and precedence — the fastest way to find 'where is this value coming from?'. If you cannot enable Actuator, an EnvironmentAware bean can print the property source list at startup for the same purpose. For any property you care about, always ask: which of the twelve sources has it, and does anything higher-precedence override it?

An interview-quality answer names the general rule (command line > env vars > profile files > base files) rather than reciting all twelve, gives the SERVER_PORT example, and mentions @Profile / profile groups and Actuator's env endpoint as the practical tools. That shows you understand configuration as a precedence system, not as scattered @Value lookups.
bullets: Command-line args and env vars beat all file config; profile files beat non-profile files at the same location.
SERVER_PORT env var overrides server.port from application.yml — relaxed binding maps UPPER_SNAKE_CASE to dot.case automatically.
spring.profiles.active activates profiles; application-{profile}.yml overrides application.yml; multiple profiles merge left-to-right with the rightmost winning.
Profile groups (spring.profiles.group.production=prod-db,prod-metrics) let one flag activate several profiles.
@Profile("prod") on a @Bean or @Configuration makes it conditional on the active profile.
Actuator /actuator/env shows every property with its source and precedence — the fastest 'where does this value come from?' tool.
cards.code:
# Layered config
# application.yml              (base, lowest in-jar priority)
server.port: 8080
spring.datasource.url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/app

# application-prod.yml         (overrides base in prod)
spring.datasource.url: jdbc:postgresql://db.prod:5432/app
spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size: 30

# Run with:
java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod --server.port=9090
# effective server.port: 9090     (command line wins)
# effective datasource.url: prod  (profile file wins over base)

# Container override
#   docker run -e SERVER_PORT=7070 -e SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod app
#   SERVER_PORT overrides server.port from any file

# Profile group -- one switch, multiple profiles
# spring.profiles.group.production=prod-db,prod-metrics
# java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=production

# Inspect everything live
# GET /actuator/env    -> every property + source + precedence

// Conditional bean by profile
@Configuration
@Profile("prod")
class ProdConfig {
    @Bean DataSource dataSource() { ... }
}

cards.title: @ConfigurationProperties vs @Value: Type Safety, Relaxed Binding, and When to Use Each
bullets: @Value injects one scalar; @ConfigurationProperties binds an entire prefix tree to a POJO.
@ConfigurationProperties gives relaxed binding (kebab, camel, snake, env-var forms all match the same field), type conversion (Duration, DataSize, enums), JSR-380 validation, and IDE metadata.
@Value does no validation, no relaxed binding, no autocomplete, and fails cryptically when a required property is missing.
@ConfigurationProperties class must become a bean — @Component, @ConfigurationPropertiesScan, or @EnableConfigurationProperties.
Rule of thumb: @Value for one-off scalars, @ConfigurationProperties for anything with 3+ related fields, nesting, or validation.

cards.title: @Transactional Internals and the Six Silent Failures
cards.summary:
@Transactional is the most misused annotation in the Spring ecosystem. It is a thin, easy-to-write annotation that looks like it 'just works', but its semantics are governed by proxies, propagation rules, and rollback contracts — and it fails silently in six common ways that ship to production and cause data corruption or phantom transactions.

How it actually works. @Transactional is implemented by a BeanPostProcessor (AbstractAutoProxyCreator via InfrastructureAdvisorAutoProxyCreator) that wraps the finished bean in a proxy (JDK dynamic proxy if it implements interfaces, CGLIB otherwise). External callers hit the proxy, which starts a transaction (or joins one), invokes the target method, commits if it returns normally, and rolls back if it throws. This is why self-invocation (this.someMethod()) bypasses @Transactional — the internal call skips the proxy. This is also why final methods break — CGLIB cannot override them.

Propagation controls what happens when a transactional method calls another. REQUIRED (default) joins the existing transaction if one exists, otherwise starts a new one. REQUIRES_NEW always suspends the current transaction and starts a fresh one — useful when you need to persist audit logs even if the outer transaction rolls back. NESTED creates a savepoint inside the current transaction; it rolls back to the savepoint, not the whole transaction. MANDATORY requires an existing transaction or throws. NEVER forbids one. SUPPORTS uses one if present, else runs non-transactionally. NOT_SUPPORTED suspends any existing transaction. Most bugs live in REQUIRES_NEW (people forget it commits independently) and NESTED (savepoints need database support).

Isolation levels map to the database's own: READ_COMMITTED (default), READ_UNCOMMITTED, REPEATABLE_READ, SERIALIZABLE. Setting anything stricter than the database default has real cost — locks, retries, deadlocks — so choose deliberately, not by habit.

The six silent failures:

1. Self-invocation. this.method() bypasses the proxy. Calls inside the same class do not start a new transaction. The fix is to move the inner method to another bean, use TransactionTemplate, or use AspectJ load-time weaving.

2. Checked exceptions do not roll back. @Transactional only rolls back on RuntimeException and Error by default. If your method throws a checked exception (IOException, a custom Exception), the transaction commits. Fix: @Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class), or throw an unchecked exception, or handle and rethrow wrapped.

3. Final methods and final classes cannot be proxied by CGLIB. @Transactional on a final method is silently ignored — no transaction starts, no warning. Fix: remove final, extract into an interface (JDK proxy handles it), or use AspectJ.

4. Private methods are not proxied. Spring's proxy-based AOP only intercepts public methods (and protected for CGLIB, but the common contract is public). @Transactional on a private method does nothing. Fix: make the method public or restructure.

5. Wrong proxy target in injection. If you @Autowired the concrete class but Spring produced a JDK proxy of the interface, injection fails at startup with BeanNotOfRequiredTypeException. Fix: inject the interface, or force proxyTargetClass=true.

6. readOnly=true on a method that writes. readOnly is a hint to Hibernate to skip dirty-checking and to the JDBC driver to mark the connection read-only. If the method writes, the write is either silently ignored or fails when the driver enforces read-only. Fix: remove readOnly on write methods; use it only for genuine reads.

Additional common pitfalls worth knowing: long transactions holding database locks across network calls to downstream services (never do IO inside a transaction); @Transactional on @Async methods (async executes on a different thread with a different transaction context — the transaction often does not propagate as expected); and nested @Transactional where the inner REQUIRES_NEW bean is actually the same bean invoked via self-invocation, so REQUIRES_NEW silently does nothing.

An interview answer that names the proxy model, the six failure modes, and the REQUIRED vs REQUIRES_NEW distinction is far stronger than 'it makes methods transactional'. Bonus points for mentioning TransactionTemplate (imperative, no proxy, no self-invocation risk) as the escape hatch when @Transactional's proxy model gets in the way.
bullets: @Transactional uses a runtime AOP proxy (JDK or CGLIB) — external callers hit the proxy, which manages begin/commit/rollback.
Six silent failures: self-invocation, checked exceptions, final methods/classes, private methods, wrong injection type, readOnly on writes.
Rollback default: only RuntimeException and Error. Use rollbackFor = Exception.class for checked exceptions.
Propagation: REQUIRED (join or create), REQUIRES_NEW (suspend outer, always new), NESTED (savepoint), MANDATORY, NEVER, SUPPORTS, NOT_SUPPORTED.
Never do network IO inside a transaction — long-held locks cause cascading timeouts.
TransactionTemplate is the imperative escape hatch — no proxy, no self-invocation trap.

cards.title: Actuator: Health, Metrics, Env, and the Endpoints That Make Spring Boot Production-Ready
cards.summary:
Actuator is the module that gives a running Spring Boot app an HTTP interface for introspection and operations. Add spring-boot-starter-actuator and Boot exposes a set of endpoints under /actuator by default: /actuator/health (are you up?), /actuator/info (build and git metadata), /actuator/metrics (JVM and application metrics), and a few others, depending on what is on the classpath. The full set of possible endpoints includes env, beans, configprops, mappings, loggers, threaddump, heapdump, httptrace, scheduledtasks, and prometheus — but most are disabled by default because they can leak sensitive data.

/actuator/health is the endpoint Kubernetes readiness and liveness probes talk to. It aggregates multiple HealthIndicators (database reachable, disk space, Redis ping, Kafka broker reachable) into an overall status: UP, DOWN, OUT_OF_SERVICE, UNKNOWN. You can write custom HealthIndicators by implementing the interface and registering them as beans, and you can control what is shown to unauthenticated users with management.endpoint.health.show-details (default never; use when_authorized to reveal DB details only to authenticated callers).

/actuator/metrics exposes Micrometer meters — JVM memory, GC pauses, HTTP request timings, thread pool stats, DataSource pool utilization, and any custom counters or timers you register. Meter names follow Micrometer conventions (http.server.requests, jvm.memory.used, hikaricp.connections.active). The /actuator/prometheus endpoint (when the micrometer-registry-prometheus dependency is present) exports these in Prometheus text format, ready to be scraped.

/actuator/env lists every property with its source and precedence — the single best tool for 'where is this value coming from?' debugging. /actuator/configprops shows the bound @ConfigurationProperties beans. /actuator/beans shows every bean in the context with its type and dependencies. /actuator/mappings shows all HTTP routes. /actuator/threaddump dumps thread stacks (great for hanging requests). /actuator/heapdump produces a .hprof file you can open in a profiler — be careful with this in production, it can be hundreds of MB.

Security is critical. By default, most endpoints are disabled. Even health and info should generally not be exposed on the public internet — Kubernetes probes work fine on an internal port. The recommended production setup: management.server.port=8081 puts Actuator on a separate internal port, unreachable from the outside; secure it with Spring Security on that port; enable only the endpoints you need (management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,prometheus); and put health behind authentication with management.endpoint.health.show-details=when_authorized.

Custom endpoints are easy: annotate a class with @Endpoint(id = "features") and @ReadOperation methods for GET-like reads, @WriteOperation for POST-like writes. Custom health indicators: implement HealthIndicator and register the bean — Boot's aggregate picks it up automatically.

An interview answer that names health, metrics, env, and loggers specifically (with the security warning) shows real production experience. An answer that only says 'it exposes endpoints' is superficial.
bullets: Actuator exposes operational endpoints under /actuator: health, info, metrics, env, beans, configprops, loggers, threaddump, heapdump.
/actuator/health aggregates multiple HealthIndicators (DB, disk, Redis, custom) into UP/DOWN — used by Kubernetes probes.
/actuator/metrics exposes Micrometer meters; /actuator/prometheus exports them for scraping.
/actuator/env shows property sources and precedence — best tool for config debugging.
Security: most endpoints disabled by default; put Actuator on a separate port (management.server.port) and expose only what you need (exposure.include).
Custom: @Endpoint for operations, HealthIndicator for health checks.

cards.title: Embedded Server and Graceful Shutdown: How java -jar Actually Serves HTTP
cards.summary:
In classic Java web deployments, your application was a WAR file dropped into a pre-installed Tomcat, and the server lived outside your build. Spring Boot flips this: the application IS the server. spring-boot-starter-web brings spring-boot-starter-tomcat, which brings the Tomcat embed jar, and Spring Boot creates a Tomcat instance programmatically inside the JVM. When you run java -jar app.jar, your main method runs, the context refreshes, and around step 7e of the startup sequence Boot instantiates Tomcat, binds the port, deploys the DispatcherServlet, and starts accepting requests. There is no external install, no war file, no container — one JVM, one jar, one server.

The default is Tomcat, but Jetty and Undertow are drop-in swaps: exclude spring-boot-starter-tomcat, add spring-boot-starter-jetty or spring-boot-starter-undertow. Jetty is often chosen for lower memory and better support of long-lived connections like WebSockets; Undertow has the smallest footprint and is optimized for very high concurrency. Configuration is uniform via server.* properties regardless of choice: server.port, server.servlet.context-path, server.tomcat.max-threads, server.undertow.io-threads.

server.tomcat.max-threads (default 200) is the maximum number of worker threads — if it saturates, new requests queue in the OS accept backlog or are rejected depending on the OS. This is different from the HikariCP connection pool size; if max-threads is 200 but the DB pool is 10, 190 threads will block on connection acquisition, which is where many production latency incidents originate. Sizing those two together (threads ≈ pool × expectedIOwaitRatio) is a real engineering decision, not a checkbox.

Graceful shutdown is the property that separates a toy app from a production app. When a pod receives SIGTERM (Kubernetes rolling update, deploy), the default behavior in Spring Boot pre-2.3 was to kill the JVM immediately — in-flight requests get 500 errors and clients see broken responses. With server.shutdown=graceful (since Boot 2.3, default in 3.x is still immediate unless enabled), Boot stops accepting new requests on the connector, waits up to spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase (default 30s) for in-flight requests to finish, then proceeds to close the context and run @PreDestroy / DisposableBean / custom destroy-method on beans. Kubernetes should set terminationGracePeriodSeconds greater than the timeout so the pod does not get SIGKILLed mid-drain.

Graceful shutdown is a chain: stop accept connector → wait for in-flight requests → stop the servlet container → publish ContextClosedEvent → run @PreDestroy on beans → run DisposableBean.destroy → run custom destroy-method → close the JVM. If you have background executors or message listeners (Kafka, Rabbit, SQS pollers), they must be stopped during shutdown too — that is what @PreDestroy and SmartLifecycle implementations are for. Kafka consumers should stop their pollers, commit offsets cleanly, and leave the consumer group so partitions reassign without a rebalance storm. Getting this right is the difference between a deploy that loses zero in-flight requests and one that drops a small percentage on every rollout.

An interview answer that explains (1) the server is inside the JVM, not external, (2) Tomcat is the default but Jetty/Undertow are drop-in swaps, (3) graceful shutdown is opt-in and needs Kubernetes terminationGracePeriodSeconds coordination, and (4) background processors must be stopped in @PreDestroy, is a complete answer.
bullets: Spring Boot embeds the server (Tomcat default) inside the JVM; the app jar is the web server, no external Tomcat install.
Jetty and Undertow are drop-in alternatives via starter swap; same server.* properties apply.
server.tomcat.max-threads (default 200) is worker-thread limit; mismatch with DB pool size causes connection-acquire latency spikes.
server.shutdown=graceful stops accepting new requests, drains in-flight up to spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase, then destroys beans.
Kubernetes terminationGracePeriodSeconds must exceed the shutdown timeout, or the pod is SIGKILLed mid-drain.
Background processors (Kafka, Rabbit, executors) must be stopped in @PreDestroy / SmartLifecycle for clean shutdown.

cards.title: What Is Kafka? The Distributed Append-Only Log Mental Model
cards.summary:
Apache Kafka is best understood not as a message queue but as a distributed, append-only, immutable log that many independent readers can consume at their own pace[reference:0]. A traditional queue (RabbitMQ, SQS) is a mailbox: a producer drops a message, one consumer picks it up, and the broker deletes it. Consumption is destructive — once processed, the message is gone[reference:1]. Kafka inverts this. Records are never deleted by consumers; they persist on disk until a retention policy (time or size) removes them[reference:2]. Each consumer tracks its own position (offset) in the log. Two consumer groups can read the same partition at completely different positions simultaneously, and neither affects the other. Consuming changes nothing about the data; readers simply move forward[reference:3]. This is the single most important mental model: if you design Kafka topics around deletion (as you would a queue), you will get single-partition bottlenecks, aggressive retention mistakes, and consumer-lag panic — all symptoms of queue habits applied to a log[reference:4].

The core architecture has four pieces. Brokers are the servers that store data and serve client requests; a cluster is a set of brokers[reference:5]. Topics are named, categorized streams of data. Each topic is split into partitions, which are ordered, append-only sequences of records distributed across brokers[reference:6]. Producers are applications that publish records to topics. Consumers are applications that subscribe to topics and read records, typically as part of a consumer group[reference:7]. An offset is a monotonically increasing integer assigned to each record within a partition, acting as its unique position identifier[reference:8]. Offsets give consumers a durable bookmark: store the offset of the last processed record, and you can resume from there after a crash or deploy[reference:9].

The log abstraction unlocks capabilities a queue cannot provide. Replay: because data persists, you can reset a consumer group's offsets to the earliest record and reprocess history — essential for bug fixes, event sourcing, and rebuilding derived state[reference:10]. Fan-out: many independent consumer groups can read the same topic without interfering; each group maintains its own offsets, so analytics, billing, and alerting pipelines can all consume the same event stream at different speeds. Ordering is per-partition, not per-topic: Kafka guarantees that records within one partition are read in the order they were written, but records across different partitions of the same topic have no ordering guarantee relative to each other[reference:11]. This is why key-based partitioning matters: all events for a given entity (user_id, order_id) hash to the same partition, preserving order for that entity while other entities flow in parallel[reference:12].

The durability and performance story explains why Kafka is used for streaming at scale. Kafka writes sequentially to disk, which is far faster than random writes, and it uses the operating system's zero-copy feature to stream data from the page cache straight to the network without copying it through user space[reference:13]. This combination allows single clusters to sustain millions of messages per second[reference:14]. Replication across brokers provides fault tolerance: each partition has a leader and followers, and the leader coordinates all reads and writes while followers replicate the log. If the leader broker dies, one of the in-sync followers is promoted[reference:15].

In an interview, the strongest opening answer for 'What is Kafka?' is: 'Kafka is a distributed append-only log, not a queue. Consumers read at their own offsets and never delete data; retention is a storage policy. Ordering is per-partition, replay is a first-class operation, and many consumer groups can independently consume the same stream.' That framing immediately distinguishes you from candidates who only know Kafka as 'a faster RabbitMQ'[reference:16].
bullets: Kafka is a distributed append-only log, not a queue — consumers track offsets; consumption never deletes data; retention is a storage policy.
Core components: brokers (servers), topics (named streams), partitions (ordered append-only slices), producers (writers), consumers (readers), offsets (per-record positions).
Consumers can replay history by resetting offsets — a queue cannot do this because messages are deleted after acknowledgment.
Ordering is guaranteed only within a partition, not across partitions; use key-based partitioning to preserve per-entity order while parallelizing across entities.
Kafka achieves high throughput via sequential disk writes and OS zero-copy, streaming data from the page cache to the network without user-space copies.
Fan-out: many consumer groups read the same topic independently, each tracking its own offsets, without interfering with one another.
cards.code:
Queue mental model (RabbitMQ, SQS)

  Producer --> [ mailbox ] --> Consumer
                                   |
                                   v
                              ACK -> DELETE
  (message is gone; cannot replay; one consumer)


Kafka mental model (append-only log)

  Producer --> [ partition: offset 0,1,2,3,4,5 ... ]
                          ^      ^      ^
                          |      |      |
             ConsumerA ---+      |      |       (offset 3)
             ConsumerB ----------+      |       (offset 1)
             ConsumerC -----------------+       (offset 5)

  - retention deletes old segments by time/size, NOT by consumption
  - each consumer group stores its own committed offset
  - replay = reset offsets to an earlier point

cards.title: Topic, Partition, and Offset: The Three Words Everything Else Builds On
cards.summary:
A topic is a logical name for a stream of records — think 'orders', 'clicks', or 'payments'. But a topic is not a file on one disk. It is split into partitions, and each partition is a separate append-only log that lives on a specific broker[reference:17]. The number of partitions determines the maximum parallelism of consumption: within a consumer group, each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer, so a topic with four partitions can have at most four active consumers doing work in that group[reference:18]. If you add a fifth consumer, it sits idle until a partition becomes available. This is why partition count is a capacity-planning decision, not an afterthought.

An offset is a sequential, monotonically increasing integer assigned to every record within a partition[reference:19]. It is not a global identifier across the topic — offset 42 in partition 0 is a different record from offset 42 in partition 1. Offsets serve three purposes. First, they define position: a consumer's current offset tells Kafka where it is in the log. Second, they enable resumption: commit the offset of the last processed record, and after a crash the consumer restarts from that position[reference:20]. Third, they enable replay: reset offsets to an earlier point and reprocess records[reference:21]. Crucially, offsets are not timestamps and are not stable forever — when old log segments are deleted by retention, the earliest available offset advances, so code that tries to calculate offsets from timestamps will break when segments expire[reference:22].

Partitions are stored as segment files on disk. A partition is not one giant file; it is a series of rolling segments, each with a base offset. The active segment receives writes; when it reaches a size or time threshold, it is closed and a new active segment is created. Retention and compaction operate at the segment level, which is why you cannot delete an individual record — you can only delete whole segments or compact them by key. This is a deliberate design: immutable, append-only files enable sequential I/O and zero-copy reads, which is the foundation of Kafka's throughput[reference:23].

The relationship between topic, partition, and offset can be summarized as: a topic is a logical stream, a partition is a physical ordered log within that stream, and an offset is a record's position within that log. A consumer group's progress is tracked per partition: it stores a committed offset for each partition it owns. When a group rebalances, partitions are reassigned among consumers, and each consumer resumes from the committed offset of its newly assigned partition. This is why rebalances can cause latency spikes — consumers must fetch the committed offsets and seek to those positions before processing resumes.

The interview trap is to treat offset as a message ID. It is not. Two records in different partitions can have the same offset. Offsets are positional, not globally unique. The second trap is to assume you can always replay from offset 0. If retention has deleted the earliest segments, the earliest available offset is greater than 0, and a reset to 'earliest' will start from whatever is still on disk, not from the true beginning of time. The mental model is: topic = logical stream; partition = ordered physical log; offset = cursor position within that log; retention = the window of history that still exists.
bullets: A topic is a logical stream; it is split into partitions, each an ordered append-only log on a broker.
An offset is a per-partition monotonically increasing position, not a global message ID — offset 42 in partition 0 differs from offset 42 in partition 1.
Partition count caps consumer-group parallelism: one partition is assigned to at most one consumer in the group.
Partitions are stored as rolling segment files; retention deletes whole segments, not individual records, so the earliest available offset advances over time.
Offsets enable resumption (commit and restart) and replay (reset to earlier), but replay is limited to the retention window.
Kafka's throughput comes from immutable segment files enabling sequential writes and zero-copy reads.

  Partition 0  [offset 0][offset 1][offset 2][offset 3][offset 4] ...
  Partition 1  [offset 0][offset 1][offset 2][offset 3] ...
  Partition 2  [offset 0][offset 1][offset 2][offset 3][offset 4][offset 5] ...

Consumer group 'billing':
  Consumer-1 -> Partition 0 (committed offset = 3)
  Consumer-2 -> Partition 1 (committed offset = 1)
  Consumer-3 -> Partition 2 (committed offset = 5)

  (4th consumer joins -> sits idle until a partition is freed)

  00000000000000000000.log   (base offset 0, closed)
  00000000000000100000.log   (base offset 100000, closed)

Retention deletes whole segments -> earliest available offset
advances from 0 to 100000, then to 200000, ...

cards.title: Producer, Consumer, Broker, Cluster: Who Talks to Whom and How
cards.summary:
A Kafka cluster is a set of brokers — individual servers, each identified by a numeric broker ID, each storing a subset of partitions and serving client requests[reference:24]. When you create a topic with replication factor 3 and 6 partitions, the cluster distributes those 18 partition-replicas across brokers. For each partition, one replica is the leader and the others are followers. All producer writes and consumer reads go to the leader; followers replicate the leader's log in the background. If the leader broker dies, a follower whose log is sufficiently caught up (an in-sync replica, or ISR) is promoted to leader and clients transparently reconnect.

A producer is any application that publishes records. Internally, the producer is not a single-threaded send-and-wait loop. The application thread calls send(record), which serializes the key and value, determines the target partition (by key hash, by explicit partition, or round-robin if no key), and appends the record to a per-partition in-memory buffer called the RecordAccumulator. A background I/O thread then drains batches from this accumulator, compresses them as a unit, and sends them to the appropriate broker leaders[reference:25]. This separation between application thread and I/O thread is why send() returns a Future immediately — the actual network call happens asynchronously. Batching (batch.size) and waiting (linger.ms) are the two knobs that trade latency for throughput: a larger batch and a longer linger mean fewer, fuller network requests and better compression ratios, at the cost of higher per-record latency[reference:26].

A consumer reads records by repeatedly calling poll(). Each poll returns a batch of records from the partitions assigned to that consumer. The consumer does not push records to you; you pull them. Under the hood, the consumer tracks its position in each partition and periodically commits that position (the offset) back to Kafka. In a consumer group, partitions are assigned across the group's consumers so that each partition is owned by exactly one consumer at a time[reference:27]. This assignment is coordinated by a broker acting as the group coordinator, and it can change during a rebalance — for example, when a consumer joins, leaves, or is declared dead because it stopped sending heartbeats.

The flow of a single record is worth tracing end to end. Producer send(record) → serialize → choose partition → buffer in RecordAccumulator → background I/O thread drains batch → compress → network request to the partition leader → leader appends to its local log → followers fetch and append → leader responds according to acks setting → producer's Future completes. On the consumer side: poll() → fetch request to leaders of assigned partitions → broker returns records from the consumer's current position → consumer processes records → consumer commits offsets (auto or manual) → next poll() continues from the new position. Every durability, ordering, and delivery-semantics guarantee is a consequence of the details inside this flow: acks controls when the producer considers a write successful; ISR determines what 'replicated' means; auto vs manual commit determines whether a crash before processing causes data loss or duplicates.

In interviews, the most common mistake is to describe producers and consumers as talking to 'the cluster' generically. They talk to specific partition leaders, which are specific brokers. The second most common mistake is to forget that consumers pull, not push — this pull model is what allows consumers to process at their own pace and to replay. The third is to understate the producer's internal buffering: send() is not a network call, it is an enqueue; the actual write happens on a background thread, which is why configuring batch.size and linger.ms has such a large effect on throughput.
bullets: A cluster is a set of brokers; each partition has one leader replica and zero or more follower replicas distributed across brokers.
All producer writes and consumer reads go to the partition leader; followers replicate in the background; ISR replicas are eligible for promotion on leader failure.
Producer send() is asynchronous: records are buffered per-partition in the RecordAccumulator and drained by a background I/O thread in compressed batches.
Consumers pull by calling poll(); each poll returns records from assigned partitions; consumers commit offsets to track progress.
Consumer-group partition assignment is coordinated by a broker acting as group coordinator; heartbeats determine liveness; rebalances reassign partitions.
acks, ISR, and commit mode (auto vs manual) are the three levers that determine durability, ordering, and delivery semantics.

Cluster layout (replication factor 3, 3 brokers)

  Broker 1            Broker 2            Broker 3
  ----------          ----------          ----------
  P0 leader           P0 follower         P0 follower
  P1 follower         P1 leader           P1 follower
  P2 follower         P2 follower         P2 leader

Producer flow

  send(record)
    -> serialize key/value
    -> choose partition (key hash | explicit | round-robin)
    -> append to RecordAccumulator (one deque per TopicPartition)
    -> [background I/O thread]
       -> drain batch
       -> compress (lz4/snappy/zstd)
       -> network send to partition leader
       -> leader appends, followers fetch
       -> leader responds per acks
    -> Future completes

Consumer flow

  while (true) {
      records = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(100));
      for (record : records) process(record);
      consumer.commitSync();   // or auto-commit
  }

cards.title: Why Kafka Over a Database or a Simple Queue? Replay, Fan-Out, and the Cost of Deletion
cards.summary:
The question 'why not just use a database table as a queue?' has a precise answer: databases are optimized for mutable state and transactional consistency, not for append-heavy sequential reads with many independent consumers. A database queue table requires polling (or LISTEN/NOTIFY), row-level locking to prevent two workers from grabbing the same row, index maintenance on the status column, and vacuuming as rows are deleted. Throughput is bounded by row-level write contention. Kafka, by contrast, appends sequentially to immutable segment files, serves reads from the page cache, and uses zero-copy to move data to the network without user-space copies[reference:28]. The result is that Kafka can sustain millions of messages per second per cluster[reference:29] while a database-backed queue typically tops out orders of magnitude lower without significant tuning.

The comparison with a traditional queue (RabbitMQ, SQS) is more subtle because both Kafka and queues decouple producers from consumers. The difference is the lifecycle of a message. A queue deletes a message after acknowledgment; if a consumer crashes after acking but before finishing its work, the message is gone. Kafka retains records until retention expires, independent of consumption[reference:30]. This changes the failure model. With a queue, you need an explicit dead-letter queue and careful ack timing to avoid loss. With Kafka, a bug in your consumer is recoverable: fix the code, reset the group's offsets to an earlier point, and replay[reference:31]. That replay capability is also the foundation of event sourcing and change data capture — the log is the source of truth, and downstream materialized views can be rebuilt by replaying it.

Fan-out is the second major differentiator. A queue is designed to deliver each message to one consumer. If three services need to react to the same order event, a queue requires either a fan-out exchange (RabbitMQ) or separate queues per consumer with a routing layer (SQS + SNS). Kafka gives you fan-out natively: many consumer groups can subscribe to the same topic, each maintaining its own offsets, each reading the full stream independently. Analytics, fraud detection, and billing can all consume 'orders' at their own pace without interfering with one another. This is not just convenience — it removes an entire category of coordination logic from your architecture.

Ordering is the trade-off. A single queue preserves global order across all messages. Kafka preserves order only within a partition[reference:32]. If you need total order for all events, you must use a single partition, which caps parallelism at one consumer. If you need per-entity order (all events for one order_id in sequence) while processing different entities in parallel, key-based partitioning gives you both: hash(order_id) routes all events for that order to the same partition, preserving order for that key, while other keys distribute across partitions for parallel consumption[reference:33]. This is the standard Kafka design pattern, and it is why choosing the right key is a business decision, not an infrastructure detail.

The decision matrix in one sentence: use Kafka when you need high throughput, replay, durable event history, or multi-consumer fan-out; use a traditional queue when you need per-message routing, complex routing rules (RabbitMQ exchanges), simple task distribution with low operational overhead, or serverless integration (SQS). Do not use Kafka as a general-purpose RPC mechanism or as a database replacement — it has no query language, no random-access lookup by primary key (unless you build one with compacted topics + external indexing), and no transactional multi-record updates across partitions.
bullets: Databases and queues delete after consumption; Kafka retains records until retention expires — this enables replay, recovery, and event sourcing.
Kafka's sequential immutable segment writes + zero-copy reads give orders-of-magnitude higher throughput than row-level-locking queue tables.
Fan-out is native: many consumer groups read the same topic independently with their own offsets; queues require fan-out exchanges or SNS-to-multiple-SQS wiring.
Ordering is per-partition; use key-based partitioning to preserve per-entity order while parallelizing across entities.
Use Kafka for high-throughput event streaming, replay, and fan-out; use RabbitMQ/SQS for per-message routing, task queues, and serverless integration.
Kafka is not a database: no query language, no random-access lookup, no cross-partition transactional updates.

Why not a database queue table?

  CREATE TABLE queue (
      id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
      payload JSONB,
      status TEXT DEFAULT 'PENDING'
  );
  -- polling: SELECT ... WHERE status='PENDING' FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
  -- contention on status index; vacuum on delete; row-level locks
  -- throughput ceiling: ~thousands/sec with tuning

Kafka equivalent:

  -- append-only segment file, sequential write
  -- page-cache reads, zero-copy to network
  -- millions/sec per cluster

Queue lifecycle vs Kafka lifecycle:

  RabbitMQ/SQS:
    produce -> consume -> ACK -> DELETE
    (crash after ACK = data loss)

  Kafka:
    produce -> append to log -> consumer reads at offset
    (retention deletes old segments by time/size, not by ACK)
    crash -> restart -> resume from committed offset OR reset to replay

Fan-out:

  Queue:    one consumer per message (or fan-out exchange)
  Kafka:    N consumer groups, each reads full stream independently

cards.title: Producer Mechanics: RecordAccumulator, Batching, Compression, and acks
cards.summary:
A Kafka producer is not a synchronous request-response client. When your application calls send(record), the call returns almost immediately with a Future; the record has only been serialized and appended to an in-memory buffer. The actual network write happens on a separate background I/O thread. This two-thread model — application thread produces, I/O thread sends — is the foundation of producer throughput and the reason batching parameters matter so much[reference:34].

The buffer is called the RecordAccumulator. Internally it holds one double-ended queue (deque) of ProducerBatch objects per topic-partition. When a record arrives, it is appended to the current batch for its target partition. A batch is sent when either (a) it reaches batch.size bytes (default 16 KB), or (b) linger.ms has elapsed since the batch was created (default 0, meaning send immediately)[reference:35]. This is the core latency-versus-throughput trade-off: linger.ms=0 minimizes latency but produces many small requests; linger.ms=10 with a larger batch.size produces fewer, fuller requests and better compression ratios, at the cost of up to 10 ms of additional latency per record. In high-throughput pipelines, the throughput gain from batching and compression far outweighs the latency cost.

Before a batch is sent, it is compressed as a unit using the codec configured in compression.type (none, gzip, snappy, lz4, zstd). Compressing a batch is significantly more effective than compressing individual records because the compressor sees more repeated patterns across the batch. This is another reason batching is central: larger batches compress better, reducing network I/O and broker disk usage. The compressed batch is then sent to the leader broker of the target partition.

The acks setting controls durability — when the producer considers a write successful. acks=0 means fire-and-forget: the producer does not wait for any broker acknowledgment; the record may be lost if the broker is unavailable, but throughput is maximal. acks=1 means the leader broker writes to its local log and acknowledges; if the leader crashes before followers replicate, the record is lost. acks=all (or -1) means the leader waits for all in-sync replicas (ISR) to acknowledge; combined with min.insync.replicas=2, this guarantees that the record survives the loss of any single broker. The standard production setting for critical data is acks=all with idempotence enabled and retries set to a high value[reference:36].

Idempotence deserves separate treatment because it is the default in modern Kafka clients. When enable.idempotence=true, the producer is assigned a Producer ID (PID) by the broker, and each batch for a given partition carries a monotonically increasing sequence number. If a network blip causes the producer to retry a batch that the broker already wrote, the broker recognizes the duplicate (PID, partition, sequence) and silently drops it. This eliminates the duplicate-on-retry problem that plagues non-idempotent producers[reference:37]. Constraints: idempotence requires acks=all, retries > 0, and max.in.flight.requests.per.connection ≤ 5. It guarantees deduplication within one producer session only — a producer restart gets a new PID, so cross-session exactly-once requires transactions.

Partition selection is the final piece. If the record has a key, the default partitioner computes murmur2(key) % numPartitions — this is deterministic, so the same key always lands on the same partition, preserving order for that key. If the key is null, the producer uses a sticky partitioner (since Kafka 2.4): it picks one partition and sticks to it until the batch is full or linger expires, then switches. This avoids the round-robin behavior of older clients, which produced many tiny batches. If the record specifies an explicit partition, the partitioner is bypassed.

The interview answer that distinguishes a strong candidate: explain the two-thread model (send() is an enqueue, not a network call), name RecordAccumulator and the batch.size/linger.ms trade-off, state the acks ladder precisely, and mention that idempotence is now the default and what it protects against. Bonus points for explaining that key-based partitioning is what gives Kafka per-key ordering.
bullets: send() serializes and enqueues into the RecordAccumulator; a background I/O thread drains batches and performs network writes.
RecordAccumulator holds one batch deque per topic-partition; batches are sent when batch.size bytes are reached or linger.ms elapses.
Compression (lz4/snappy/zstd) is applied per batch — larger batches compress better, which is why batching improves both throughput and network efficiency.
acks ladder: 0 = fire-and-forget, 1 = leader only, all = all ISR replicas; production critical data uses acks=all + min.insync.replicas=2.
Idempotent producer (default in modern clients) assigns a PID and per-partition sequence numbers; the broker deduplicates retries within a producer session.
Key-based partitioning preserves per-key ordering; null-key records use a sticky partitioner to fill batches efficiently.

Producer internals

  Application thread                Background I/O thread
  ------------------                ----------------------
  send(record)
    -> serialize
    -> choose partition
    -> append to RecordAccumulator
       (one ProducerBatch deque per TopicPartition)
                                      drain batch
                                        -> compress (lz4/snappy/zstd)
                                        -> send to partition leader
                                        -> handle acks / retries
    <- Future completes            <-

Batch trigger:
  batch.size reached (default 16 KB)  OR  linger.ms elapsed (default 0)

acks ladder:
  acks=0    fire-and-forget, max throughput, may lose data
  acks=1    leader confirms, loses data if leader dies before followers replicate
  acks=all  all ISR confirm; use with min.insync.replicas=2 for durability

Idempotent producer:
  enable.idempotence=true
  acks=all
  retries=Integer.MAX_VALUE
  max.in.flight.requests.per.connection <= 5

Partition selection:
  key != null  -> murmur2(key) % numPartitions  (same key -> same partition)
  key == null  -> sticky partitioner (fills one batch before switching)

cards.title: Consumer Mechanics: poll(), Offset Commit, and the Auto-Commit Data-Loss Trap
cards.summary:
A Kafka consumer is a pull-based client. It does not receive records via callbacks; instead, the application calls poll(Duration) in a loop, and each call returns a batch of ConsumerRecord objects from the partitions currently assigned to this consumer. Behind poll(), the consumer sends fetch requests to the leaders of those partitions, requesting records starting from its current position. The returned batch is bounded by max.poll.records (default 500) and by fetch size limits, which is why poll() may return an empty batch even when data exists — it respects the timeout and fetch constraints[reference:38].

The consumer's position is tracked as an offset per partition. After processing records, the consumer commits the offset of the next record it wants to read (or the last processed record, depending on the client's convention) back to Kafka. Committed offsets are stored in an internal Kafka topic called __consumer_offsets. When a consumer restarts or a rebalance assigns it a partition, it fetches the committed offset for that partition and seeks to that position. This is how progress survives crashes and deploys.

The single most important configuration decision for a consumer is auto-commit vs manual commit. With enable.auto.commit=true (the default), the consumer periodically commits the latest offset returned by poll(), at the interval set by auto.commit.interval.ms (default 5 seconds)[reference:39]. The failure mode is severe: imagine poll() returns records 100–199, auto-commit fires and commits offset 200, and then the consumer crashes while processing record 150. On restart, the consumer fetches from offset 200, and records 150–199 are lost forever[reference:40]. Auto-commit provides at-most-once delivery: records may be lost, but never duplicated (because the committed offset is always ahead of or equal to the processed position). For any workload where data loss is unacceptable, enable.auto.commit must be false, and the application must commit manually after processing.

Manual commit gives you at-least-once semantics. The pattern is: poll() → process each record (or the whole batch) → commitSync() or commitAsync(). commitSync() blocks until the broker acknowledges the commit and retries on retriable errors; commitAsync() does not block but provides a callback for errors and does not retry automatically (to avoid overwriting a newer commit). The trade-off between them is latency vs safety: commitSync() is slower but ensures the commit succeeded before proceeding; commitAsync() is faster but may leave the group with a stale committed offset if the commit fails silently[reference:41]. A common production pattern is commitAsync() during the loop and commitSync() in the shutdown hook or rebalance listener to ensure a final, durable commit.

At-least-once delivery means duplicates are possible. If a consumer processes a record, crashes before committing, and restarts from the last committed offset, it will process that record again. This is why every Kafka consumer must be idempotent: use an idempotency key (the record's unique business ID) and make the downstream write conditional on that key not already existing. The consumer does not guarantee exactly-once by itself — it guarantees at-least-once, and idempotent processing bridges the gap to effectively-once.

Two more mechanics matter for interviews. First, max.poll.interval.ms (default 5 minutes) is the maximum time between poll() calls before the consumer is considered dead and a rebalance is triggered. If processing a batch takes longer than this, the consumer is kicked out of the group, its partitions are reassigned, and another consumer reprocesses the same records. This is a common cause of duplicate processing under load — reduce max.poll.records or process asynchronously to keep the loop fast. Second, auto.offset.reset (earliest or latest) only applies when there is no committed offset for a partition — for example, on first consumption or after the committed offset has been deleted by retention[reference:42]. It is not a rebalance-time fallback; it is a no-committed-offset fallback. Confusing these two is a classic interview trap.
bullets: Consumers pull via poll(); each call returns up to max.poll.records (default 500) from assigned partitions.
Committed offsets are stored in __consumer_offsets; on restart or rebalance, the consumer seeks to the committed position.
Auto-commit (enable.auto.commit=true) commits the latest polled offset on a timer — crash before processing causes data loss (at-most-once).
Manual commit (enable.auto.commit=false) + process-then-commit gives at-least-once; duplicates are possible and require idempotent processing.
max.poll.interval.ms (default 5 min) kicks a consumer out of the group if poll() is not called frequently enough — long processing causes duplicate work.
auto.offset.reset applies only when no committed offset exists, not on every rebalance.
cards.code:
Auto-commit data-loss scenario

  poll() -> records 100..199
  auto-commit fires -> committed offset = 200
  crash while processing record 150
  restart -> fetch from offset 200
  records 150..199 are LOST

Manual commit for at-least-once

  props.put("enable.auto.commit", "false");
  while (true) {
      records = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(100));
      for (record : records) {
          processIdempotently(record);
      }
      consumer.commitSync();   // or commitAsync()
  }

Commit variants:
  commitSync()    blocks, retries on retriable errors, safe but slower
  commitAsync()   non-blocking, callback for errors, no retry,
                  may leave stale committed offset

Common pattern:
  commitAsync() in the loop
  commitSync() in shutdown hook / rebalance listener

max.poll.interval.ms (default 5 min):
  if poll() is not called within this window -> consumer is kicked,
  rebalance fires, partitions reassign, records reprocessed

auto.offset.reset:
  earliest | latest
  applies only when NO committed offset exists
  (first consumption, or committed offset deleted by retention)

cards.title: Consumer Groups and Rebalancing: How Kafka Divides Work and Why Rebalances Hurt
cards.summary:
A consumer group is a set of consumers that jointly consume a topic, with the guarantee that each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer in the group at any moment. This is how Kafka achieves parallelism without coordination between consumers: the group protocol assigns partitions so that no two consumers process the same partition simultaneously. If a topic has six partitions and a group has three consumers, each consumer gets two partitions. Add a seventh consumer, and one consumer sits idle — the maximum parallelism of a consumer group equals the number of partitions. This is the single most important capacity fact about consumer groups: you cannot scale consumption beyond the partition count by adding more consumers.

A broker is elected as the group coordinator, and it manages the group's state machine. Each consumer periodically sends a HeartbeatRequest to the coordinator. If the coordinator does not receive a heartbeat within session.timeout.ms (default 45 seconds in newer protocols, historically 10 seconds with a range), it marks that consumer as dead and triggers a rebalance. The coordinator also tracks a generation ID — a monotonically increasing number that increments on every rebalance. Offset commits are tagged with the generation ID they belong to; a commit from a stale generation (an old consumer that has not yet realized it was kicked out) is rejected with IllegalGeneration, preventing a zombie consumer from committing offsets that would cause data loss or duplication.

A rebalance is the process of redistributing partitions among the current members. It has several triggers: a new consumer joins, an existing consumer leaves gracefully, a consumer is declared dead (missed heartbeats), the partition count of the topic changes, or the subscribed topic list changes via pattern matching. The rebalance protocol has two phases. In the first phase, all consumers stop fetching, commit their current offsets, and send a JoinGroupRequest to the coordinator. The coordinator picks one consumer as the group leader and returns the full member list to it. In the second phase, the leader computes the partition assignment (using the configured assignor, such as Range, RoundRobin, Sticky, or CooperativeSticky) and sends it to the coordinator, which distributes it to all members. Only after all members acknowledge the assignment does normal consumption resume.

The pain of rebalancing comes from the stop-the-world nature of the classic eager protocol: during the rebalance, every consumer in the group pauses consumption, even partitions that are not changing owners. A large group rebalancing every few minutes (because of rolling deploys or flaky network) can spend more time rebalancing than processing. The incremental cooperative rebalancing protocol (introduced via CooperativeStickyAssignor) reduces this by only revoking the partitions that actually move, so consumers that keep their partitions continue processing. Spring for Apache Kafka and the Java client both support cooperative rebalancing, and it is the recommended mode for production groups.

In an interview, the strongest answer traces the full lifecycle: coordinator election, heartbeats, session timeout, generation ID, the two-phase JoinGroup/SyncGroup protocol, the eager vs cooperative distinction, and the partition-count cap on parallelism. That demonstrates you understand consumer groups as a distributed coordination protocol, not just as a configuration block.
bullets: A consumer group assigns each partition to exactly one consumer at a time; parallelism is capped by partition count.
The group coordinator (a broker) tracks membership via heartbeats; session.timeout.ms expiry triggers a rebalance.
A generation ID increments on every rebalance; stale-generation offset commits are rejected with IllegalGeneration.
Rebalance triggers: consumer join/leave, missed heartbeats, partition count change, subscription change.
Classic eager rebalancing pauses all consumers stop-the-world; cooperative rebalancing (CooperativeStickyAssignor) only moves the partitions that change owners.
The two-phase protocol: JoinGroup (all members sync) then SyncGroup (leader distributes assignment).
cards.code:
Consumer group protocol (classic eager rebalance)

  1. Consumer A sends JoinGroupRequest to coordinator
  2. Consumer B sends JoinGroupRequest
  3. Coordinator picks leader (e.g. A), returns full member list
  4. Leader computes assignment (Range / RoundRobin / Sticky)
  5. Leader sends SyncGroupRequest with assignments
  6. Coordinator distributes assignments to all members
  7. All consumers resume fetching from committed offsets

  During phases 1-6: EVERY consumer pauses fetching (stop-the-world)

Cooperative rebalancing (incremental)

  - Only partitions that change owner are revoked
  - Consumers that keep their partitions continue processing
  - Faster convergence, fewer processing stalls

Key configs:
  session.timeout.ms           (default 45s new protocol, 10s classic)
  heartbeat.interval.ms        (typically 1/3 of session timeout)
  max.poll.interval.ms         (default 5 min; kicks consumer if poll not called)
  partition.assignment.strategy = CooperativeStickyAssignor  (recommended)

cards.title: Replication, ISR, and the High Watermark: Why a Broker Can Die Without Losing Data
cards.summary:
Kafka replicates at the partition level. Each partition has one leader replica and zero or more follower replicas on different brokers. The replication factor is the total number of copies; a replication factor of 3 means one leader and two followers. Producers write to the leader, and consumers read from the leader under normal conditions. Followers do not receive pushed data — each follower sends fetch requests to the leader (much like a consumer) and appends what it receives to its own log. This pull-based replication is what allows followers to catch up at their own pace after a pause.

The in-sync replica set (ISR) is the list of replicas that are fully caught up with the leader. The leader is always in the ISR. A follower stays in the ISR as long as it keeps fetching and keeps up with the leader's log end offset. The rule is controlled by replica.lag.time.max.ms (default 30 seconds): if a follower has not sent a fetch request, or has not caught up to the leader's log end offset, for at least this long, the leader removes it from the ISR. The ISR shrinks and grows dynamically — a follower that falls behind because of a slow disk, a long GC pause, or network trouble drops out, and once it catches up it is added back. Frequent ISR shrink/expand usually points to an overloaded broker or unstable network, not a Kafka bug. The metric to watch is UnderReplicatedPartitions, which every broker reports; in a healthy cluster it sits at zero.

The high watermark (HW) is the highest offset that every in-sync replica has copied. Consumers can only read records up to the high watermark — they never see a record that could vanish if the leader failed before replicating it. This is the mechanism that makes Kafka's durability guarantee precise: with acks=all and min.insync.replicas=2, the producer only considers a write successful after all ISR replicas have acknowledged it, and the high watermark only advances when at least min.insync.replicas ISR members have replicated it. If the ISR shrinks below min.insync.replicas, the high watermark stops advancing, and the producer's acks=all writes start failing — which is the correct behavior: Kafka prefers to reject writes rather than accept data that is not durably replicated.

The durability configuration that prevents data loss is a small set of settings working together. replication.factor=3 gives three copies. min.insync.replicas=2 requires at least two of them to acknowledge. acks=all on the producer waits for the full ISR. unclean.leader.election.enable=false prevents an out-of-sync replica from being elected leader (which would silently truncate data that the old leader had acknowledged). With this combination, acknowledged writes survive the loss of any single broker. If unclean leader election is enabled, Kafka may elect a follower that is behind, and records that the old leader had acknowledged are lost — this is the classic data-loss window that unclean election opens, and why it should normally stay false.

In an interview, the strongest answer connects the ISR to the high watermark and to the producer's acks contract. A candidate who can explain that consumers never read past the high watermark, that min.insync.replicas is what prevents acks=all from degrading to acks=1 when the ISR shrinks, and that unclean leader election trades durability for availability, has demonstrated genuine understanding of Kafka's replication model.
bullets: Each partition has a leader and followers; followers pull from the leader, and the leader tracks how far each follower has fetched.
The ISR is the set of replicas fully caught up with the leader; replica.lag.time.max.ms (default 30s) controls eviction from the ISR.
The high watermark is the highest offset replicated to all ISR members; consumers never read past it, so they never see uncommitted-to-replication data.
min.insync.replicas=2 with acks=all guarantees acknowledged writes survive a single broker failure; if the ISR drops below min.insync.replicas, writes fail rather than risk data loss.
unclean.leader.election.enable=false prevents an out-of-sync replica from becoming leader and silently truncating acknowledged data.
UnderReplicatedPartitions is the metric to monitor; frequent ISR shrink/expand indicates broker or network instability.
cards.code:
Durability configuration (production)

  replication.factor=3
  min.insync.replicas=2
  acks=all
  unclean.leader.election.enable=false

Flow of a write with acks=all:

  Producer -> Leader (append to local log)
           -> Follower 1 (fetch, append)
           -> Follower 2 (fetch, append)
           <- Leader waits for all ISR acks
           <- acks=all satisfied -> write success -> Future completes

High watermark:

  HW = max offset replicated to ALL ISR members
  Consumers read only up to HW

  If ISR size < min.insync.replicas:
    - HW stops advancing
    - acks=all producer writes fail
    - Kafka rejects writes rather than accept non-durable data

Unclean leader election:

  false -> only ISR replicas can become leader (no data loss)
  true  -> an out-of-sync replica can become leader
           (records acknowledged by the old leader are silently lost)

cards.title: Delivery Semantics: At-Most-Once, At-Least-Once, and Exactly-Once in Plain English
cards.summary:
Delivery semantics describe what happens to a message when failures occur. Kafka supports all three, but the guarantee depends on how producers and consumers are configured — it is not a single switch. The three models are: at-most-once (message may be lost but never duplicated), at-least-once (message is never lost but may be duplicated), and exactly-once (message is processed exactly once, with no loss and no duplication).

At-most-once delivery happens when the consumer commits the offset before processing, or when the producer uses acks=0 (fire-and-forget). If the consumer crashes after committing but before processing, the message is skipped on restart — data loss. If the producer sends with acks=0 and the broker never receives the record, the producer does not know and does not retry — data loss. This model is acceptable for high-throughput telemetry or metrics where an occasional lost data point is tolerable, and it offers the lowest latency because no retry or coordination is involved.

At-least-once delivery is the practical default for most systems. The consumer processes the message, then commits the offset — so if it crashes before committing, the message is redelivered on restart (duplicate). The producer uses acks=all with retries enabled, so if the broker does not acknowledge, the producer retries (which can also produce a duplicate if the original write actually succeeded but the acknowledgement was lost). At-least-once never loses data, but it requires every consumer to be idempotent — the same message may be processed more than once, and the effect must be the same as processing it once. A typical example: updating a customer's address twice with the same address produces the same result, which is naturally idempotent; charging a credit card twice is not.

Exactly-once semantics (EOS) in Kafka is achieved through two mechanisms working together. The idempotent producer assigns a Producer ID (PID) and a per-partition sequence number to each batch; the broker deduplicates retries within a producer session by recognizing the same (PID, partition, sequence) triple. Transactions extend this to atomic multi-partition writes: a producer can write to multiple partitions and commit the offsets of the consumed input in the same transaction, so that either all outputs and the offset commit become visible together, or none do. Consumers using isolation.level=read_committed only see records from committed transactions; read_uncommitted (the default) sees all records, including those from aborted transactions. Exactly-once has a cost: slightly higher latency (typically 2–5 ms) and lower throughput (10–20% reduction) compared to at-least-once, plus the complexity of transactional APIs and the requirement that the consume-transform-produce loop stays within Kafka. When writing to an external system (a database, an HTTP API), Kafka's EOS does not extend across that boundary — you still need idempotent writes or a transactional outbox.

In an interview, the strongest answer maps each semantic to its configuration: at-most-once (commit before process, or acks=0), at-least-once (process then commit, acks=all with retries), exactly-once (idempotent producer + transactions + read_committed). It also states the boundary: Kafka EOS is end-to-end only within Kafka; external systems require application-level idempotency. That framing shows you understand both what Kafka guarantees and what it does not.
bullets: At-most-once: commit before process or acks=0 — data loss possible, no duplicates, lowest latency.
At-least-once: process then commit, acks=all with retries — no loss, duplicates possible; requires idempotent consumers.
Exactly-once (Kafka EOS): idempotent producer (PID + sequence dedup) + transactions (atomic multi-partition writes + offset commit) + read_committed consumers.
Kafka EOS holds end-to-end only within Kafka; writes to external databases or APIs need application-level idempotency.
EOS costs 2–5 ms extra latency and 10–20% throughput versus at-least-once.
isolation.level: read_uncommitted (default) sees aborted-transaction records; read_committed hides them.

cards.title: Consumer Crash Mid-Processing: What Happens, Why Duplicates Occur, and How to Recover Safely
cards.summary:
A consumer crash mid-processing is the canonical Kafka failure scenario, and the correct answer depends on one thing: was the offset committed before the crash? Kafka's guarantee is at-least-once under manual commit, which means the answer in almost every production case is: the message will be redelivered, and your downstream system will see it twice unless you make processing idempotent.

The mechanics are simple. The consumer calls poll(), receives a batch of records, and begins processing them. It commits offsets only after processing succeeds. If the process crashes — OOM kill, pod eviction, deploy, or a caught exception that kills the poll loop — the committed offset remains at the position before the crash. When a new consumer instance takes over the partition (after a rebalance), it fetches the committed offset and seeks there, redelivering every record that was polled but not yet committed. If the batch had 500 records and the consumer crashed after processing 200, the next instance reprocesses the remaining 300 (and possibly the 200 that were processed but not committed, depending on where exactly the crash happened relative to the commit call).

There is a second, less obvious source of duplicates: the crash can happen after the downstream side effect but before the offset commit. The consumer wrote to the database, sent the email, or called the payment API, then crashed before commitSync() succeeded. On restart, the same record is redelivered and the side effect happens again. Kafka cannot see that the side effect already occurred — it only knows the offset was not committed. This is the dual-write problem: the consumer is writing to two systems (Kafka offset store and the downstream system) that cannot be updated atomically. The classic solution is to make the downstream write idempotent and to store the Kafka offset alongside the domain change in the same database transaction (the inbox pattern), or to use Kafka transactions when the downstream is another Kafka topic.

Auto-commit flips the failure direction. With enable.auto.commit=true, the consumer periodically commits the latest offset returned by poll(), independent of whether processing finished. If the consumer crashes after auto-commit but before processing, the messages that were polled are lost — at-most-once semantics. This is why auto-commit is unsuitable for any workload where data loss is unacceptable. The two configurations are not just 'different defaults' — they represent opposite failure models: manual commit risks duplicates, auto-commit risks loss.

Recovery is a three-part discipline. First, disable auto-commit and commit only after processing succeeds. Second, make every handler idempotent using a stable idempotency key that survives redelivery — the best choice is a business key generated at the origin (payment_id, order_id + operation) or an eventId UUID placed in the record header, not topic-partition-offset (because offsets change across replays and cluster moves). Third, keep the poll loop fast enough that max.poll.interval.ms is not exceeded — if processing a batch takes longer than 5 minutes, the consumer is kicked out of the group, its partitions are reassigned, and another consumer reprocesses the same records while the original is still working, compounding the duplicate problem.

In an interview, the strongest answer names the three failure windows: crash before process (message redelivered — fine if idempotent), crash after process before commit (side effect duplicated — requires idempotency), and auto-commit before process (message lost — requires manual commit). It then states the fix: manual commit + idempotent handler + a dedup table or inbox table for the offset-plus-side-effect atomicity. That is the complete answer.
bullets: Crash before offset commit → message redelivered on restart; processing must be idempotent to avoid duplicate side effects.
Crash after downstream side effect but before commit → the same record is reprocessed and the side effect happens twice (dual-write problem).
Auto-commit commits the latest polled offset regardless of processing → crash causes data loss (at-most-once).
Fix: enable.auto.commit=false, process then commit; make handlers idempotent with a stable business/event idempotency key.
Store the offset in the same database transaction as the domain write (inbox pattern) to avoid the dual-write gap.
Keep processing under max.poll.interval.ms (default 5 min) or the consumer is kicked and its records are reprocessed concurrently.

cards.title: Message Ordering Across Partitions: What Is Guaranteed, What Is Not, and How to Design for It
cards.summary:
Kafka guarantees ordering only within a single partition. Records in partition 0 are read in the order they were written to partition 0, and consumers see them in that order. Records across partition 0, partition 1, and partition 2 have no ordering guarantee relative to each other — the broker does not coordinate across partitions, and consumers process different partitions concurrently. This is not a limitation to work around; it is the design that enables parallelism. A single partition can only be consumed by one consumer in a group, so total order means total serialization. The moment you have more than one partition, you have given up global order in exchange for throughput.

Key-based partitioning is how you recover per-entity order while keeping parallelism. When a producer sends a record with a key, the default partitioner computes murmur2(key) % numPartitions. This is deterministic: the same key always maps to the same partition (as long as the partition count does not change). All events for order_id=123 land in the same partition, so they are produced and consumed in order. Events for different order_ids may land in different partitions and be processed in parallel. This is the standard pattern: partition by the entity whose events must be ordered, and accept that entities are independent. The critical caveat is that adding partitions to an existing topic changes the modulo mapping — messages with the same key may route to a different partition after repartitioning, breaking the ordering guarantee for keys that were previously co-located. Plan partition counts with future growth in mind, or use a partitioner that is stable across partition-count changes (custom logic, or co-partitioning designs).

Null-key records use a sticky partitioner (since Kafka 2.4). Instead of round-robin across all partitions, the producer picks one partition and sends batches to it until the batch is full or linger.ms expires, then switches to another partition. This improves batching efficiency but explicitly provides no ordering guarantee: a null-key record can land anywhere, and consecutive null-key records may be reordered relative to each other. If order matters, you must provide a key.

A second ordering subtlety is producer retries. Without idempotence, a failed batch may be retried, and if the retry succeeds but the original write actually landed, the broker's log contains the record twice — and the ordering between the two copies depends on which arrived first. With enable.idempotence=true (the default in modern clients), the broker deduplicates by (PID, partition, sequence), so retries do not create duplicates and do not break per-partition order. The producer's max.in.flight.requests.per.connection also matters: with more than one in-flight request, a later batch can succeed before an earlier failed batch is retried, potentially reordering records unless idempotence is enabled. The safe configuration for ordered, duplicate-free production is enable.idempotence=true and max.in.flight.requests.per.connection ≤ 5.

The global-order question is a common interview follow-up: 'How would you guarantee ordering across the entire topic?' The answer is: use a single partition. That gives total order but caps consumer parallelism at one consumer, which is almost never acceptable for high-throughput topics. The practical design is to order by key, not by topic — preserve order for the entities that require it, and let independent entities flow in parallel. For cases where cross-entity order genuinely matters (a saga with steps that must interleave across multiple entities), use a single partition for that specific coordination topic, or move the ordering logic into the application layer with sequence numbers and reordering buffers.
bullets: Kafka guarantees ordering only within a partition, not across partitions of the same topic.
Key-based partitioning (murmur2(key) % partitions) routes all events for the same key to the same partition, preserving per-key order while parallelizing across keys.
Adding partitions to an existing topic breaks the key-to-partition mapping — keys may move, and per-key order is no longer guaranteed.
Null-key records use a sticky partitioner and have no ordering guarantee.
Idempotent producer + max.in.flight.requests.per.connection ≤ 5 prevents retry-induced reordering and duplicates.
Global order requires a single partition, which serializes consumption — use it only for topics that genuinely need total order.
cards.code:
Per-partition order (guaranteed):

  Partition 0:  [order-123: created] [order-123: paid] [order-123: shipped]
  Partition 1:  [order-456: created] [order-456: paid]
  Partition 2:  [order-789: created]

  order-123 events are in order (same partition)
  order-456 and order-789 events are independent (different partitions)

Key-based partitioning:

  murmur2("order-123") % 3 = 0  -> all order-123 events -> partition 0
  murmur2("order-456") % 3 = 1  -> all order-456 events -> partition 1

No key = no order:

  producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>("orders", value))  // key null
  -> sticky partitioner -> round-robin-ish -> no ordering guarantee

Producer settings for ordered, duplicate-free writes:

  enable.idempotence=true
  max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=5   (or lower)
  acks=all

Global order (rarely acceptable):

  topic with 1 partition -> total order, max 1 consumer in the group
  -> throughput ceiling = single consumer's processing rate

cards.title: Idempotency in Distributed Systems: Why Kafka Forces It and How to Implement It Correctly
cards.summary:
Idempotency means that performing an operation multiple times has the same effect as performing it once. In a distributed system, this is not a nice-to-have; it is the bridge between at-least-once delivery (which Kafka guarantees) and effectively-once processing (which is what the business actually wants). Kafka will redeliver records after crashes, rebalances, and retries. If the consumer's handler is not idempotent, redelivery means duplicate side effects: double charges, duplicate emails, double inventory decrements. Idempotency is the consumer's responsibility, not Kafka's.

The producer side has its own idempotence mechanism, and it is important not to confuse the two. The idempotent producer (enable.idempotence=true, default in modern clients) assigns a Producer ID (PID) to each producer session and a monotonically increasing sequence number to each batch per partition. The broker tracks the highest sequence number it has seen for each (PID, partition) and drops any batch whose sequence number is less than or equal to the last committed one. This deduplicates retries within a single producer session — if the producer retries a batch that the broker already wrote, the broker recognizes the duplicate and returns success without writing again. But this does not make the consumer idempotent, and it does not survive a producer restart (a new PID is assigned). The two mechanisms solve different problems at different layers.

Consumer idempotency requires a stable idempotency key that is identical on every redelivery of the same message. The best choice is a key generated at the origin and carried in the record — either a business key (payment_id, order_id plus operation) or an eventId UUID in the record header. Topic-partition-offset is a poor key because offsets change across replays and cluster moves; the same logical message may have a different offset after a retention reset or a MirrorMaker failover. The idempotency key must be stable across producer retries, consumer crashes, dead-letter replays, and cross-cluster moves.

The implementation pattern is the inbox (or dedup) table. In the same database transaction that applies the domain change, insert the idempotency key into an inbox table with a unique constraint. If the insert succeeds, the domain change is applied; if it fails with a duplicate-key error, the message has already been processed and the handler returns success without applying the change again. This makes the side effect and the dedup record atomic — either both happen or neither does.
