The table needs a TTL at least as long as the maximum redelivery window (which could be days if dead-letter queues are replayed much later).

For operations that call external APIs, true atomicity is impossible across systems, so you rely on the external system's idempotency support. Stripe, for example, accepts an Idempotency-Key header; if the same key is used for a retry, Stripe returns the original response instead of charging again. When the external system does not support idempotency keys, the best you can do is make the operation naturally idempotent (upserts instead of inserts, compare-and-set on version numbers) and accept a small risk window, or wrap the external call in a saga with a compensating action.

In an interview, the strongest answer distinguishes producer idempotence (PID + sequence, session-scoped, broker-side dedup) from consumer idempotence (application-level idempotency key + dedup store), explains why topic-partition-offset is a bad key, and gives the inbox-table pattern with the unique constraint. It also notes the boundary: exactly-once within Kafka does not extend to external systems, so external calls need their own idempotency mechanisms. That answer shows you understand idempotency as a layered problem, not a single configuration.
bullets: Idempotency: performing an operation multiple times has the same effect as performing it once — the bridge from at-least-once to effectively-once.
Producer idempotence (PID + per-partition sequence) deduplicates retries within one producer session; it does not make consumers idempotent.
Consumer idempotency needs a stable key: business key (payment_id, order_id+operation) or eventId UUID in the header — not topic-partition-offset.
Inbox/dedup table with a unique constraint, updated in the same transaction as the domain change, makes side effect + dedup atomic.
External APIs need their own idempotency keys (e.g., Stripe Idempotency-Key); Kafka EOS does not cover them.
The dedup table TTL must cover the maximum redelivery window (including DLQ replay and cross-cluster failover).

cards.title: Kafka vs RabbitMQ vs SQS: A Decision Framework, Not a Winner
cards.summary:
The interview question is never 'which is best?' — it is 'which fits this communication pattern, durability requirement, and replay need?' Kafka, RabbitMQ, and SQS descend from different lineages and solve different problems. Kafka is a distributed, replicated append-only log built for high-throughput event streaming, replay, and multi-consumer fan-out. RabbitMQ is a smart broker built around AMQP, designed for flexible routing (exchanges, bindings, headers), per-message acknowledgment, and task queues. SQS is a managed, simple, highly available queue designed for decoupling producers and consumers with minimal operational overhead, especially inside AWS.

The decision tree has three questions. First: do you need replay? If you need to reprocess history — for event sourcing, rebuilding a derived view, or recovering from a consumer bug — Kafka is the only one of the three that retains records after consumption and lets you reset offsets. RabbitMQ and SQS delete messages after acknowledgment; replay requires external storage. Second: do you need per-message routing or task-queue semantics with individual acknowledgment and push delivery? RabbitMQ excels here with exchanges (direct, topic, fanout, headers) and per-consumer QoS. SQS Standard is simpler but offers no routing — you need SNS fan-out to multiple queues. Third: do you need native multi-consumer fan-out without duplicating messages? Kafka gives you many independent consumer groups on one topic; RabbitMQ needs a fanout exchange (and still deletes after ack); SQS needs SNS to replicate the message into multiple queues.

Durability and ordering trade-offs differ. Kafka with acks=all, replication.factor=3, and min.insync.replicas=2 gives strong durability but only per-partition ordering. RabbitMQ quorum queues give durability and per-queue ordering; classic queues are faster but not replicated. SQS Standard gives at-least-once with best-effort ordering; SQS FIFO gives exactly-once-per-message-group with strict ordering within a group, at lower throughput. None of these is 'more durable' in the abstract — the guarantee depends on the configuration and what you are willing to pay in latency and throughput.

The operational model is the final axis. Kafka requires running brokers, tuning partitions, monitoring consumer lag, and managing retention. RabbitMQ requires managing exchanges, queues, bindings, and clustering. SQS is fully managed — no servers, no partitions, no retention tuning — but it ties you to AWS and has per-message pricing. For a small team shipping a task queue on AWS, SQS is almost always the pragmatic choice. For a team building an event-driven platform where replay and fan-out are core requirements, Kafka's operational cost is justified. RabbitMQ fits the middle: complex routing, task queues, and push delivery without the log-management overhead.

In an interview, never say 'Kafka is the best.' Say: 'I would choose based on whether replay is required, whether routing is complex, and whether the team can operate the cluster. For this scenario, because X, I would pick Y, and here is the trade-off I am accepting.' That framing demonstrates engineering judgment, which is what senior interviews actually test.
bullets: Kafka: durable replicated log, replay, multi-consumer fan-out, high throughput — but per-partition ordering and operational overhead.
RabbitMQ: smart broker with flexible routing (exchanges/bindings), per-message ack, push delivery — ideal for task queues and complex routing.
SQS: managed simple queue, at-least-once (Standard) or FIFO with ordering — minimal ops, AWS-native, no replay.
Replay is the deciding factor: Kafka retains after consumption; RabbitMQ and SQS delete on ack.
Fan-out: Kafka natively via consumer groups; RabbitMQ via fanout exchange; SQS via SNS-to-multiple-queues.
Never say one is 'best' — choose by communication pattern, durability requirement, and operational capacity.
cards.code:
Decision tree

  Need messaging?
    No  -> synchronous calls with retries/timeouts/circuit breakers
    Yes -> What is the primary pattern?
            Point-to-point task queue?
              Need strict FIFO ordering? -> SQS FIFO or RabbitMQ quorum queue
              No                         -> SQS Standard or RabbitMQ work queue
            Fan-out broadcast pub/sub?
              Need durable retention?    -> Kafka (topics + consumer groups + replay)
              No                         -> SNS / lightweight pub-sub
            Internal async event reactions?
              Need replay later?         -> Kafka event log
              No                         -> RabbitMQ or SQS task/event queue

Capability matrix

  Replay after consumption   Kafka YES | RabbitMQ NO  | SQS NO
  Per-message ACK            Kafka via offset (batch) | RabbitMQ YES | SQS YES
  Complex routing            Kafka NO  | RabbitMQ YES (exchanges) | SQS NO
  Native multi-consumer fan-out Kafka YES | RabbitMQ via fanout exchange | SQS via SNS
  Managed (no ops)           Kafka NO  | RabbitMQ NO  | SQS YES
  Ordering                   per-partition | per-queue | FIFO per message group

cards.title: Retention vs Compaction: Two Different Ways to Keep Data, and When Each Applies
cards.summary:
Kafka topics have a cleanup policy that determines how old data is removed. There are two fundamentally different strategies, and confusing them is a common interview trap. Retention (cleanup.policy=delete) deletes whole log segments based on time or size. Compaction (cleanup.policy=compact) retains at least the latest record for every key, indefinitely, by rewriting segments and discarding older records with the same key.

Retention operates at the segment level, not per-record. A partition is a series of rolling segment files. When a segment's newest record is older than log.retention.ms (default 7 days), or when the partition's total size exceeds log.retention.bytes (per-partition, default unlimited), the oldest segments are deleted. The active segment is never deleted, so recent data is always retained even if it is older than the configured time. This segment-level granularity is why you cannot delete an individual record by retention — you can only wait for the segment it belongs to become eligible. Time-based and size-based retention can be combined; whichever threshold is hit first triggers deletion, which is the recommended production setup for bounded storage with a time-based safety net.

Compaction is a per-key retention policy. The Log Cleaner thread runs in the background, reads the dirty (not-yet-compacted) portion of the log, builds an offset map of key → latest offset, and rewrites segments containing only the latest record for each key. Older records with the same key are discarded. The cleaner activates when the dirty ratio (dirty_bytes / total_bytes) exceeds min.cleanable.dirty.ratio (default 0.5), so compaction is not continuous — it happens in batches. Compaction is how Kafka implements changelog topics and state stores: a compacted topic represents the current state of each key, not the full history of changes. If a consumer reads a compacted topic from the beginning, it sees at least the latest value for every key that has not been tombstoned.

A tombstone is a record with a null value. In a compacted topic, a tombstone marks a key for deletion: the cleaner retains the tombstone for delete.retention.ms (default 24 hours) to give consumers time to see the deletion, then removes both the tombstone and any earlier records for that key. Without tombstones, a compacted topic has no way to express 'this key was deleted' — the previous value would persist forever.

The decision between retention and compaction maps to the semantics of the stream. Use retention when the stream is a sequence of events and consumers need the history within a time window (clicks, orders, logs). Use compaction when the stream is a changelog and consumers need the current state per key (user profiles, configuration, inventory snapshots). Some topics combine both policies (cleanup.policy=compact,delete): compact for the current state, but also delete segments older than a retention window to bound storage — this is common for changelog topics that must not grow forever.

In an interview, the strongest answer names both policies, explains that retention is segment-level time/size deletion while compaction is per-key latest-value retention, mentions tombstones and delete.retention.ms, and gives the changelog-vs-event-stream distinction as the decision criterion.
bullets: Retention (delete): deletes whole segments by time (log.retention.ms) or size (log.retention.bytes) — segment-level, not per-record.
Compaction (compact): retains at least the latest record per key indefinitely by rewriting segments; older duplicates are discarded by the Log Cleaner.
The Log Cleaner runs when dirtyRatio > min.cleanable.dirty.ratio (default 0.5) — compaction is batched, not continuous.
A tombstone (null value) marks a key for deletion; delete.retention.ms (default 24h) gives consumers time to see it before the key is removed.
Use retention for event streams that need history within a window; use compaction for changelogs that need current state per key.
cleanup.policy=compact,delete combines both: compact for current state, delete old segments to bound storage.
cards.code:
# Time-based retention (default 7 days)
log.retention.ms=604800000

# Size-based retention (per partition, default unlimited)
log.retention.bytes=-1

# Combined (recommended): delete when either threshold hits
log.retention.ms=604800000
log.retention.bytes=10737418240   # 10 GB per partition

# Compaction
cleanup.policy=compact
min.cleanable.dirty.ratio=0.5
delete.retention.ms=86400000      # 24h for tombstones

# Both: compact for current state, delete old segments
cleanup.policy=compact,delete

Retention vs compaction at a glance

  Retention (delete)           Compaction (compact)
  -------------------          --------------------
  segment-level deletion       per-key latest value
  time/size based              key-based
  history window               current state
  event streams                changelogs / state stores
  records vanish wholesale     old duplicates vanish, latest stays

cards.title: Kafka Transactions and Exactly-Once Semantics: Transactional ID, Epoch Fencing, and read_committed
cards.summary:
Kafka's exactly-once semantics (EOS) is built on two layers that work together: the idempotent producer, which deduplicates retries within a producer session, and transactions, which extend atomicity across multiple partitions and across the consume-transform-produce loop. Without transactions, a consumer that reads from one topic, transforms, and writes to another can crash after writing but before committing its offset — and on restart it writes the same output again. Transactions make the output writes and the offset commit atomic: either both become visible, or neither does.

The mechanism requires a stable transactional.id. Unlike the idempotent producer's PID (which is assigned per session and changes on restart), the transactional.id is chosen by the application and must survive restarts. Kafka uses it to fence zombies: when a new producer instance initializes with the same transactional.id, the Transaction Coordinator increments an epoch counter. Any request from the old producer instance — the zombie — carries an older epoch and is rejected with ProducerFencedException. This is how Kafka prevents a paused or partitioned producer from waking up and committing a transaction that a newer instance has already superseded. Fencing is not optional; it is what makes transactions safe under producer restarts.

The API sequence is: producer.initTransactions() on startup (registers the transactional.id and obtains the current epoch); producer.beginTransaction(); produce records to one or more partitions; optionally call producer.sendOffsetsToTransaction(offsets, groupId) to include consumer offset commits in the same transaction; then producer.commitTransaction() or producer.abortTransaction(). On the consumer side, isolation.level=read_committed is mandatory. Without it, the consumer sees records from aborted transactions and the transaction control markers (BEGIN, COMMIT, ABORT). With read_committed, the consumer only returns records that belong to committed transactions, and it waits for the transaction outcome before exposing them. This is the half that candidates most often forget — describing only the producer side is an incomplete answer.

The performance cost is real: roughly 20% throughput reduction and a few milliseconds of added latency, because each transaction requires coordination with the Transaction Coordinator (beginTransaction, commitTransaction). The cost is justified for financial transactions, order processing, inventory updates, and any domain where duplicates or lost messages cause business errors. For high-volume telemetry where occasional duplicates are tolerable, at-least-once with idempotent consumers is cheaper.

The boundary is the most important part of the interview answer. Kafka's EOS is end-to-end only within Kafka. If the consumer writes to an external PostgreSQL database or calls a third-party API, that write is outside the Kafka transaction. A crash between the Kafka commit and the external write (or vice versa) leaves the two systems inconsistent. External systems require their own idempotency mechanisms — an idempotency key with the payment provider, an upsert with a unique constraint, or an inbox table that atomically records the event ID and the domain change. Kafka transactions do not solve the dual-write problem across system boundaries; they only solve it within Kafka.

In an interview, the strongest answer names transactional.id, epoch fencing, sendOffsetsToTransaction, read_committed, the ~20% cost, and the external-system boundary. That demonstrates you understand both the mechanism and its limits.
bullets: Kafka EOS = idempotent producer (PID + sequence, session dedup) + transactions (atomic multi-partition writes + offset commit).
transactional.id is application-chosen and stable across restarts; the Transaction Coordinator increments an epoch and fences zombies (ProducerFencedException).
API: initTransactions → beginTransaction → produce → sendOffsetsToTransaction → commitTransaction / abortTransaction.
Consumer must set isolation.level=read_committed to hide aborted records and transaction markers.
Cost: ~20% throughput reduction and a few ms latency due to Transaction Coordinator coordination.
EOS holds only within Kafka — external DBs/APIs require application-level idempotency (idempotency keys, upserts, inbox tables).

cards.title: Kafka Connect and Kafka Streams: Integration vs Stream Processing
cards.summary:
Kafka Connect and Kafka Streams solve two different problems that both involve moving data through Kafka. Connect is an integration framework: it moves data between Kafka and external systems (databases, S3, Elasticsearch, Salesforce) using pre-built connectors, without writing producer/consumer code. Streams is a stream-processing library: it lets you write Java applications that read from Kafka topics, transform the data (filter, map, join, aggregate, window), and write results back to Kafka, with exactly-once guarantees and local state stores.

Kafka Connect runs as a cluster of worker processes. A source connector pulls data from an external system and writes it to Kafka topics; a sink connector reads from Kafka topics and writes to an external system. Connectors are configured via JSON, not code, and Connect handles offset tracking, retries, scaling (by running multiple workers and splitting connectors into tasks), and schema integration with Schema Registry. Single Message Transforms (SMTs) allow lightweight per-record modifications (mask a field, rename a column, route to a different topic) without writing a full Streams application. Connect is the right tool when the job is 'get data in or out of Kafka reliably' and there is an existing connector — writing custom producer/consumer code for a JDBC source or an S3 sink is reinventing Connect badly.

Kafka Streams is a library, not a cluster. You embed it in a Java application; it starts one or more StreamThreads, each running a Kafka consumer and producer. The core abstractions are KStream (an unbounded stream of records) and KTable (a changelog-backed table representing the current value per key). Operations include filter, map, flatMap, join (stream-stream, stream-table, table-table), groupByKey + aggregate (count, reduce), and windowing (tumbling, hopping, sliding, session). Stateful operations use local state stores (RocksDB by default) backed by compacted changelog topics, so state survives restarts and can be restored by replaying the changelog. Exactly-once in Streams is enabled with processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2 (Kafka 2.5+), which uses the transactional producer internally.

The decision between them is straightforward. If the task is 'move data between Kafka and system X' and a connector exists, use Connect. If the task is 'compute something from Kafka streams — enrich, aggregate, join, detect patterns — and write the result back to Kafka', use Streams. If the task requires calling an external API per record or has complex business logic with side effects outside Kafka, a plain consumer application is often clearer than Streams. Connect is not a processing engine; Streams is not an integration framework. They complement each other: a common architecture uses Connect to ingest database changes into Kafka, Streams to process them, and Connect again to sink the results to a data warehouse.

In an interview, the strongest answer distinguishes configuration-driven integration (Connect) from code-driven stream processing (Streams), names KStream vs KTable, mentions state stores and changelog topics, and states that exactly-once in Streams uses the transactional producer. That shows you know where each tool fits rather than treating them as interchangeable Kafka add-ons.
bullets: Kafka Connect: configuration-driven integration framework — source connectors (external → Kafka) and sink connectors (Kafka → external), with offset tracking, retries, and scaling via tasks.
Single Message Transforms (SMTs) allow lightweight per-record changes without a full processing app.
Kafka Streams: a Java library for stream processing — KStream (events) vs KTable (current state per key), stateless and stateful operations, windowing, joins.
Stateful Streams operations use local state stores (RocksDB) backed by compacted changelog topics for fault tolerance and restore.
Streams exactly-once: processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2 uses the transactional producer internally.
Connect = integration; Streams = processing. They complement rather than compete.

cards.title: Schema Registry and Schema Evolution: Why Unstructured JSON Breaks Consumers
cards.summary:
Kafka does not validate message contents. A producer can write any bytes to a topic, and a consumer that expects a different structure will fail at deserialization or, worse, silently misinterpret fields. In a system with many producers and consumers evolving independently, this is a coordination problem: how do you change an event schema without breaking downstream consumers you may not even know about? The answer is Schema Registry combined with a serialization format that supports schema evolution — typically Avro, Protobuf, or JSON Schema.

Schema Registry is a separate service (often Confluent Schema Registry) that stores versioned schemas and enforces compatibility rules. When a producer registers a schema for a subject (by convention, <topic>-value or <topic>-key), the Registry assigns it a globally unique schema ID and stores it. The producer serializes each record by writing the schema ID (5 bytes) followed by the encoded payload. The consumer reads the schema ID, fetches the corresponding schema from the Registry (cached locally), and deserializes using that schema. This decouples the wire format from any single producer or consumer's compiled classes: the schema is the contract, and the Registry is the source of truth for which versions are valid.

Compatibility modes determine which schema changes are allowed. BACKWARD (the default) means a consumer using the new schema can read data written with the old schema — you can add optional fields and remove fields that consumers do not require. FORWARD means a consumer using the old schema can read data written with the new schema — you can add fields and remove optional fields. FULL requires both. NONE disables checks. The practical rule is: choose a mode, and let the Registry reject incompatible changes at registration time. Without this, a producer deploy silently breaks consumers at runtime.

Avro is the most common choice because it has a compact binary encoding, a schema that is defined alongside the data, and first-class support for schema evolution (default values, union types, aliases). Protobuf is also supported and is preferred in polyglot environments where gRPC is already in use. JSON Schema is supported but produces larger payloads and has weaker evolution semantics. The choice is less important than the discipline: every topic that carries structured data should have a registered schema, and producers should be prevented from writing without one (for example, by using a serializer that requires a schema ID).

A subtle but important point: Schema Registry does not enforce that the serialized bytes actually match the schema ID written in the header. A misbehaving producer could write bytes that do not conform. Serializers provided by the Registry client libraries guarantee conformance on the producer side; consumers assume the producer is honest. This is why the Registry is a contract registry, not a validator of every record.

In an interview, the strongest answer explains the problem (unstructured data breaks independent evolution), the mechanism (schema ID in the record header, Registry as source of truth, compatibility modes), and the practical rule (choose BACKWARD or FULL, reject incompatible changes at registration, use Avro/Protobuf with a schema-aware serializer). That demonstrates you understand data contracts, which is what separates a senior Kafka answer from a 'I know what a topic is' answer.
bullets: Kafka does not validate payloads — without schemas, changing an event structure breaks consumers silently or at deserialization.
Schema Registry stores versioned schemas per subject and assigns a schema ID; producers write the ID in the record header, consumers fetch the schema by ID.
Compatibility modes: BACKWARD (new consumers read old data), FORWARD (old consumers read new data), FULL (both), NONE.
The Registry rejects incompatible schema changes at registration time — this is the enforcement point that prevents runtime breakage.
Avro is most common (compact binary, strong evolution support); Protobuf fits polyglot/gRPC environments; JSON Schema is larger and weaker.
Schema Registry is a contract registry, not a per-record validator — producers must use schema-aware serializers.
cards.code:
Wire format (Confluent style)

  [ magic byte (1) ][ schema ID (4) ][ Avro/Protobuf payload ]

Producer (schema-aware serializer)

  props.put("schema.registry.url", "http://schema-registry:8081");
  props.put("value.serializer",
      "io.confluent.kafka.serializers.KafkaAvroSerializer");

Consumer

  props.put("value.deserializer",
      "io.confluent.kafka.serializers.KafkaAvroDeserializer");

Compatibility modes (set per subject)

  BACKWARD  new consumer reads old data    (add optional fields, remove fields)
  FORWARD   old consumer reads new data    (add fields, remove optional fields)
  FULL      both directions
  NONE      no checks (dangerous)

Subject naming:

  <topic>-value  (for record values)
  <topic>-key    (for record keys)

cards.title: Kafka Operations: Consumer Lag, Partition Sizing, and the Tuning That Prevents Outages
cards.summary:
Operating Kafka in production is mostly about two things: keeping consumer lag under control and sizing partitions correctly. Consumer lag is the difference between the log-end offset (LEO) — the latest offset written to a partition — and the last committed offset of a consumer group on that partition. Per-partition lag = LEO − committed offset; group lag is the sum across partitions. Lag is the single most important operational metric because it directly measures how far behind real time the consumer is. A lag of 1 million records means nothing without context; convert it to time: lag_time = lag_records / consumption_rate. If the consumer processes 5,000 records/second and lag is 1 million, the consumer is about 200 seconds behind. That is the number that matters for freshness SLOs.

Alerting on raw offset counts is a mistake because throughput varies across topics and time. Better alerts: (1) lag growing monotonically for 10+ minutes — the consumer is falling behind and will not catch up on its own; (2) lag exceeding the equivalent of a few minutes of peak production — the consumer is under-provisioned; (3) records-consumed-rate dropping to zero for 2+ minutes — the consumer is stuck (rebalance loop, poison message, thread deadlock); (4) partition imbalance — one partition has 10x the lag of others, indicating a hot key or a stuck consumer thread. Tools include kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe, JMX metrics (records-lag-max, records-consumed-rate), Burrow (which evaluates lag trends, not just current values), and Prometheus/Grafana via JMX Exporter.

Partition sizing is the other operational lever. Partition count determines maximum consumer-group parallelism (one partition per consumer) and the topic's write throughput ceiling. The formula is: partitions = max(peak throughput ÷ per-partition throughput, peak consumer count), plus ~50% headroom for growth. You can add partitions later, but you cannot remove them — reducing partition count requires creating a new topic and migrating, which is disruptive. Over-partitioning has real costs: each partition consumes memory and file handles on every broker, increases replication network traffic, and lengthens leader-election and rebalance times. Under-partitioning caps parallelism and forces you to repartition under pressure, which breaks key-based ordering for keys that move partitions.

Key selection is the third operational concern. A low-cardinality key (for example, a boolean isPremium flag) routes almost all messages to one or two partitions, creating a hotspot while other partitions sit idle. A high-cardinality key (user_id, order_id) distributes load evenly and preserves per-entity order. If the natural key is skewed (one celebrity user, one hot product), use key salting (append a random suffix to spread across partitions) or a compound key, accepting that per-key order may be relaxed. The monitoring signal for a hotspot is partition imbalance in lag or byte rate — one partition consistently higher than the rest.

Rebalance storms are the fourth operational failure mode. If consumers are rolling-deployed frequently or processing takes longer than max.poll.interval.ms, the group rebalances repeatedly, pausing consumption and reassigning partitions. Symptoms: lag spikes correlate with deploy times, frequent generation ID changes in logs, and consumers spending more time joining than polling. Fixes: use cooperative rebalancing (CooperativeStickyAssignor), keep processing under max.poll.interval.ms (reduce max.poll.records or process asynchronously), and use static group membership (group.instance.id) so a restarting consumer reclaims its partitions without triggering a full rebalance.

In an interview, the strongest answer names consumer lag as the primary metric, explains the time-conversion, gives the partition-sizing formula with headroom, mentions key skew and rebalance storms as failure modes, and states that partitions cannot be decreased. That demonstrates you have operated Kafka, not just consumed it.
bullets: Consumer lag = log-end offset − committed offset per partition; group lag is the sum. Convert to time: lag_records / consumption_rate.
Alert on trends, not raw counts: monotonically growing lag, lag exceeding minutes of production, zero consumption rate, partition imbalance.
Partition sizing: max(peak throughput ÷ per-partition throughput, peak consumer count) + ~50% headroom; partitions can be added but never removed.
Low-cardinality keys create hotspots; high-cardinality keys distribute load and preserve per-entity order. Use salting or compound keys for skewed natural keys.
Rebalance storms from frequent deploys or slow processing cause lag spikes; fix with cooperative rebalancing, max.poll.interval.ms alignment, and static group membership.
Over-partitioning increases per-broker memory/file-handle overhead and slows leader election; under-partitioning caps parallelism.
cards.code:
Lag calculation

  per-partition lag = log_end_offset - committed_offset
  group lag         = sum(per-partition lag)
  lag_time_seconds  = lag_records / consumption_rate_records_per_sec

CLI

  kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server broker:9092 \
      --describe --group my-group

Alert rules (examples)

  - lag > 1,000,000 for > 5 min            -> page
  - lag increasing monotonically 10+ min   -> warn
  - records-consumed-rate = 0 for 2+ min   -> critical
  - max partition lag > 10x median lag     -> hotspot / stuck thread

Partition sizing

  partitions = max(
      peak_throughput / per_partition_throughput,
      peak_consumer_count
  ) + ~50% headroom

  add partitions: allowed (breaks key ordering across the change)
  remove partitions: NOT supported (must create new topic + migrate)

Hotspot mitigation

  low-cardinality key (e.g. isPremium) -> hotspots
  high-cardinality key (user_id, order_id) -> even distribution
  skewed natural key -> key salting (key + random suffix) or compound key

cards.title: Singleton Pattern: The One-Instance Rule, Thread-Safe Implementations, and Why It Is Often an Anti-Pattern
cards.summary:
The Singleton pattern guarantees that a class has exactly one instance and provides a global point of access to it. The problem it solves: some resources are inherently singular — a database connection pool, a configuration registry, a logging facility, a hardware driver handle. Creating multiple instances wastes resources or causes corruption (two pools competing for the same limited connections, two loggers interleaving and producing garbled files). Singleton centralizes control so everyone shares the same instance.

The naive implementation is a private constructor plus a public static field or method. This is easy to break in five ways, and each break is a common interview question. First, reflection: setAccessible(true) on the private constructor lets anyone create a second instance. Second, serialization: deserializing a serialized singleton produces a new instance unless you implement readResolve(). Third, classloaders: in an application server with multiple classloaders, the same class can be loaded twice, yielding two statics and two 'singletons'. Fourth, cloning: implementing Cloneable without overriding clone() allows duplication. Fifth, testing: because the instance is global and static, tests cannot easily substitute a fake, and state leaks between tests.

The correct thread-safe implementations differ in cost and subtlety. Eager initialization (a static final field assigned at class-load time) is simple and thread-safe because the JVM guarantees class initialization happens once — but it wastes work if the instance is never used. Lazy with double-checked locking (DCL) requires volatile on the instance field; without volatile, a partially constructed object can be seen by a second thread (this is covered in depth in the Core Java card java-dcl-1). The initialization-on-demand holder idiom is the elegant solution: a private static nested class holds the instance, and the JVM's class-initialization guarantees do the synchronization for free — no volatile, no DCL, no eager cost. The enum singleton is the safest of all: a single-element enum is thread-safe, protects against reflection, protects against serialization, and is guaranteed by the JLS to be a singleton. Joshua Bloch (Effective Java) recommends it as the default.

The crucial interview point is that the classic Singleton pattern is often an anti-pattern in modern applications, and the alternatives matter more than the pattern itself. In Spring, every bean is a singleton by default — but it is Spring's container that manages the singleton, not a static field on the class. This is DI (dependency injection), not the GoF Singleton pattern, and it is strictly better: the class has a normal constructor, it can be mocked in tests, and the container can create a prototype instead if the scope should change. Storing mutable state in a singleton field is a classic bug — because the instance is shared across threads, any request-specific data written to a field leaks to all other requests. Singletons must be stateless or thread-safe. In interviews, a strong answer explicitly contrasts 'GoF Singleton via static' (mostly a code smell, hard to test) with 'container-managed singleton via DI' (the modern, correct approach).
bullets: Singleton guarantees exactly one instance of a class; use it for resources that are inherently singular (connection pool, config, hardware driver).
Five ways a naive singleton breaks: reflection, serialization, multiple classloaders, cloning, and testing (global state leaks across tests).

Thread-safe implementations: eager static final (simple), DCL with volatile (requires careful memory model knowledge), holder idiom (best without enum), enum singleton (safest overall, JLS-guaranteed).
The classic Singleton pattern is often an anti-pattern — it hides dependencies, prevents testing with fakes, and stores state that cannot be scoped per request.
Spring's @Component/@Service singletons are DI-managed, not GoF Singleton — the class has a normal constructor and is testable. This is the modern correct approach.
Singletons must be stateless or thread-safe; request-specific data in a singleton field is a data-leak bug.

cards.title: Factory Method Pattern: Decoupling Object Creation from Usage
cards.summary:
The Factory Method pattern defines an interface or abstract class with a method for creating an object, and lets subclasses (or implementations) decide which concrete class to instantiate. The caller asks a factory for 'a PaymentProcessor' and gets a StripePaymentProcessor, PayPalPaymentProcessor, or any other implementation — without ever writing new StripePaymentProcessor() in its own code. The pattern's value is not the factory method itself; it is the decoupling of 'which class to instantiate' from 'how to use it', which lets you add new implementations without touching the client.

The problem it solves is the tight coupling created by direct new calls. If OrderService does new StripeClient(...), then testing OrderService requires a real Stripe, and switching to PayPal requires editing OrderService. With Factory Method, OrderService calls processorFactory.create(type), receives a PaymentProcessor interface, and is unaware of the concrete class. Adding a new payment provider means adding a new implementation and a factory registration — no change to OrderService. This is the Open/Closed Principle in practice: open for extension (add new implementations) but closed for modification (do not edit existing code).

Where Factory Method appears in Java and Spring matters for interviews. The classic Java example is Calendar.getInstance(), which returns a Calendar implementation appropriate to the default locale — the caller does not know or care which subclass. JDBC's DriverManager.getConnection() is arguably a factory: you ask for a connection by URL, and the driver manager picks the correct driver implementation. In Spring, FactoryBean<T> is a factory-method mechanism: when you register a FactoryBean, the bean the container exposes is the object returned by its getObject() method, not the FactoryBean itself. This is how frameworks create proxies, SqlSessionFactory, and other wrapper objects. Spring Boot's auto-configuration is essentially a factory: given what is on the classpath, it decides which implementation to provide.

The distinction between Factory Method and Abstract Factory is a common interview follow-up. Factory Method creates one product (with variation by subclass); Abstract Factory creates a family of related products that must be used together. If you only need to choose between two payment providers, Factory Method is enough. If you need to choose between 'Stripe stack' (payment + refund + webhook handlers all Stripe-aware) and 'PayPal stack' (the same three, all PayPal-aware), you need Abstract Factory so the three products are guaranteed to be compatible.

The trap with Factory Method is over-engineering. If you have exactly one implementation and no expectation of a second, a factory is unnecessary indirection — it is a common GoF over-application that makes code harder to follow. The pattern earns its keep when there are two or more implementations, when the concrete class is chosen at runtime based on configuration or input, or when creation has setup steps (initialize the client, register callbacks, warm up a pool) that you want to centralize. In an interview, name the problem (tight coupling to concrete classes), show the before/after with real code, and mention when you would NOT use it.
bullets: Factory Method defines a creation method; subclasses or implementations decide which concrete class to instantiate — the caller only knows the interface.
Solves tight coupling created by new: caller depends on interface, factory decides implementation, adding a new type requires zero changes to the caller.
Real examples: Calendar.getInstance(), DriverManager.getConnection(), Spring FactoryBean<T>.getObject().
Factory Method vs Abstract Factory: Factory Method creates one product with variation; Abstract Factory creates a family of related products.
Avoid when there is only one implementation and no plan for a second — over-engineering hides simple code behind indirection.
Spring's container is itself a factory: auto-configuration chooses an implementation based on the classpath, and FactoryBean exposes the created object as the bean.

cards.title: Abstract Factory Pattern: Creating Families of Related Objects
cards.summary:
Abstract Factory provides an interface for creating a family of related or dependent objects without specifying their concrete classes. Where Factory Method creates a single product with subclass-based variation, Abstract Factory creates an entire set of products that are designed to work together. The classic example is a cross-platform UI toolkit: a WindowsUIFactory creates WindowsButton, WindowsScrollbar, and WindowsWindow; a MacUIFactory creates MacButton, MacScrollbar, and MacWindow. Code that builds a UI depends only on UIFactory and the abstract product interfaces — swapping the factory at construction time changes the entire look and feel with no other changes.

The problem it solves is accidental incompatibility. If your application creates buttons and scrollbars independently, a bug or a developer mistake can pair a Windows button with a Mac scrollbar — they compile, but render inconsistently or crash. Abstract Factory guarantees that products from the same factory are compatible: they belong to the same family. This is why it is sometimes called the 'kit' pattern — a factory produces a matched kit.

Real-world examples in Java and Spring are plentiful. JDBC drivers are effectively an Abstract Factory: DriverManager gives you Connection, Statement, and ResultSet objects that all come from the same vendor (Postgres, MySQL) and are guaranteed to be compatible. Hibernate's Dialect and its related object graph work similarly. In Spring, when you have a set of beans that must be used together and selected by a profile (@Profile("prod") provides a ProdDatabaseFactory that creates a ProdConnection, ProdTransactionManager, ProdAuditor), the profile-scoped @Configuration is an Abstract Factory: it guarantees the family is consistent.

The distinction from Factory Method is the most-tested interview question. Factory Method: one product, subclass decides. Abstract Factory: N related products, one factory instance creates all of them consistently. The tell in code is the number of creation methods on the factory interface — one creation method suggests Factory Method; multiple related creation methods suggest Abstract Factory. Another tell is whether you need a family to be compatible: if yes, Abstract Factory.

The cost of Abstract Factory is complexity and rigidity. Adding a new product to the family means adding a method to every factory interface — a breaking change. Adding a new family (LinuxUIFactory) is easy and requires no changes to client code (which is the point). This asymmetry is the Open/Closed principle applied to families but not to products: easy to add families, hard to add products. In interviews, mention this asymmetry — it shows you understand the pattern's shape, not just its definition. Also mention the modern Java alternative: sealed interfaces with pattern matching can sometimes express families more cleanly than a factory hierarchy, at the cost of losing the runtime selection benefit.
bullets: Abstract Factory creates families of related objects guaranteed to be compatible — swap one factory, swap the entire family.
Solves accidental incompatibility (mixing products from different families) by making the factory the single source of every product.
Real examples: JDBC DriverManager (Connection + Statement + ResultSet from same vendor), Hibernate Dialect, profile-scoped Spring @Configuration.
Factory Method vs Abstract Factory: one product vs a family; one method vs multiple related methods on the factory interface.
Asymmetry: easy to add a new family, hard to add a new product (breaks every factory interface).
Overkill when there is only one family or no risk of mixing — an interface with a single implementation is just indirection.

cards.title: Builder Pattern: Constructing Complex Objects Without Telescoping Constructors
cards.summary:
The Builder pattern separates the construction of a complex object from its representation, allowing the same construction process to create different representations. In practical Java terms, it lets you assemble an object step by step — builder.withUrl(...).withTimeout(...).withRetry(3).build() — instead of writing a constructor with ten parameters, half of which are optional, which forces every caller to pass every value (or use overloaded constructors — the 'telescoping constructor anti-pattern').

The problem it solves is the readability and correctness of construction with many optional parameters. Consider new HttpClient(url, 30, 3, true, false, null, null, "GET", null). Which number is the timeout? Which boolean is retry-on-5xx? Every caller must consult the Javadoc or the source, and adding a new optional parameter breaks every caller. A Builder turns this into new HttpClient.Builder(url).timeout(30).retries(3).retryOn5xx(true).build() — self-documenting, order-independent, and safe to extend because callers only pass what they care about.

Where Builder appears in Java is everywhere once you start looking. StringBuilder is a simplified builder for strings — you append fragments and call toString() once. The Java Stream.Builder is a real Builder. Protocol Buffers generate builders for every message type. Lombok's @Builder generates a builder from a class's fields automatically. HTTP request libraries (OkHttp, Spring's WebClient, HttpClient in Java 11) use builders pervasively. Spring's UriComponentsBuilder is a builder. The pattern is so common in modern Java that interviewers assume fluency.

The 'build()' method deserves its own discussion because it is where the interesting correctness lives. Builder should validate mandatory fields in build() and throw a descriptive exception (IllegalStateException or IllegalArgumentException) if any are missing or invalid — not in each setter, which makes the failure late but the diagnosis late too. If the object being built is meant to be immutable, the builder copies all fields into an immutable target and the builder can then be discarded. If the builder is reused, you must not let it leak references to mutable collections — defensive copy on build(). A subtle bug: builders are almost never thread-safe; sharing one builder instance across threads causes corruption. Either document that builders are not thread-safe, or make them per-call.

The distinction from other patterns matters. Builder is often used alongside Factory: the factory decides which concrete builder to use; the builder assembles the object; the finished product is returned. Builder is not the same as 'static factory method' (which is just a named constructor) — Builder is specifically about step-by-step assembly of a complex object. The pattern is also different from Abstract Factory in that Builder's job is assembly, not family compatibility. In interviews, name the telescoping-constructor anti-pattern as the motivating problem, show the before/after with real code, and mention that Lombok @Builder generates exactly this if you do not want to write it by hand.
bullets: Builder assembles a complex object step by step; avoids the telescoping-constructor anti-pattern where every optional parameter forces a new overload.
The build() method should validate mandatory fields and throw a descriptive exception — not fail silently or in a setter.
The finished product is typically immutable; the builder copies all fields on build() so further builder mutations do not affect the result.
Builders are almost never thread-safe — do not share a builder instance across threads.
Real examples: StringBuilder, Stream.Builder, Protocol Buffers, Lombok @Builder, OkHttp Request.Builder, Spring UriComponentsBuilder.
Builder and Factory are complementary: factory decides which builder; builder assembles; the finished product is returned.

cards.title: Adapter Pattern: Making Incompatible Interfaces Work Together
cards.summary:
The Adapter pattern converts the interface of one class into another interface that clients expect. It lets classes work together that otherwise could not because of incompatible interfaces — without modifying either the client or the adaptee. The pattern is deliberately mundane: it is just a wrapper class that translates method calls. Its value comes from isolating the translation in one place, so the rest of the codebase depends only on the target interface.

The problem it solves is legacy and third-party integration. You have a modern OrderService that calls PaymentClient.charge(amount). The third-party payment library exposes LegacyPay.chargeRupees(long paise) or even XML-in, XML-out. You cannot modify the library (you do not own it), and you do not want to pollute OrderService with the library's vocabulary. The adapter sits between them: PaymentClientAdapter implements PaymentClient, holds a reference to the library's object, and translates charge(amount) into library-specific calls. The rest of the application sees only PaymentClient.

There are two flavors. Object adapter (composition — the adapter holds a reference to the adaptee) is the standard approach in Java because Java does not support multiple inheritance; it is more flexible and can adapt to an interface. Class adapter (inheritance — the adapter extends the adaptee and implements the target) is possible in Java but rarely used because it requires the adapter to inherit from a concrete class, which is fragile. Use composition.

Where Adapter appears in Java and Spring matters for interviews. The java.io stream hierarchy is a classic example: InputStreamReader adapts an InputStream (bytes) to a Reader (characters); BufferedReader wraps a Reader to add buffering — these are decorators (a related pattern discussed next), but the byte-to-character translation in InputStreamReader is genuinely an adapter. In Spring MVC, HandlerAdapter is the framework's way of adapting different controller types (annotated @Controller, functional handlers, HttpRequestHandler) to a common handler invocation interface — the DispatcherServlet only talks to HandlerAdapter, not to any specific handler. In slf4j, the Simple Logging Facade for Java is a facade (different pattern) but slf4j-to-log4j2 bindings are adapters: they implement slf4j's interfaces by delegating to log4j2. In tests, Mockito's mocks are effectively adapters when they stand in for real services with a compatible interface.

The distinction between Adapter and Decorator is a common interview trap. Adapter changes the interface (InputStreamReader makes a Reader out of an InputStream — the interface is different). Decorator keeps the same interface and adds behavior (BufferedReader is a Reader, wrapping another Reader, adding buffering). Adapter is usually used for integration; Decorator is used for composition of behavior. A tricky case: an adapter can be seen as 'making something look like what the client expects'; a decorator makes 'something behave in a modified but still compatible way'. If interfaces are different → Adapter. If interfaces are the same → Decorator.

The interview-quality answer explains the problem (incompatible interfaces from third-party or legacy code), shows the two implementation styles (object vs class adapter, with a preference for object), contrasts Adapter with Decorator, and gives Spring examples (HandlerAdapter) and Java examples (InputStreamReader, slf4j bindings). Mentioning that adapters are cheap to write but easy to over-apply — one adapter per third-party dependency is healthy, ten adapters for the same interface is a design smell.
bullets: Adapter converts one interface to another that the client expects — used for integrating third-party or legacy code without modifying either side.
Object adapter (composition) is the standard in Java; class adapter (multiple inheritance) is rare and fragile.
Real examples: InputStreamReader (bytes → characters), Spring MVC HandlerAdapter, slf4j-to-log4j2 bindings, Mockito mocks standing in for real services.
Adapter vs Decorator: Adapter changes the interface; Decorator keeps the same interface and adds behavior.
One adapter per third-party dependency is healthy; multiple adapters for the same interface signals a design problem.
The client depends only on the target interface — the adaptee's vocabulary (XML, legacy APIs, weird units) stays out of domain code.

cards.title: Decorator Pattern: Adding Behavior by Wrapping, Not Subclassing
cards.summary:
The Decorator pattern attaches additional responsibilities to an object dynamically. Decorators wrap the original object, implement the same interface, and add behavior before, after, or around the wrapped call. The key insight is that wrapping composes behaviors at runtime, whereas subclassing composes them at compile time — so you can stack three decorators to get three behaviors without creating a class for every combination.

The problem it solves is class explosion from inheritance. Suppose you have an InputStream, and you want to support buffering, gzip decompression, and progress reporting — each optionally, in any combination. Subclassing gives you 2^3 = 8 concrete classes for every combination, and 2^N for N behaviors. Wrapping gives you three decorators that can be stacked in any order: new Progress(new Gzip(new Buffered(new FileInputStream(f)))). Three classes handle all eight combinations. This is why java.io uses decorators pervasively, and why the pattern is sometimes called 'the wrapping pattern'.

Where Decorator appears in Java and Spring matters for interviews. java.io is the canonical example: BufferedInputStream wraps an InputStream, GZIPInputStream wraps an InputStream, DataInputStream wraps an InputStream — each adds one behavior. In Spring MVC, HttpServletRequestWrapper and HttpServletResponseWrapper are decorators used by filters to add caching, header injection, request body reading, or logging without modifying the underlying request. Spring Security's filter chain decorates requests with authentication context. In the wider ecosystem, Reactor and RxJava operators (map, filter, buffer) are decorators — they wrap a Mono/Flux and add behavior. Spring AOP's proxies are conceptually decorators too (wrapping the bean and adding transaction/security/caching behavior), though the implementation is proxy-based rather than hand-written.

The order of decorators matters, and getting it wrong is a common bug. new Gzip(new Buffered(stream)) compresses buffered data; new Buffered(new Gzip(stream)) buffers compressed data — both are valid but produce different memory profiles and performance. Progress reporting placed inside a buffer will report per-buffer-flush counts; placed outside, per-byte counts. You must decide the order based on what you are trying to achieve, and document it.

The subtle trap is identity. A decorated object is not the same as the underlying object: wrapped.equals(wrapped) may not hold depending on implementation, and instanceof checks against the wrapper may fail when callers expect the concrete type. For example, a List decorator that overrides get/size but delegates everything else cannot be cast to ArrayList — callers using ArrayList-specific methods will break. This is the same reason Spring AOP proxies fail when callers inject the concrete class instead of the interface (the same topic as the spring-aop-1 card). The decorator must implement the same interface, not just the concrete class, and callers must depend on the interface.

The distinction from related patterns: Adapter changes the interface (different contract); Decorator keeps the same interface (same contract, more behavior); Proxy also keeps the same interface but adds cross-cutting concerns (security, caching, lazy loading) and controls access rather than layering behavior. In practice, the line between Decorator and Proxy is often blurred — a ProgressInputStream is a decorator (adds behavior to every call); a CachingProxy that returns cached results without calling the wrapped object is a proxy. In interviews, explain the 'wrapping instead of subclassing' motivation, show java.io and Spring HttpServletRequestWrapper as examples, mention the order-dependency and identity caveats, and distinguish from Adapter and Proxy.
bullets: Decorator wraps an object to add behavior dynamically — same interface, layered behavior, composed at runtime instead of subclassed at compile time.
Solves class explosion: N optional behaviors need 2^N subclasses but only N decorators, stackable in any order.
Real examples: java.io (Buffered/GZIP/DataInputStream), Spring HttpServletRequestWrapper/ResponseWrapper, Spring Security filter chain, Reactor operators.
Order of decorators matters — Gzip(Buffered(x)) vs Buffered(Gzip(x)) are both valid but behave differently; document the intended order.
Identity caveat: wrapped != underlying, and casting a decorator to a concrete class fails — callers must depend on the interface.
Distinction: Adapter changes the interface, Decorator adds behavior to the same interface, Proxy controls access to the same interface.

cards.title: Facade Pattern: One Simple Door to a Complex Subsystem
cards.summary:
The Facade pattern provides a simplified, unified interface to a set of interfaces in a subsystem. It does not remove complexity — it hides it behind one clean entry point so that clients do not have to coordinate multiple objects themselves. The subsystem classes remain fully accessible; the facade is an additional convenient surface, not a replacement.

The problem it solves is coordination overhead. Consider a video conversion pipeline: you must open the file, decode audio, decode video, resample audio, re-encode both, mux them together, and write the output — in that specific order, with the correct intermediate buffers, and with error handling at each step. A caller who just wants to 'convert this file' should not have to know that order. A VideoConverter facade exposes convert(input, output), calls the seven subsystem classes internally, and lets callers treat the pipeline as one operation. If the subsystem changes (a new codec added, an intermediate step removed), only the facade changes; every caller remains untouched.

Where Facade appears in Java and Spring matters for interviews. SLF4J (Simple Logging Facade for Java) is the textbook example — it is literally named after the pattern. The org.slf4j.Logger interface is the facade; underneath, the actual logging happens through a binding to logback, log4j2, or java.util.logging. Application code depends only on slf4j interfaces, so the logging backend can be swapped at deployment time. Spring's JdbcTemplate is a facade over the JDBC API: callers write jdbcTemplate.query(sql, mapper) instead of openConnection → createStatement → executeQuery → iterate ResultSet → close everything in finally blocks. Spring's JmsTemplate, RestTemplate, and WebClient are similar facades. Spring Boot's DataSourceAutoConfiguration can be seen as a configuration facade: it wires HikariCP, dialect selection, transaction manager, and connection validation behind one DataSource bean.

The crucial interview distinction is Facade vs Adapter and Facade vs Mediator. Adapter translates one interface to another (different contracts); Facade simplifies many interfaces into one (same underlying contracts, easier access). Mediator centralizes communication between objects that need to talk to each other bidirectionally; Facade is one-way — the client calls the facade, the facade calls the subsystem, nothing calls back. A common trap is to claim a Facade 'wraps each subsystem class' — it does not wrap them, it composes them and orchestrates the calls. Wrapping each class individually would be Decorator or Adapter territory.

The trade-off with Facade is that it can become a God Object if misused. A facade that exposes fifty methods across ten subsystems is no longer simplifying — it is a monolith with a friendly name. The healthy discipline is: one facade per coherent subsystem, with a narrow interface focused on the operations clients actually need. If clients need fine-grained control, they should still be able to drop down to the subsystem classes (which is why Facade never hides them). In interviews, name the coordination problem, show the before/after with a real subsystem, mention SLF4J and JdbcTemplate as production examples, and note the God Object risk.
bullets: Facade provides one simplified interface to a complex subsystem — it hides coordination, not capability; subsystem classes remain accessible.
Solves coordination overhead: a caller that wants one operation does not need to sequence seven subsystem calls correctly.
Real examples: SLF4J (facade over logging backends), Spring JdbcTemplate (facade over JDBC), JmsTemplate, RestTemplate, WebClient.
Facade vs Adapter: Facade simplifies many interfaces into one; Adapter translates one interface to another.
Facade vs Mediator: Facade is one-way (client → facade → subsystem); Mediator is bidirectional communication between peers.
Beware God Object — a facade should be narrow and per-subsystem, not a 50-method catch-all.

cards.title: Proxy Pattern: Controlled Access to an Object
cards.summary:
The Proxy pattern provides a stand-in or placeholder for another object, allowing you to control access to it. The proxy implements the same interface as the real subject and delegates calls to it, but inserts behavior before, after, or instead of the delegate call. Unlike Decorator (which adds behavior to every call), a Proxy typically controls whether and when the real object is accessed at all.

The pattern comes in several important flavors. A Virtual Proxy defers creating the expensive real object until the first call — this is how Hibernate's lazy loading works: the entity is a proxy, and the SQL query fires only when a getter on a lazily loaded field is called. A Remote Proxy represents an object in a different process — RMI stubs, gRPC stubs, and feign clients are remote proxies. A Protection Proxy controls access based on permissions — Spring Security's method-level proxies (@PreAuthorize) check the caller's authorities before invoking the target method. A Caching Proxy returns a cached result without touching the real object — HTTP caches and memoization layers are caching proxies. A Logging Proxy records calls without altering behavior.

Spring AOP is entirely proxy-based, which is why this pattern comes up in every Spring interview. When you annotate a method with @Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async, or @PreAuthorize, Spring wraps the bean in a proxy. The proxy intercepts the call, decides whether to open a transaction, consult a cache, dispatch to a thread pool, or check permissions, then invokes the real bean's method. Two proxy mechanisms are used: JDK dynamic proxy (requires the bean to implement interfaces) and CGLIB (subclasses the bean). This is the same mechanism discussed in detail in spring-aop-1 — the failure modes (self-invocation bypass, final methods, concrete-class injection) are all consequences of the proxy pattern.

The critical interview distinction is Proxy vs Decorator. Both implement the same interface and wrap the real object. Decorator's purpose is to add behavior — every call is delegated, and the wrapper layers on functionality. Proxy's purpose is to control access — the proxy may not call the real object at all (cache hit, security denial, lazy deferral). In practice they are hard to distinguish, and many implementations mix both concerns. The clean rule: 'is the real object always called?' If yes → Decorator. If sometimes → Proxy.

The second trap is Proxy vs Adapter. Adapter changes the interface (the wrapper implements a different interface from the wrapped object). Proxy keeps the same interface. If a client can treat the proxy and the real object interchangeably without code changes, it is a Proxy.

In an interview, name the four proxy types (virtual, remote, protection, caching), describe Spring AOP as the production example, mention the self-invocation trap as a direct consequence of proxy-based interception, and distinguish from Decorator with the 'real object always called?' test.
bullets: Proxy controls access to a real object — same interface as the subject, but may not call it at all (cache hit, security denial, lazy deferral).
Four flavors: virtual (lazy loading, Hibernate), remote (RMI, gRPC, feign), protection (Spring Security @PreAuthorize), caching (memoization, HTTP cache).
Spring AOP is entirely proxy-based — @Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async, @PreAuthorize all work by intercepting via a proxy.
Two proxy mechanisms: JDK dynamic proxy (interface-based) and CGLIB (subclass-based). The choice determines the failure modes.
Proxy vs Decorator: 'is the real object always called?' If yes → Decorator; if sometimes → Proxy.
Proxy vs Adapter: Adapter changes the interface; Proxy keeps the same interface.
Self-invocation (this.method()) bypasses the proxy — the biggest gotcha for any annotation-driven proxy in Spring.

cards.title: Composite Pattern: Treating Individual and Group Uniformly
cards.summary:
The Composite pattern composes objects into tree structures and lets clients treat individual objects (leaves) and groups of objects (composites) uniformly through a common interface. A composite holds a collection of children — which may themselves be leaves or composites — and delegates operations to them. The client never has to check 'is this a leaf or a container?'; it just calls the common method.

The problem it solves is the leaf-vs-container distinction leaking into client code. Without Composite, a client walking a file system has to branch on 'is this a file or a directory?' at every level — check its type, decide whether to recurse, aggregate results differently. With Composite, both File and Directory implement a Node interface with size() and print(), and the client writes one recursive call: node.print(). This eliminates a whole class of bugs (forgetting a branch, mishandling empty directories, off-by-one in aggregation).

Where Composite appears in Java and Spring matters for interviews. java.io.File is a composite-shaped API (a directory can contain files and directories). java.awt.Container extends Component and holds a list of children — classic Composite. In Spring, Spring Security's AccessDecisionVoter chain is not composite per se, but the ApplicationContext's bean factory hierarchy (parent-child BeanFactory) is composite-shaped. The Spring MVC ViewResolver chain (a CompositeViewResolver delegating to a list of view resolvers in order) is a real Composite. JSF, Wicket, and Vaadin UI component trees are composites. Anywhere you see 'tree of nodes, uniform operations', it is Composite.

The crucial design decision is where to put child management methods (add/remove/getChild). You have two options. (1) Declare add/remove on the Component interface — uniform, but leaves have to implement them (throw UnsupportedOperationException or no-op). This violates the Interface Segregation Principle but is simpler for clients. (2) Declare add/remove only on Composite — cleaner interface, but clients must downcast to Composite to add children. The common production choice is the first (uniform interface) because clients rarely need to add children through the leaf-facing interface, and the UnsupportedOperationException is a rare fallback. The interview trap is to say 'one of these is correct' — both are valid trade-offs and the right answer is context-dependent.

The second trap is misuse in a concurrent context. A composite that holds a mutable List of children is not thread-safe by default. If children are added or removed while a tree walk is in progress, you get ConcurrentModificationException or inconsistent results. Production composites either use CopyOnWriteArrayList for the children or snapshot the list before delegating. In Spring, this is why a list of sorted resolvers injected with @Autowired List<SomeInterface> is immutable — the container gives you a snapshot that does not change after startup.

In an interview, name the problem (leaf-container branching), the uniform interface (both implement the same methods), the recursive delegation (composite iterates over children calling the same method), and the two placement choices for child management. Mention Spring's CompositeViewResolver or a UI component tree as real examples.
bullets: Composite composes objects into trees; leaves and composites implement the same interface so clients treat them uniformly.
Solves leaf-container branching: without it, every client has to check 'is this a file or directory?' and aggregate differently.
The composite holds a collection of children and delegates operations recursively; leaves implement the operation directly.
Child management (add/remove) placement is a trade-off: on Component (uniform, leaves throw UnsupportedOperationException) vs on Composite only (clean, but callers downcast).
Real examples: java.io.File hierarchy, java.awt.Container, Spring CompositeViewResolver, JSF/Wicket/Vaadin component trees.
Composites with mutable child lists are not thread-safe — snapshot or use CopyOnWriteArrayList for concurrent tree walks.

cards.title: Strategy Pattern: Swappable Algorithms Behind a Common Interface
cards.summary:
The Strategy pattern defines a family of algorithms, encapsulates each one in its own class behind a common interface, and lets the client swap algorithms at runtime. The context class holds a reference to a Strategy and delegates the algorithm to it. The client chooses the strategy — the context does not — which is what separates Strategy from patterns where the object chooses its own behavior (like State).

The problem it solves is conditional branching that explodes over time. Without Strategy, a PaymentService has an if (type == STRIPE) { ... } else if (type == PAYPAL) { ... } else if (type == RAZORPAY) { ... } block. Every new provider edits the same method, every edit risks breaking the existing branches, and testing a new provider requires understanding all of the others. Strategy moves each branch into its own class: StripeStrategy, PayPalStrategy, RazorpayStrategy — each implementing PaymentStrategy. The PaymentService becomes paymentStrategy.charge(amount), and adding a new provider means adding one class and one entry in a factory or map, not editing production code. This is the Open/Closed Principle in action.

Where Strategy appears in Java and Spring matters for interviews. Comparator is the most famous Strategy in Java — Collections.sort(list, comparator) takes the sorting algorithm as a parameter. Runnable, Callable, and every functional interface in java.util.function is effectively a Strategy — the caller supplies the algorithm. In Spring, ResourceLoader is a strategy for loading resources (classpath, file, URL — chosen by the protocol prefix). PlatformTransactionManager is a strategy (DataSourceTransactionManager, JpaTransactionManager, JtaTransactionManager). ViewResolver is a strategy for resolving view names. MessageConverter in RestTemplate is a strategy. And Spring's @Autowired Map<String, Strategy> is the idiomatic way to inject a collection of strategies keyed by bean name — the pattern is so fundamental that Spring has first-class support for it.

The distinction from State is the most-tested interview question. Strategy: the client chooses the algorithm, and the choice usually does not change during the object's lifetime (or changes only when the client decides). State: the object transitions between states internally, and each state determines the next state. If the choice is made externally and passed in, it is Strategy. If the object changes its own behavior by moving to a new state, it is State. A second trap is confusing Strategy with Template Method: Strategy uses composition (a strategy object is injected); Template Method uses inheritance (the base class defines the skeleton and subclasses override the steps). If you have one algorithm and many variations of its steps → Template Method. If you have many independent algorithms and the caller chooses one → Strategy.

The trade-off with Strategy is extra classes and client awareness. The client must know which strategies exist and how to select them, which is why a factory or a map injection is usually paired with the pattern. Over-applying Strategy to a method with one implementation and no plan for a second is a common over-engineering mistake — the branching has to be real before the pattern pays off. In interviews, name the branching problem, show the before/after, mention Comparator and Spring's Map<String, Strategy> injection as real examples, and clearly distinguish Strategy from State.
bullets: Strategy encapsulates a family of algorithms behind one interface and lets the client choose at runtime — the context does not choose.
Solves conditional branching explosion: if-else chains become separate strategy classes, adding a new algorithm requires no changes to existing code.
Real examples: Comparator, Runnable/Callable, Spring's PlatformTransactionManager, ResourceLoader, ViewResolver, and @Autowired Map<String, Strategy>.
Strategy vs State: Strategy is chosen externally by the client; State transitions internally within the object.
Strategy vs Template Method: Strategy uses composition (injected algorithm); Template Method uses inheritance (subclass overrides steps).
Avoid when there is only one implementation — branches must be real for the pattern to earn its keep.

cards.title: Observer Pattern: One Event, Many Listeners, and the Memory Leak You Will Hit
cards.summary:
The Observer pattern defines a one-to-many dependency between objects: when the subject changes state, all its registered observers are notified and updated automatically. The subject holds a list of observers, provides register and unregister methods, and iterates over them on each event. The pattern is the foundation of every event system — UI listeners, pub-sub, message buses, reactive streams, and Spring's ApplicationEvent framework.

The problem it solves is tight coupling between a state change and its consequences. Without Observer, when an Order is placed, the OrderService must call the email service, the inventory service, the analytics tracker, and the loyalty-points service — every consequence becomes a hardcoded dependency. Adding a new consequence edits OrderService. With Observer, OrderService publishes an OrderPlaced event; email, inventory, analytics, and loyalty each register as observers. Adding loyalty means adding a new observer class — no change to OrderService. This is the same Open/Closed idea as Strategy but applied to events instead of algorithms.

Java's built-in Observer/Observable (java.util.Observer, java.util.Observable) is deprecated since Java 9 for good reasons: Observable is a class, not an interface, forcing inheritance; its setChanged()/notifyObservers() contract is awkward; and it is not thread-safe. The modern replacements are java.util.concurrent.Flow (Java 9+, the Reactive Streams API), the listener interfaces in every framework (Spring's ApplicationListener, ServletContextListener), and reactive libraries (Reactor, RxJava) whose onNext/onError/onComplete model is Observer + backpressure.

Spring's ApplicationEventPublisher is the production example to mention. Services call applicationEventPublisher.publishEvent(new OrderPlacedEvent(id)); and any bean implementing ApplicationListener<OrderPlacedEvent> or annotated @EventListener receives it. By default events are synchronous (delivered on the publishing thread), which is a common interview trap — a slow listener blocks the publisher. For async delivery, @EventListener + @Async, or an ApplicationEventMulticaster configured with an executor, is required. Spring Boot 3 adds @TransactionalEventListener for events that fire only after a transaction commits — this is the correct way to publish an event whose side effects must see committed data, avoiding the dual-write problem the Kafka cards discuss.

The most important interview topic in Observer is the memory leak. If an observer is registered but never unregistered, the subject holds a strong reference to it and prevents garbage collection. In long-lived subjects (a singleton publisher), the leak accumulates: every transient observer that forgot to unregister stays alive forever. Real-world examples: Android activities registered to a global bus, event listeners in web frameworks that outlive their session, custom observers in a long-running service. The fixes are: (1) unregister in a @PreDestroy or finally block; (2) store observers as WeakReference so the subject does not prevent collection; (3) use a lifecycle-aware framework (Spring events are tied to the bean lifecycle — a bean that goes out of scope is unregistered automatically). The second trap is reentrancy and ordering: if an observer publishes another event during notification, you can get infinite loops or unpredictable ordering. A robust subject either queues events and processes them after the current notification completes, or documents that reentrant notifications are forbidden.

In an interview, name the problem (one change, many consequences), show the register/notify/unregister contract, mention Spring events and reactive streams as production examples, and importantly — call out the memory leak and the sync-vs-async delivery distinction. That shows you have used Observer in production, not just read about it.
bullets: Observer defines a one-to-many dependency: subject state changes trigger notifications to all registered observers automatically.
Solves tight coupling between a state change and its consequences — publish an event, let observers react, do not hardcode each consequence in the publisher.
Java's Observable/Observer is deprecated; modern equivalents are Spring ApplicationEvent, java.util.concurrent.Flow (Reactive Streams), Reactor, RxJava.
Spring events are synchronous by default — a slow listener blocks the publisher. Use @Async or an async ApplicationEventMulticaster for async delivery.
Memory leak: unregister in @PreDestroy, use WeakReference, or rely on lifecycle-aware frameworks — long-lived subjects leak forgotten observers.
Spring Boot 3 @TransactionalEventListener fires only after transaction commit — avoids the dual-write problem.

cards.title: Command Pattern: Encapsulating Requests as Objects, Enabling Undo, Queueing, and Transactions
cards.summary:
The Command pattern turns a request into a standalone object. A Command encapsulates the action to perform, the receiver it operates on, and any parameters, behind a common execute() (and often undo()) method. The invoker holds commands and calls execute() without knowing what the command does or who will perform it. The receiver is the object that actually carries out the work.

The problem it solves is decoupling the request from its execution context. Without Command, a UI button's onClick handler is a hardcoded method call: button.onClick → editor.saveFile().
