That couples the button to the editor, prevents queueing, and makes undo impossible. With Command, the button holds a Command reference. The client constructs SaveCommand(editor) and passes it to the button; the button calls command.execute(). Now the same button can trigger any command, undo is enabled by calling command.undo(), and commands can be queued, logged, or retried because they are just objects.

Where Command appears in Java and Spring matters for interviews. java.lang.Runnable is the simplest Command — a parameterless execute(). java.util.concurrent's ExecutorService.submit(Callable) executes a Command and returns a Future. Spring's TransactionCallback is a Command executed inside TransactionTemplate — the pattern is what gives imperative transaction control without the AOP proxy. Spring Batch's Tasklet is a Command. Undo/redo in editors, transactional queues in event-sourcing systems, macro recording, and every 'task' abstraction (Jira's Issue, Gradle's Task, Kubernetes' Job) is Command-shaped.

The undo capability deserves separate attention because it is what distinguishes Command from most other patterns. To undo, each command stores enough state to reverse itself — SaveCommand stores the previous file content, DeleteCommand stores the deleted bytes, MoveCommand stores the original position. An UndoStack holds executed commands; undo() pops the last command and calls its undo(). Redo stacks the popped command for re-execution. The pattern gets tricky when commands interact: undo of command N must be safe even if command N+1 partially succeeded, which is why production undo systems usually use mementos (saved snapshots) rather than hand-written inverse operations.

The distinction from Strategy and State is a common interview question. Strategy replaces an algorithm inside a context — the context still does the work, the strategy decides how. State changes the context's behavior based on internal state. Command packages an action to be performed by someone else — the invoker and receiver are separate, and the command holds the parameters. If the caller knows the receiver and calls it directly, it is not Command. The tell is the invocation indirection: the invoker holds the command and calls execute(), not 'does the thing'.

In an interview, name the problem (request execution coupled to invocation context), show the invoker/command/receiver triangle, give Runnable and TransactionTemplate as examples, and explain how undo, queueing, and transactions all fall out of the same indirection. Mention the queueing use case — commands can be persisted, delayed, retried, or reordered in ways that direct method calls cannot — because that is what makes Command a distributed-systems tool, not just a UI tool.
bullets: Command encapsulates a request as an object with execute() (and often undo()), decoupling the invoker from the receiver.
Solves request-execution coupling: a button holds a Command reference; the same button can trigger any action, and commands can be queued, logged, or undone.
Real examples: Runnable, ExecutorService.submit, Spring TransactionCallback/TransactionTemplate, Spring Batch Tasklet, UI button handlers.
Undo requires storing inverse state per command; UndoStack holds executed commands and pops + undo()s on user request.
Command vs Strategy: Strategy replaces an algorithm inside a context; Command packages an action to be performed by a separate receiver.
The queueing use case is what makes Command a distributed-systems tool — commands can be persisted, delayed, retried, or reordered.

cards.title: Template Method Pattern: Skeleton in the Base Class, Steps in Subclasses
cards.summary:
The Template Method pattern defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a base class, deferring some steps to subclasses. The base class's template method calls a fixed sequence of steps — some concrete (shared implementation), some abstract or overridable (subclass-specific). Subclasses can customize individual steps without changing the overall algorithm's structure. This is inheritance-based composition: the base class controls the flow, the subclass fills in the variation points.

The problem it solves is duplication of the algorithm's control flow across variations. Imagine three data importers: CSV, JSON, and XML. Each reads the file, parses it, validates each row, writes it to the database, and logs a summary. Only the parse step differs. Without Template Method, all three duplicate the read-validate-write-log flow, and a bug in that flow must be fixed in three places (and the fourth, fifth, sixth that come later). With Template Method, an AbstractImporter defines importFile() that calls read(), parse(), validate(), write(), and logSummary() in order. CSVImporter, JsonImporter, and XmlImporter extend AbstractImporter and override only parse(). The flow is written once, fixed once, tested once. This is the 'Hollywood principle': don't call us, we'll call you — the base class calls the subclass's methods, not the other way around.

Where Template Method appears in Java and Spring matters for interviews. java.io.InputStream has read(byte[]) implemented in terms of the abstract read() — the template method orchestrates reading and subclasses implement the byte source. java.util.AbstractList defines most List behavior in terms of get() and size(), which subclasses provide. Spring's JdbcTemplate.query() is a textbook Template Method: it opens a connection, creates a PreparedStatement, binds parameters, executes, iterates the ResultSet, handles exceptions, and closes everything — while the caller supplies only the RowMapper (the varying step). JmsTemplate, TransactionTemplate, and RestTemplate follow the same shape. Spring Security's AbstractAuthenticationProcessingFilter defines the filter flow and leaves the actual authentication to subclasses. The pattern is pervasive in framework code because it lets a framework own the cross-cutting concerns (resource management, exception handling) while the application owns the domain logic.

The 'hook' concept distinguishes Template Method from simple inheritance. A hook is an overridable method with a default (often empty) implementation that subclasses MAY override — like afterPropertiesSet() in Spring's InitializingBean, or the onSuccess/onFailure callbacks around a network call. Abstract steps are mandatory (subclasses MUST override); hooks are optional. The base class calls both in the same template method, but the base class never assumes hooks do anything.

The crucial design rule is that template methods should be final (or at least not overridable) to preserve the algorithm's structure. If a subclass overrides the template method itself, it can reorder or skip steps, which defeats the entire purpose. Making the template method final is a defensive choice — it tells subclasses 'you can vary the steps, but not the sequence'. This is also why Template Method is criticized in modern Java: inheritance is a tight coupling, and the subclass is coupled to the base class's private step structure. Composition-based alternatives (Strategy) are often preferred when the variations are independent.

The distinction from Strategy is the most-tested interview question. Template Method uses inheritance: one algorithm skeleton, subclass overrides steps, variation at compile time. Strategy uses composition: many independent algorithms, injected at runtime. If the algorithm's structure is fixed and only individual steps vary → Template Method. If the entire algorithm can be swapped → Strategy. If you find yourself writing a Template Method with only one subclass and no plan for a second, that is a smell — the abstract class is unnecessary indirection. In interviews, name the flow-duplication problem, show the JdbcTemplate.query() example, mention the final-on-template-method rule, and clearly distinguish from Strategy.
bullets: Template Method defines an algorithm skeleton in a base class; subclasses override individual steps without changing the flow.
Solves flow duplication: the control sequence (read-validate-write-log) lives in one place; subclasses only supply the varying steps.
Real examples: InputStream.read(byte[]) via abstract read(), AbstractList via get()/size(), Spring JdbcTemplate.query(), JmsTemplate, TransactionTemplate, AbstractAuthenticationProcessingFilter.
Abstract steps are mandatory (subclass must override); hooks are optional (default empty implementation, may be overridden).
The template method should be final — overriding it defeats the pattern by allowing subclasses to reorder or skip steps.
Template Method vs Strategy: Template Method uses inheritance (fixed flow, varying steps); Strategy uses composition (whole algorithm swapped at runtime).

cards.title: State Pattern: Behavior That Changes with Internal State, Without if-else Explosion
cards.summary:
The State pattern lets an object change its behavior when its internal state changes. The object appears to change its class: a method that behaved one way in state A behaves differently in state B, without the caller knowing or caring. Internally, the context delegates to a state object representing the current state, and state transitions replace that state object.

The problem it solves is conditional explosion over state-dependent behavior. An Order has states: PLACED, PAID, SHIPPED, DELIVERED, CANCELLED, REFUNDED. It has operations: pay(), ship(), deliver(), cancel(), refund(). Each operation is legal in some states and forbidden in others. Without State, every operation begins with a big switch over the current state: if (state == PLACED) allow; else if (state == PAID) allow; else throw. Every new state edits every operation. Every new operation duplicates the state matrix. After three months the Order class is a 2,000-line method with a subtle cross-product of rules.

With State, each state is a class. PlacedState implements pay(), ship(), cancel(); calls to deliver() or refund() throw IllegalStateException. PaidState implements ship(), refund(), cancel(); calls to pay() throw 'already paid'. The Order holds a State reference and delegates: state.pay(order). The state object knows which transitions are valid and calls order.setState(new PaidState()) when a transition succeeds. Adding a new state means adding a new class — no edits to existing states, no edits to Order. This is the Open/Closed Principle applied to state machines.

The State pattern appears in production wherever a finite state machine lives. TCP connection states (LISTEN, SYN_SENT, ESTABLISHED, CLOSE_WAIT) are the canonical example. Spring's state machine project (spring-statemachine) makes the pattern explicit, but most code uses a hand-written State without naming it. Workflow engines (Airflow tasks, Camunda BPMN) are State-based. Order/payment/subscription lifecycles in e-commerce are State-based. Any 'current status' field in a database table with rules about which transitions are legal is asking for State.

The crucial interview distinction is State vs Strategy. Both involve a context holding a reference to an interface implementation and delegating. The difference is who changes the reference. In Strategy, the client chooses the algorithm and the context does not change it (or only changes it on explicit external command). In State, the state objects themselves trigger transitions — calling pay() on a PlacedState causes it to set the context's state to PaidState. If a state can initiate a transition to another state, it is State. If the caller always chooses the algorithm, it is Strategy. A second tell: Strategy algorithms are usually stateless and interchangeable; State objects usually reference the context (to trigger transitions) and are not freely swappable.

The trade-off with State is class proliferation. A state machine with 15 states and 30 operations can become 15 classes each with 30 methods — too much boilerplate for simple cases. The pragmatic rule: use State when the state matrix is genuinely complex (many states, many rules, frequent additions); use an enum + switch when the matrix is simple and stable. Spring's @Transactional propagation, for example, uses enum + switch because the rules are stable. A payment lifecycle that gains a new state every quarter uses State. In interviews, name the conditional-explosion problem, show the before/after with a payment example, explain the self-transition mechanism, and distinguish from Strategy with the 'who changes the state?' test.
bullets: State lets an object's behavior change with its internal state by delegating to a state object that represents the current state.
Solves conditional explosion: each state becomes a class implementing only its legal operations; adding a state does not edit existing states.
Real examples: TCP connection states, order/payment lifecycles, workflow engines (Camunda, Airflow), Spring StateMachine.
State vs Strategy: State transitions internally (state objects set the context's next state); Strategy is chosen externally by the client.
The state object usually holds a reference to the context so it can call context.setState(next).
Class proliferation is the cost — use State only when the state matrix is complex and growing; use enum + switch for stable simple rules.

cards.title: Chain of Responsibility: Passing a Request Along a Pipeline Until Someone Handles It
cards.summary:
The Chain of Responsibility pattern passes a request along a chain of handlers. Each handler decides either to process the request, to pass it to the next handler, or both. The client sends the request to the first handler and does not know which handler will ultimately process it — or whether any will. This decouples the sender from the receiver and lets you compose processing as a pipeline.

The problem it solves is ordered, flexible processing without a monolithic dispatcher. A request may need authentication, then authorization, then rate-limiting, then input validation, then logging, then the actual business logic. Without a chain, all of these live in one handler method and the order is hardcoded. With a chain, each concern is a handler; the chain is assembled declaratively; a request that fails authentication never reaches business logic because the auth handler short-circuits. The chain is what makes middleware middleware.

Where the pattern appears is everywhere in production. Servlet Filters are the canonical Java example: a Filter chain (in web.xml or Spring's FilterChain) processes every HTTP request. Each filter can inspect the request, modify it, call chain.doFilter(req, res) to continue, or return without calling it to short-circuit. Spring Security is a chain of filters: SecurityContextPersistenceFilter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter, ExceptionTranslationFilter, FilterSecurityInterceptor — each handles its concern and passes to the next. Netty pipelines, gRPC interceptors, Kafka's producer/consumer interceptors, and Spring's HandlerInterceptor are all chains. Even try/catch blocks form an implicit chain — each catch is a handler that decides to handle or rethrow.

The two variants — pure and impure — are important to name. A pure chain guarantees that exactly one handler processes the request (classic Gang of Four). An impure chain lets multiple handlers act and pass through — this is the middleware variant that dominates in practice. Servlet filters are impure (each filter can modify the request and pass it on). Load balancers and reverse proxies in a request path form an impure chain too. When you say 'Chain of Responsibility' in an interview, clarify which variant you mean — this shows you understand the pattern beyond the textbook definition.

The design decisions are: how to assemble the chain, and where to stop. Assembly can be static (each handler holds a reference to next at construction) or dynamic (a list of handlers iterated by the chain manager). The dynamic list is more flexible and is what most frameworks use — you can add, remove, or reorder handlers via configuration. The stop decision is each handler's choice: some always pass (logging), some conditionally pass (auth — pass if authenticated, short-circuit if not), some never pass (a terminal handler that writes the response). The classic bug is a handler that forgets to call the next one — silently dropping requests. The defense is to make each handler's pass-or-stop decision explicit in code, and to test the chain end-to-end, not just individual handlers.

The distinction from Decorator is subtle but worth naming. Decorator wraps a specific target and always delegates; the chain has a variable number of participants and any handler may not pass. Decorator's goal is to add behavior to a specific call; Chain's goal is to find the right handler among many. In practice, the two are hard to distinguish — a servlet filter chain is both an impure chain AND structurally a series of decorators — but naming the intent ('this is about finding a handler' vs 'this is about enriching a call') is what matters.

In an interview, name the problem (ordered processing, sender should not know the receiver), show the middleware pipeline (Servlet Filters, Spring Security), explain pure vs impure, and mention the 'handler forgot to call next' bug as the classic failure mode.
bullets: Chain of Responsibility passes a request along handlers; each handler processes, passes, or both, decoupling sender from receiver.
Solves ordered processing without a monolithic dispatcher: auth, rate limit, validation, logging, business logic each become a handler.
Real examples: Servlet Filters (chain.doFilter), Spring Security filter chain, Netty pipeline, gRPC interceptors, Kafka interceptors.
Pure chain: exactly one handler processes. Impure chain: multiple handlers act and pass through — middleware-style, the dominant variant in practice.
Dynamic assembly (list of handlers) beats static chaining — enables configuration-driven ordering, addition, and removal.
Classic bug: a handler that forgets to call next silently drops requests — make pass/stop explicit and test the chain end-to-end.

cards.title: Iterator Pattern: Traversing a Collection Without Exposing Its Internals
cards.summary:
The Iterator pattern gives a way to access the elements of an aggregate object sequentially without exposing the aggregate's underlying representation. The collection provides an iterator(); the iterator provides hasNext() and next(); the client consumes elements without knowing whether the collection is an array, a linked list, a tree, or a lazily generated stream.

The problem it solves is coupling between the collection's storage and the code that traverses it. Without Iterator, a client that walks an ArrayList uses indices (for (int i = 0; i < list.size(); i++) list.get(i)), which does not work on a LinkedList without O(n²) cost and does not work at all on a hash-based structure or a tree. Every collection would need a different traversal API, and switching the collection would require rewriting the client. With Iterator, the client uses the same for-each loop against any collection — the array-backed list, the linked list, the hash set, the tree — because they all implement Iterable<T> and expose an Iterator<T>.

Java's Iterator is one of the most-used interfaces in the language. The for-each loop (for (T x : collection)) is pure syntactic sugar for an iterator-based loop — the compiler translates it. Collection extends Iterable, and every collection in java.util provides an Iterator. Stream<T> is the modern alternative for functional-style traversal: collection.stream() gives a lazy, composable pipeline that is iterated internally. The two coexist: iterator for imperative control (break, remove), streams for declarative transformations.

The two important behaviors of Java iterators are fail-fast and remove(). Fail-fast iterators (the default for all java.util collections except concurrent ones) detect structural modification during iteration and throw ConcurrentModificationException. They do this by checking a modCount field against the expected count on every next() call — the modification may be on the same thread or another thread, and the iterator does not distinguish. This is why removing from a collection inside a for-each loop throws: the collection's structural modification counter changes and the iterator notices. The correct pattern is iterator.remove() (which updates both the collection and the modCount atomically) or the Collection.removeIf(predicate) method, or iterating over a snapshot (new ArrayList<>(collection)).

The second behavior is that fail-fast is a detection, not a guarantee. It is best-effort: a modCount check on next() catches most concurrent modification, but a modification between hasNext() and next() may or may not be detected, and there is no memory visibility guarantee. For multi-threaded use, the concurrent collections (ConcurrentHashMap, CopyOnWriteArrayList) provide weakly consistent iterators that do not throw ConcurrentModificationException — they may or may not reflect modifications made during iteration, but they never corrupt. This is a deliberate design trade-off: fail-fast favors correctness by failing loudly, weakly consistent favors availability at the cost of snapshot semantics.

The Iterator pattern in production takes many forms. A database ResultSet is an iterator — next() advances, getXxx() reads fields. Kafka consumers iterate over poll() results. JPA's ScrollableResults, jOOQ's Cursor, Jackson's JsonParser — all iterators over potentially very large streams of data, so you never load everything into memory. The pattern's value is more visible when the data is large or unbounded than in a simple List.

In an interview, name the problem (traversal coupled to representation), show the hasNext/next contract and the for-each desugaring, explain fail-fast via modCount and why ConcurrentModificationException happens, and mention that Stream is the modern declarative alternative. Bonus points for noting that fail-fast is best-effort detection, not a guarantee.
bullets: Iterator provides sequential access to elements without exposing the aggregate's representation — one API works for arrays, lists, trees, hash structures.
Java's for-each loop is compiler-translated into an iterator-based loop — every collection's for-each is Iterator under the hood.
Fail-fast iterators (java.util, non-concurrent) throw ConcurrentModificationException by checking modCount on next().
Structural modification during for-each is the #1 cause of ConcurrentModificationException — use iterator.remove(), Collection.removeIf(), or a snapshot.
Concurrent collections (ConcurrentHashMap, CopyOnWriteArrayList) provide weakly consistent iterators that never throw — they favor availability over snapshot correctness.
Stream<T> is the modern declarative alternative for functional traversal; Iterator remains for imperative control (break, remove, external iteration).

cards.title: Visitor Pattern: Adding Operations to a Class Hierarchy Without Modifying It
cards.summary:
The Visitor pattern lets you define new operations on a class hierarchy without modifying the classes themselves. It works by separating the operation into a separate Visitor class that knows how to visit each element type, and by adding a single accept(Visitor) method to each element that dispatches back to the visitor's type-specific method (double dispatch). When you need a new operation, you add a new Visitor; you do not touch the element classes.

The pattern exists because of a fundamental trade-off in OOP. Adding a new class is easy: create the class, implement the interface, done. Adding a new operation is hard: edit every class in the hierarchy. Visitor flips this: adding a new operation is easy (add a Visitor), and adding a new element class is hard (add a method to every Visitor). Visitor is the right choice when the element hierarchy is stable but operations evolve — a compiler's AST is the canonical example: the node types (Add, Multiply, Variable, Literal) change rarely, but the operations (type-check, code-gen, optimize, pretty-print) grow every release.

The mechanism is double dispatch. A single call like node.accept(visitor) dispatches on two types: first, which concrete node (Java's virtual method call picks the override of accept), then which visitor method (the accept implementation calls visitor.visitXxx(this), where xxx is the concrete node type). Neither type is selected by a single dynamic dispatch — you need the two-step call. In Java's single-dispatch model, this is the only way to write 'call the right visitor method for this element type' without reflection or instanceof chains.

Where Visitor appears in production is worth knowing. Java's javax.lang.model uses it: ElementVisitor and TypeVisitor are interfaces that let you traverse the compiler's AST without modifying javax.lang.model.element.* classes. The JDK's java.nio.file.FileVisitor is a Visitor: walkFileTree() calls your FileVisitor.preVisitDirectory, visitFile, visitFileFailed, postVisitDirectory — you write the operation, not the traversal. ANTLR-generated parsers use Visitor. Spring's BeanDefinitionVisitor (deprecated) walked bean definitions. Reflection-free serializers, pretty-printers, and interpreters are visitor-shaped.

The trade-off is real. Visitor is criticized for several reasons. First, adding a new element type is painful: every existing Visitor must add a new visitXxx method, and abstract base visitors must be updated. Second, the Visitor interface usually cannot be sealed — third parties may add visitors, so you cannot use Java's sealed types to close the hierarchy (though sealed element hierarchies make Visitor safer). Third, the accept() method allows the visitor to see every field of the element, which can break encapsulation if not disciplined. Fourth, in modern Java, sealed interfaces + pattern matching (switch on type) is often a cleaner alternative: it gives you exhaustiveness checking without the double-dispatch ceremony. When the hierarchy is sealed, prefer pattern matching; when the hierarchy is extensible by third parties, Visitor is the mechanism.

The classic interview question is 'when would you use Visitor over inheritance?' The answer: when the set of classes is stable but the set of operations is not, or when you want to centralize related operations (all type-checking logic in one class rather than scattered across node classes). If both are changing, neither pattern is right — you need a different decomposition. Also mention: Java 21's pattern matching makes Visitor less attractive for sealed hierarchies; Visitor is still the right tool when visitors are supplied by external code or when you need a formal 'traversal contract'.

In interviews, name the operation-vs-class trade-off, show the double-dispatch accept() mechanism, give FileVisitor or ElementVisitor as a production example, and honestly discuss the cost (adding element types is painful; sealed + pattern matching is often better today).
bullets: Visitor adds operations to a class hierarchy without modifying the classes — new operation = new Visitor, not edits to every element.
Mechanism is double dispatch: element.accept(visitor) → visitor.visitConcrete(this), selecting both the element type and the visitor type.
Real examples: javax.lang.model.ElementVisitor (compiler AST), java.nio.file.FileVisitor (walkFileTree), ANTLR visitor pattern, reflection-free serializers.
The trade-off is asymmetric: adding an operation is easy; adding a new element type breaks every existing Visitor.
Sealed interfaces + Java 21 pattern matching often replace Visitor when the element hierarchy is closed — exhaustiveness without double dispatch.
Use Visitor when the hierarchy is stable but operations grow (compilers, serializers) or when external code must supply operations.

cards.title: Memento and Mediator: Snapshot/Restore and Centralized Communication
cards.summary:
Memento and Mediator are two Behavioral patterns that solve different problems but appear together in interviews because they often confuse candidates. Memento captures and externalizes an object's internal state so it can be restored later, without violating encapsulation. Mediator defines an object that encapsulates how a set of objects interact, so the objects no longer refer to each other directly.

Memento is the pattern behind every 'undo' and every transactional rollback. The originator (the object whose state must be saved) creates a memento containing a snapshot of its state; a caretaker (the undo stack, the transaction log) stores the memento without inspecting it; when a restore is needed, the caretaker returns the memento to the originator, which uses it to reset itself. The key discipline is that the caretaker cannot read or modify the memento's contents — only the originator knows how to interpret its own snapshot. This is what makes Memento safer than exposing getters/setters for every field: the state can be saved and restored without breaking encapsulation.

Memento appears in production at many levels. Undo/redo in editors, IDEs, and design tools uses Memento (a snapshot of the document state on each edit). Database transactions are memento-like: the undo log records before-images of modified rows so a ROLLBACK can restore them. Version control (Git commits) is memento-shaped: each commit is a snapshot, and checking out restores it. Java's Serializable interface is a generic (and often too heavy) memento mechanism — serialize the object to a byte array, store it, deserialize to restore. The trade-off is always the same: memory cost vs undo capability. A full snapshot of a large document for every keystroke is expensive; production editors use command-based undo (Command pattern) for fine-grained edits and Memento for coarse checkpoints. In interviews, name the encapsulation benefit (caretaker cannot see memento contents), describe the originator-caretaker-memento triangle, and mention the snapshot-cost trade-off.

Mediator centralizes communication. Without Mediator, N objects that need to coordinate with each other hold N × (N-1) references — the classic 'everything talks to everything' mess that becomes untestable and unmodifiable. With Mediator, each object holds a reference only to the mediator; the mediator holds references to all participants and routes messages. The result is O(N) references instead of O(N²), a single point of control for coordination logic, and an easy way to add cross-cutting concerns (logging, transaction boundaries, retries) in the mediator.

Mediator appears in Java and Spring in ways candidates often do not recognize. Spring's ApplicationContext is a mediator: beans do not call each other directly — they publish events and the context routes them. A message broker (Kafka, RabbitMQ) is a distributed mediator: producers and consumers do not know about each other; they communicate through topics. Air traffic control is the textbook metaphor: planes do not talk to each other, they talk to the tower. In UI frameworks, dialog boxes often mediate between widgets (a 'Save' button's enabled state depends on the text field, the checkbox, and the file picker — the dialog coordinates all of them). In service meshes, the sidecar proxy is a mediator: services talk to their sidecar, and sidecars handle discovery, retries, mTLS — services no longer need to know each other's addresses.

The cost of Mediator is that the mediator itself can become a God Object. If N is large and the coordination logic is complex, the mediator accumulates all of it. The pattern is best used when the coordination is a genuine cross-cutting concern (routing, discovery, transaction management) and the participants can be simple. When the coordination is domain logic, it often belongs in the domain, not in a mediator.

The distinction between Memento and Command is worth stating: Command is about executing a request (often with undo as a bonus); Memento is about capturing state (undo is the primary purpose). Command-based undo stores the inverse of an operation; Memento-based undo stores a snapshot. Command scales better for many small edits; Memento is simpler when the state is small or when snapshots are coarse. In interviews, name both patterns' problems, give production examples (Git/DB-transactions for Memento; message brokers/ApplicationContext for Mediator), and call out the trade-offs — snapshot cost for Memento, God Object risk for Mediator.
bullets: Memento captures and externalizes an object's state (originator creates memento, caretaker stores without inspecting, restore returns to originator) — undo without breaking encapsulation.
Mediator centralizes communication: N participants talk to the mediator, not to each other — reduces O(N²) coupling to O(N).
Memento examples: undo/redo editors, database ROLLBACK via undo logs, Git commits as snapshots, Serializable as a heavy generic memento.
Mediator examples: Spring ApplicationContext (event routing), message brokers (Kafka, RabbitMQ), UI dialog boxes coordinating widgets, service mesh sidecars.
Trade-offs: Memento costs memory (snapshot size); Mediator risks becoming a God Object (coordination logic accumulates).
Memento vs Command: Command stores the inverse of an operation; Memento stores a state snapshot. Command scales for fine-grained edits, Memento for coarse checkpoints.

cards.title: REST Constraints and HTTP Semantics: Safe vs Idempotent, and Why POST Retries Create Duplicates
cards.summary:
REST is not a protocol; it is an architectural style defined by six constraints. The first is Client-Server: the UI and the data store are separated so each can evolve independently. The second is Statelessness: every request must contain all the information needed to understand it — the server does not store session context between requests. This is why a JWT or an API key travels on every call; the server can be any instance behind a load balancer because no instance holds state from a previous request[reference:0]. The third is Cacheability: responses must explicitly declare whether they can be cached (Cache-Control, ETag), so clients and intermediaries can skip unnecessary calls. The fourth is a Uniform Interface — resource identification in URIs, manipulation through representations (JSON), self-descriptive messages (Content-Type), and optionally HATEOAS (hypermedia links). The fifth is a Layered System: the client cannot tell whether it is talking to the origin server or to a proxy, gateway, or CDN. The sixth is Code on Demand (optional): servers may send executable code (JavaScript) to clients.

The single most tested semantic distinction is safe versus idempotent. A method is safe if calling it does not change server state — GET, HEAD, and OPTIONS are safe. A method is idempotent if calling it multiple times produces the same server state as calling it once. GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent. POST is neither safe nor idempotent: two identical POST requests create two resources[reference:1]. PATCH is not inherently idempotent either — PATCH { "op": "increment", "value": 1 } called twice increments twice; PATCH { "name": "Alice" } called twice leaves the name as Alice. The spec does not guarantee PATCH idempotence, but a well-designed PATCH endpoint can be idempotent by using absolute values rather than deltas[reference:2].

Why does idempotence matter in interviews? Because retries are unavoidable. Network timeouts, load balancer 502s, and client crashes happen. If a client retries a GET, nothing changes. If a client retries a DELETE, the second call returns 404 but the resource is still deleted — the effect is the same. If a client retries a POST to create an order, two orders are created unless the server implements idempotency keys (covered in a separate card). This is why the HTTP specification's idempotence guarantee is the foundation of safe retry logic, and why non-idempotent POST requires application-level protection[reference:3].

Status codes are the server's three-digit verdict, and precision matters in interviews. 200 OK is success with a body; 201 Created is success for POST and must include a Location header pointing to the new resource; 204 No Content is success with no body, typical for DELETE or a PUT that returns nothing. 400 Bad Request means malformed syntax or invalid parameters; 401 Unauthorized means authentication is missing or invalid (the client is not logged in); 403 Forbidden means authentication succeeded but authorization failed (logged in, no permission); 404 Not Found means the resource does not exist; 409 Conflict means a state conflict such as a duplicate or a version mismatch; 422 Unprocessable Entity means the syntax is valid but the semantics are invalid (business rule violation); 429 Too Many Requests means rate limited, and should include Retry-After; 500 is a generic server error; 502 Bad Gateway means an upstream returned an invalid response; 503 Service Unavailable means the server is down or overloaded and should include Retry-After[reference:4][reference:5]. The interview trap is to use 400 for validation failures — many teams standardize on 422 for semantic validation and reserve 400 for malformed syntax, but consistency matters more than the specific choice.

The strongest interview answer names the six constraints (not just 'REST means JSON over HTTP'), precisely distinguishes safe from idempotent with POST and PATCH as counterexamples, and explains why idempotence is the contract that makes retries safe.
bullets: REST has six constraints: Client-Server, Statelessness, Cacheability, Uniform Interface, Layered System, and optional Code on Demand.
Safe methods do not change server state: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS. Idempotent methods produce the same state when called multiple times: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, DELETE.
POST is neither safe nor idempotent — two identical POSTs create two resources unless the server enforces idempotency keys.
PATCH is not inherently idempotent: a delta operation (increment) is not idempotent; an absolute-value operation (set name) is.
Idempotence is what makes retries safe — network failures and 502s force clients to retry, and non-idempotent methods need application-level protection.
Status code precision: 201 (POST + Location), 204 (DELETE/PUT no body), 401 (not authenticated) vs 403 (not authorized), 409 (conflict), 422 (semantic validation), 429 (rate limit + Retry-After).
cards.code:
REST constraints

  1. Client-Server       UI and data store evolve independently
  2. Stateless           every request carries all needed context
  3. Cacheable           responses declare Cache-Control / ETag
  4. Uniform Interface    resource IDs in URI, JSON representations
  5. Layered System       client cannot tell proxy from origin
  6. Code on Demand       optional: server sends executable code

Safe vs Idempotent

  Method   Safe   Idempotent   Example
  ------   ----   ----------   -------
  GET      Yes    Yes          GET /users/42
  HEAD     Yes    Yes          HEAD /users/42
  OPTIONS  Yes    Yes          OPTIONS /users
  PUT      No     Yes          PUT /users/42 { full body }
  DELETE   No     Yes          DELETE /users/42
  POST     No     No           POST /users { new user }
  PATCH    No     No*          PATCH /users/42 { op: increment }

  *PATCH can be idempotent if the operation uses absolute values
   (set name=X) rather than deltas (increment counter by 1).

Why idempotence matters

  Timeout -> client retries GET   -> safe, no change
  Timeout -> client retries DELETE -> second 404, resource still gone
  Timeout -> client retries POST   -> SECOND RESOURCE CREATED
                                    -> need idempotency key

Status code ladder (common set)

  200 OK            success with body
  201 Created       POST success + Location header
  204 No Content    DELETE or empty PUT success
  400 Bad Request   malformed syntax / invalid parameters
  401 Unauthorized  not authenticated (no/bad token)
  403 Forbidden     authenticated but not authorized
  404 Not Found     resource does not exist
  409 Conflict      duplicate or version mismatch
  422 Unprocessable valid syntax, semantic/business rule failure
  429 Too Many      rate limited; include Retry-After
  500 Internal      generic server error
  502 Bad Gateway   upstream invalid response
  503 Unavailable   server down/overloaded; include Retry-After

cards.title: Resource Modeling and URI Design: Nouns, Plural Collections, Nesting Depth, and Versioning
cards.summary:
A REST API is a map of resources, not a list of remote procedures. The first rule is: URIs identify resources (nouns), HTTP methods express actions (verbs). GET /users/42, POST /users, PUT /users/42, DELETE /users/42 — the method tells you what happens, the URI tells you what it happens to. The anti-pattern is verbs in the URI: POST /createUser, POST /getUser, GET /user?action=delete. These treat HTTP as a transport for RPC, which defeats caching, uniform tooling, and the whole point of REST[reference:6].

Collections are plural nouns in lowercase kebab-case: /users, /orders, /shipping-addresses, /order-items. A single resource is the collection plus an identifier: /users/42. Use plural consistently — /users for the collection, /users/42 for one member. Do not mix /user and /users across endpoints. For singleton sub-resources that exist per user (the current user's profile), a singular path is acceptable: /me/profile or /user-profile — but the collection naming rule still holds for any resource that can have many instances[reference:7].

Nesting expresses relationships: /users/42/orders means 'the orders belonging to user 42'. The rule is: nest only when the child cannot be identified without the parent, or when the relationship is genuinely hierarchical. Do not nest more than two to three levels deep. A path like /companies/123/departments/456/teams/789/members/012/tasks/345 is unreadable, hard to cache correctly, and forces every client to carry five parent IDs to reach a task. The fix is to promote the deep resource to a top-level collection with a filter: /tasks/345?member=012&team=789. The canonical URL for a resource should be stable and shallow; nesting is for traversal, not for permanent identity[reference:8][reference:9].

Filtering, sorting, and field selection belong in query parameters, not in path segments. GET /orders?status=shipped&sort=-created_at&fields=id,total is correct; GET /orders/shipped is not. Query parameters are optional modifiers on a collection, not new resources. Pagination is also a query-parameter concern, covered separately — but the URI shape stays clean: /orders?cursor=abc&limit=25.

Versioning is the most debated URI design decision. There are four common strategies. URI path versioning (/api/v1/users) is the most common because it is visible, easy to route, and easy to cache; its cost is that it is not 'RESTful pure' — the URI now includes a version that is not a resource. Query-parameter versioning (/api/users?version=1) keeps paths clean but pollutes the query string and makes routing and caching awkward. Header versioning (X-API-Version: 1 or Accept-Version: v1) keeps URIs clean but requires every client to set a header correctly. Media-type versioning (Accept: application/vnd.myapi.v1+json) is the purist approach — the representation format carries the version — but it is the hardest for clients and intermediaries to get right. The pragmatic industry answer: use URI path versioning for public APIs where clients need clarity, and header or media-type versioning for internal APIs where you control every client. In all cases, version for breaking changes only; additive changes (new optional fields, new endpoints) should not require a version bump[reference:10][reference:11].

HATEOAS (Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State) deserves a mention because interviewers ask about it. In a fully HATEOAS API, responses include links to related actions: an order response contains a link to cancel it, a link to its invoice, and a link to the next page. Clients navigate by following links rather than hardcoding URIs. In practice, most public APIs do not implement HATEOAS fully because the cost is high and the benefit (client decoupling) is rarely realized when clients are written by the same organization. A strong interview answer acknowledges HATEOAS as the purist ideal, explains why it is rarely implemented, and focuses on the practical rules above.

The interview-quality answer names the noun/verb rule, the plural-kebab convention, the two-to-three-level nesting limit with the flatten-to-query-parameter fix, and the versioning trade-offs. It also notes that filtering/sorting belong in query parameters, not in paths. That shows you can design an API, not just consume one.
bullets: URIs identify resources (nouns); HTTP methods express actions (verbs). /users/42 is correct; /getUser is the RPC anti-pattern.
Collections are plural lowercase kebab-case: /users, /shipping-addresses. A single resource is /users/42.
Nest only for genuine relationships, and limit depth to 2–3 levels. Beyond that, flatten to a top-level collection with filter parameters: /tasks/345?team=789.
Filtering, sorting, and field selection belong in query parameters, not in path segments: /orders?status=shipped&sort=-created_at.
Versioning strategies: URI path (most common, visible), query param (pollutes), header (clean but client-dependent), media type (purist, hard).
Version only for breaking changes — additive changes (new optional fields, new endpoints) should not require a new version.
HATEOAS is the purist ideal (responses include links to related actions) but is rarely implemented in full; mention it with the cost/benefit trade-off.
cards.code:
Resource-oriented URIs

  GET    /users              list users
  POST   /users              create user
  GET    /users/42           get user 42
  PUT    /users/42           replace user 42
  PATCH  /users/42           partial update user 42
  DELETE /users/42           delete user 42

  GET    /users/42/orders    orders belonging to user 42
  GET    /orders/789         direct access to order 789

Anti-patterns

  POST /getUser              verb in URI
  POST /createUser           verb in URI
  GET  /user?action=delete   action as query param
  /userProfiles              camelCase
  /user_profiles             snake_case
  /companies/1/depts/2/teams/3/members/4/tasks/5   too deep

Nesting depth rule

  GOOD  /users/42/orders
  GOOD  /users/42/orders/789
  BAD   /users/42/orders/789/items/012/reviews/345
  FIX   /reviews/345?order=789&item=012

Query parameters for modifiers

  GET /orders?status=shipped&sort=-created_at&limit=25&cursor=abc
  GET /users?role=admin&fields=id,name,email

Versioning strategies

  URI path        /api/v1/users          visible, cacheable, not pure REST
  Query param     /api/users?version=1   clean path, awkward routing
  Header          X-API-Version: 1       clean URL, client must set header
  Media type      Accept: application/vnd.myapi.v1+json   purist, hardest

  Public API  -> URI path versioning
  Internal API -> header or media type

cards.title: Offset vs Cursor Pagination: O(n) Deep Pages, Page Drift, and the Keyset Fix
cards.summary:
Every list endpoint eventually paginates, and the choice between offset and cursor pagination is a classic interview discriminator because it exposes whether a candidate understands database performance, not just API syntax.

Offset pagination is the tutorial default. The client sends page=3&per_page=25; the server runs LIMIT 25 OFFSET 50. It is trivial to implement, and it supports jumping to any page — a feature users expect in admin tables. The first structural problem is page drift. OFFSET counts rows from the top of the result, not from 'where the client left off'. If three new orders are inserted between page 1 and page 2, the rows the user just saw are pushed down, and page 2 repeats them. If three rows are deleted from page 1, page 2 silently skips three rows the user never saw. For a static report nobody scrolls in real time, drift is harmless; for an activity feed, a sync endpoint, or anything walked by a script while writes continue, drift means duplicates or missing records, and no error is returned[reference:12].

The second structural problem is deep-offset cost. OFFSET 500000 does not teleport to row 500,001. The database must scan and discard every row before the offset. For a primary-key-ordered table this is O(n) in the offset depth; on a table with a join or a sort, it is worse. Benchmarks commonly show cursor pagination 17× faster than offset pagination on a million-row dataset, and the gap widens as depth grows. The root cause is that offset is not using the index to jump — it is using the index to count, and counting is proportional to the offset[reference:13][reference:14].

Cursor pagination (also called keyset pagination) fixes both problems by replacing 'skip N rows' with 'start after this row'. The server returns a cursor — an opaque token that encodes the last row's sort key (and a unique tiebreaker). The client sends cursor=abc for the next page. The database runs WHERE (sort_key, id) > (last_sort_key, last_id) ORDER BY sort_key, id LIMIT 25. Because the query seeks directly into the index at the last position, each page is O(log n) or O(1) with the right index — independent of how deep the page is. Because the predicate is anchored to a row, inserts and deletes do not shift the window, so page drift disappears: the client sees a stable sequence even while writes continue[reference:15][reference:16].

The non-obvious implementation trap is the tiebreaker. A cursor built on a non-unique column (created_at, status) can skip or duplicate rows when multiple rows share the same value. The fix is to append a unique column — usually the primary key id — as the final sort key and include it in the cursor. The sort order becomes (created_at DESC, id DESC), and the WHERE predicate becomes (created_at, id) < (last_created_at, last_id). The index must match the sort order: an index on (created_at DESC, id DESC). Without this matching index, the cursor query falls back to a sort and loses its performance advantage[reference:17][reference:18].

What you give up with cursor pagination is jump-to-page and total count. The client cannot ask for 'page 47' because there is no page — there is only a cursor. If the UI genuinely needs a total count, run a separate COUNT query (which is O(n) on large tables) or maintain a cached counter. For infinite scroll, activity feeds, search results, and large exports, cursor is the right choice. For small admin tables, settings lists, and any UI with numbered pages, offset is acceptable and simpler[reference:19].

In an interview, name the two problems (drift and deep-offset cost), state the keyset query shape, insist on the unique tiebreaker and matching index, and state the trade-off (no jump-to-page, no total count). That is the complete answer.
bullets: Offset pagination uses LIMIT/OFFSET; simple, supports jump-to-page, but has page drift and O(n) deep-offset cost.
Page drift: inserts or deletes between pages shift the window — the client sees duplicates or misses rows, silently.
Deep-offset cost: OFFSET 500000 makes the database scan 500,000 rows to discard them; cost grows with depth.
Cursor (keyset) pagination anchors to the last row: WHERE (sort_key, id) > (last_key, last_id) — O(log n) per page via the index, stable under writes.
The cursor must include a unique tiebreaker (primary key) as the final sort key; without it, non-unique sort columns skip or duplicate rows.
The index must match the sort order: (created_at DESC, id DESC) for a cursor sorted by created_at then id.
Trade-off: cursor gives up jump-to-page and total count; offset is acceptable for small admin tables, cursor is mandatory for feeds, search, and large exports.
cards.code:
Offset pagination

  GET /orders?page=3&per_page=25

  SELECT id, customer_id, total_cents, created_at
  FROM orders
  ORDER BY created_at DESC
  LIMIT 25 OFFSET 50;

  -- OFFSET 500000 scans 500,000 rows before returning page 20,001
  -- page drift: new rows push old rows down -> duplicates
  -- deletions pull rows up -> missed records

Cursor (keyset) pagination

  GET /orders?cursor=eyJjcmVhdGVkX2F0IjoiMjAyNi0wOC0zMFQxNDoyMjowN1oiLCJpZCI6ODgyMX0&limit=25

  SELECT id, customer_id, total_cents, created_at
  FROM orders
  WHERE (created_at, id) < (:last_created_at, :last_id)
  ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
  LIMIT 25;

  -- seeks into index at the last row's position
  -- O(log n) per page, independent of depth
  -- stable under concurrent writes

Required index

  CREATE INDEX idx_orders_created_id
    ON orders (created_at DESC, id DESC);

  -- index order MUST match ORDER BY order

Cursor payload (opaque to client)

  {
    "created_at": "2026-08-30T14:22:07Z",
    "id": 8821
  }
  -- base64-encoded, client treats as opaque token

Trade-offs

  Offset                      Cursor
  ----------------------      ----------------------
  jump to page 47             forward-only (or backward with prev cursor)
  total count available       separate COUNT query or cached counter
  simple SQL                  moderate: encoding, tiebreaker, index
  O(n) at depth               O(log n) per page
  drifts under writes         stable under writes
  small admin tables          feeds, search, infinite scroll, exports

cards.title: Error Contracts and Idempotency Keys: RFC 7807 Problem Details and the Stripe Retry Pattern
cards.summary:
Two API design concerns are asked together in senior interviews because both are about making failures predictable. The first is the error contract: when a request fails, what exactly does the client receive, and can the client parse it programmatically without reverse-engineering your messages? The second is idempotency keys: when a client retries a non-idempotent POST, how does the server avoid doing the work twice?

The error contract problem is that every team invents its own error shape. One service returns { "error": "not found" }, another returns { "message": "...", "code": 404 }, a third returns { "errors": [{ "field": "email", "message": "invalid" }] }. Clients end up with a per-service parser. RFC 7807 (Problem Details for HTTP APIs) standardizes the shape. The media type is application/problem+json, and the body has five standard members: type (a stable URI that identifies the problem type), title (a human-readable summary), status (the HTTP status code duplicated in the body), detail (a human-readable explanation specific to this occurrence), and instance (a URI that identifies this specific occurrence, useful for support tickets). Extensions are allowed: a validation error can add an errors array with field-level details. The type URI is the machine-readable identifier — clients can switch on it without parsing prose. The instance URI lets support trace a specific failure. The status member duplicates the HTTP status code, but RFC 7807 itself warns that intermediaries (proxies, load balancers) may not respect the body's status — the HTTP status line is the authoritative one[reference:20].

The practical rule for a strong error contract is: use RFC 7807 for every error response, make the type URI stable and documented, include a correlation ID (often in the instance URI or a separate header) for tracing, and never leak stack traces or internal implementation details. Validation errors should include a machine-readable field list, not just a prose message. A 422 with a problem+json body containing errors: [{ field: "email", code: "invalid_format" }] lets the client highlight the field without string matching[reference:21][reference:22].

Idempotency keys solve the retry problem for POST. The client generates a unique key (a UUID v4 is the standard recommendation) and sends it in the Idempotency-Key header. The server stores the key alongside the response it produced, in a durable store (Redis, a database table) with a TTL. When a retry arrives with the same key, the server returns the stored response instead of executing the operation again. Stripe's implementation — the de facto reference — stores the status code and body of the first request after endpoint execution begins; retries with the same key return the saved response, including 500 errors. The key must be unique per logical operation, not per HTTP attempt. If the client retries a payment, it reuses the same key; if it makes a genuinely new payment, it generates a new key. Stripe recommends UUIDs or another random string with enough entropy to avoid collisions, and warns against using sensitive data (email addresses, personal identifiers) as keys. Keys are up to 255 characters and are pruned after at least 24 hours in API v1; a key reused after pruning starts a new request. The idempotency layer also compares the incoming parameters to the original request and errors if they differ — this prevents a client from accidentally reusing a key for a different operation[reference:23][reference:24].

The subtle failure mode is the dual-write gap. If the server executes the operation, then crashes before storing the idempotency record, a retry will re-execute the operation — duplicate charge. The fix is to store the idempotency record in the same database transaction as the domain change, so either both succeed or neither does. This is the same pattern as the inbox table in the Kafka cards: the idempotency key is the deduplication key, and the domain write and the dedup record commit atomically. If the operation calls an external system (a payment provider), the external call must also accept the same idempotency key — Stripe, for example, accepts Idempotency-Key on its own API, so the retry chain is deduplicated end to end[reference:25].

In an interview, name both halves: the error contract (RFC 7807 with stable type URIs, validation field details, and no leaked internals) and the idempotency key pattern (client-generated UUID, server-side stored response, TTL, parameter comparison, atomic dedup record). Mention Stripe as the production reference and the dual-write gap as the subtle failure. That shows you have designed APIs that survive retries, not just happy-path APIs.
bullets: RFC 7807 Problem Details standardizes error responses: application/problem+json with type, title, status, detail, and instance — plus extension fields like errors[] for validation.
The type URI is the machine-readable identifier; clients switch on it instead of parsing prose. The instance URI identifies a specific occurrence for support tracing.
Never leak stack traces or internal details in error responses — RFC 7807 explicitly warns about information disclosure.
Idempotency keys make POST retries safe: the client sends a unique key (UUID v4) in Idempotency-Key, the server stores the response, and a retry returns the stored response instead of re-executing.
The key must be unique per logical operation, not per HTTP attempt — reuse it for retries, generate a new one for a new operation.
The dual-write gap is the subtle failure: store the idempotency record in the same transaction as the domain change, or a crash between the two causes a duplicate on retry.
Stripe is the reference implementation: stores status and body after execution, returns the saved response on retry, compares parameters, prunes keys after 24 hours.
cards.code:
RFC 7807 error response

  HTTP/1.1 422 Unprocessable Entity
  Content-Type: application/problem+json

  {
    "type": "https://api.example.com/errors/validation",
    "title": "Validation failed",
    "status": 422,
    "detail": "The request body contains invalid fields.",
    "instance": "/orders/req_8f3a2c1e",
    "errors": [
      { "field": "email", "code": "invalid_format" },
      { "field": "amount", "code": "must_be_positive" }
    ]
  }

  -- type is stable and documented; clients switch on it
  -- instance identifies this occurrence for support
  -- status duplicates HTTP status, but HTTP status line is authoritative

Idempotency key flow (Stripe-style)

  Client                          Server
  ------                          ------
  POST /charges
  Idempotency-Key: 9f2a-...
  { amount: 100 }   ----------->  check key store
                                   if key exists:
                                     return stored response
                                   else:
                                     execute operation
                                     store key + response (TTL 24h)
                                     return response

  retry POST /charges
  Idempotency-Key: 9f2a-...
  { amount: 100 }   ----------->  key exists -> return stored response
                                   (no second charge)

Key rules

  unique per logical operation (not per attempt)
  UUID v4 or high-entropy random string
  do not use sensitive data (email, personal id) as key
  parameter comparison: same key + different body = error
  TTL: at least 24h (Stripe prunes after 24h in API v1)

Dual-write gap (the subtle bug)

  BEGIN;
    INSERT INTO charges(id, amount) VALUES (...);
    INSERT INTO idempotency_keys(key, response) VALUES (...);
  COMMIT;
  -- both succeed or neither does -> retry sees the key

  BAD:
    charge succeeded
    CRASH before INSERT INTO idempotency_keys
    retry -> key missing -> charge again -> duplicate

cards.title: RPC vs REST: Remote Procedure Calls, the Fallacies They Expose, and When RPC Wins
cards.summary:
Remote Procedure Call (RPC) is the oldest API style: a client invokes a method on a stub that looks like a local object, and the stub serializes the arguments, sends them over the network to a server, deserializes them, invokes the real method, and returns the result. To the caller, it feels like a local function call — getUserById(42) — even though the work happened on another machine. RPC predates REST by decades (Sun RPC, DCE, CORBA, Java RMI, SOAP), and modern gRPC is its most refined incarnation.

The reason REST became the default for public APIs is that RPC's illusion of locality is dangerous. The classic essay 'Fallacies of Distributed Computing' lists the assumptions that RPC encourages: the network is reliable, latency is zero, bandwidth is infinite, the network is secure, topology does not change, one administrator exists, transport cost is zero, and the network is homogeneous. Every one of these is false in real distributed systems. RPC's surface makes them feel true: if a local method call can throw an exception, an RPC call should too (it can, but the failure modes are entirely different — network partition, retry duplication, partial failure, unknown commit state). REST's resource-oriented style surfaces the network (HTTP status codes, idempotence rules, cacheability) and makes failures explicit. That is why REST is preferred for public, browser-facing, and cacheable APIs.

The counterargument for RPC is equally strong: for internal service-to-service calls where both sides are controlled, the resource model is artificial. Why should I model 'get the user's shipping address for order 42' as a resource with a URI and cache headers? It is a procedure — take an order ID, return an address. Modeling it as POST /getShippingAddress or GET /orders/42/shipping-address adds REST ceremony (noun-based URIs, careful status codes, hypermedia) without any real benefit — nobody caches it, nobody bookmarks it, no third party consumes it. RPC lets me write ShippingService.getAddress(orderId) and move on. This is why large tech companies (Google, Netflix, Uber, Facebook) use RPC — gRPC or Thrift — for most internal traffic and reserve REST for public APIs.

The decision matrix in one place: REST wins for public APIs (cacheable, discoverable, tooling-rich — curl, Postman, browsers), browser clients (native HTTP support, no code generation), and resource-oriented domains (CRUD, documents, catalogs). RPC wins for internal service-to-service calls (high throughput, low latency, strongly typed contracts, code generation), polyglot environments (protobuf schema shared across Java, Go, Python, Rust), streaming workloads (gRPC bidirectional streaming, which REST does not model well), and performance-critical paths (binary encoding, HTTP/2 multiplexing). GraphQL is a third style worth mentioning: it is neither RPC nor REST — it is a query language over a graph, best for aggregating multiple services for a UI (covered in a separate card).

The practical rule that senior engineers use: use REST for anything external or human-facing, use RPC for anything internal and performance-sensitive, and never let RPC's method-call syntax hide the network. In an interview, name the fallacies (reliable network, zero latency, infinite bandwidth), explain why REST surfaces the network while RPC hides it, and give the decision matrix. A candidate who says 'RPC is bad because REST is modern' or 'REST is slow, use gRPC for everything' is missing the nuance — the answer is contextual, and the strongest candidates demonstrate judgment.
bullets: RPC makes a remote call look like a local method call: stub serializes arguments, sends over network, deserializes on server, invokes real method, returns result.
RPC's illusion of locality is dangerous — it encourages the fallacies of distributed computing (reliable network, zero latency, infinite bandwidth).
REST surfaces the network (status codes, idempotence, cacheability) and is the default for public, browser-facing, and cacheable APIs.
RPC wins for internal service-to-service calls: strongly typed contracts, code generation, binary encoding, streaming, and no resource-model ceremony for procedural operations.
Real-world pattern: big tech uses gRPC/Thrift for internal traffic and REST for public APIs.
GraphQL is a third style — a query language over a graph — best for UI aggregation, not a replacement for REST or RPC.
Never let RPC hide the network: timeouts, retries, idempotency, and partial failure still apply.

cards.title: gRPC Internals: HTTP/2, Protocol Buffers, and the Four Streaming Modes
cards.summary:
gRPC is Google's open-source RPC framework, built on two technology choices that determine everything about its performance and behavior. The first is HTTP/2 as the transport. HTTP/2 gives gRPC multiplexing (many concurrent RPCs on one TCP connection, with no head-of-line blocking at the HTTP layer), header compression (HPACK, which makes the many small request/response headers cheap), binary framing (no more text parsing), flow control per stream, and server push (used for streaming). HTTP/1.1 required a new TCP connection per request or pipelining workarounds; HTTP/2 multiplexes hundreds of RPCs on one connection, which is why gRPC throughput per connection is orders of magnitude higher. gRPC over HTTP/1.1 is technically possible but loses most of the benefits.

The second choice is Protocol Buffers as the interface definition and serialization format. A .proto file defines messages (structured data) and services (RPC methods). The protoc compiler generates client stubs and server skeletons for any supported language — Java, Go, Python, C++, Rust, Ruby, C#, JavaScript, and more. Protobuf serialization is compact (fields are tagged with numbers, not names; variable-length integers; no JSON braces or quotes), fast (no reflection, schema compiled into code), and schema-evolution-friendly (fields can be added with new tag numbers, and unknown fields are preserved by the runtime). A typical protobuf payload is 3–10× smaller than JSON and 2–5× faster to serialize. The .proto file is the contract; both client and server are generated from it, so drift is impossible unless you skip regeneration.

gRPC supports four communication patterns, and knowing all four is interview table stakes. Unary: one request, one response — the same as a normal REST call. Server streaming: one request, many responses — the client asks for a feed and the server streams events as they happen. Client streaming: many requests, one response — the client uploads a stream of records and the server returns a summary. Bidirectional streaming: both sides send independent streams — used for chat, real-time sync, collaborative editing, and long-lived connections where both sides push data. In Java, the generated stub exposes a blocking variant (unary and server-streaming) and an async stub (all four patterns with StreamObserver callbacks).

Deadlines and cancellation are first-class in gRPC, and this is what makes it operationally superior to most RPC frameworks. Every RPC can carry a deadline (a point in time, not a duration) which propagates across the call graph — if service A calls B calls C, all three share a deadline budget. When the deadline expires, the whole chain is cancelled, and gRPC returns DEADLINE_EXCEEDED. This prevents the classic cascade where a slow downstream holds resources across every layer. Cancellation works the same way: if the client cancels, the server's Context.isCancelled() returns true and the server can stop work. The context carries this state; the server must check it in long-running loops or streaming handlers to avoid wasting cycles after the client has gone.

The operational details interviewers probe: gRPC uses HTTP/2 trailers to send status after the body, so error handling is separate from HTTP status codes — the response status is one of sixteen canonical gRPC codes (OK, CANCELLED, UNKNOWN, INVALID_ARGUMENT, DEADLINE_EXCEEDED, NOT_FOUND, ALREADY_EXISTS, PERMISSION_DENIED, RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED, FAILED_PRECONDITION, ABORTED, OUT_OF_RANGE, UNIMPLEMENTED, INTERNAL, UNAVAILABLE, DATA_LOSS). The mapping to HTTP is lossy — a gRPC error is not a REST status code and must not be treated as one. Metadata (headers) can carry auth tokens, trace IDs, and custom key-value pairs, and is accessible via MetadataUtils. Reflection is available for tooling (grpcurl) but should usually be disabled in production for security.

In an interview, name the two foundational choices (HTTP/2 + Protobuf), the four streaming modes with a use case for each, and the two features that elevate gRPC over naive RPC (deadlines with propagation, cancellation). That shows you understand gRPC as a system, not just as 'faster JSON'.
bullets: gRPC runs on HTTP/2 (multiplexing, HPACK header compression, binary framing) and uses Protocol Buffers for serialization and schema.
Protobuf is compact (tag numbers, varints), fast (compiled, no reflection), and schema-evolution-friendly (new tag numbers, unknown fields preserved).
Four streaming modes: unary (1-to-1), server streaming (1-to-many), client streaming (many-to-1), bidirectional streaming (many-to-many).
Deadlines propagate across the call graph — every downstream service shares the remaining budget; expiry cancels the whole chain.
Cancellation is explicit via Context.isCancelled(); long-running handlers must check it to avoid wasting work after the client leaves.
Errors use sixteen canonical gRPC status codes, delivered in HTTP/2 trailers — not REST status codes.
Metadata carries auth tokens and trace IDs; reflection (grpcurl) should be disabled in production.

cards.title: gRPC Trade-offs and Load Balancing: Long-Lived Connections vs L4 Proxies
cards.summary:
gRPC's performance comes with operational costs that interviewers love to probe because they expose whether you have actually run it in production. The biggest surprise for teams migrating from REST is load balancing: gRPC's long-lived HTTP/2 connections break the classic L4 (TCP) load balancer model, and fixing this requires understanding how HTTP/2 works at the connection level.

The root cause is HTTP/2 connection reuse. A gRPC client opens one (or a few) TCP connections to a server and multiplexes all RPCs over them for the lifetime of the connection — hours, sometimes days. An L4 load balancer (AWS NLB, an IPVS-based service, a Kubernetes Service of type LoadBalancer) distributes TCP connections, not requests. If a client opens one connection and sends ten thousand RPCs over it, all ten thousand go to the same backend pod because they share one TCP connection. Meanwhile, other pods sit idle. This is connection-level stickiness by accident: you did not configure sticky sessions, but you got them anyway because gRPC reuses connections.

The fix is L7 load balancing, which understands HTTP/2 and can distribute individual streams, not just connections. There are three common approaches. First, use an L7 proxy — Envoy, NGINX, HAProxy, or a service mesh sidecar (Istio, Linkerd) — between the client and the backend. The client connects to the proxy; the proxy maintains multiple connections to backends and load-balances per-request. This is the standard pattern in Kubernetes: gRPC services sit behind a service mesh, and Envoy handles the balancing. Second, use client-side load balancing: the client is given the list of backend addresses (via DNS, a service registry, or a control plane) and creates a subchannel per backend; the gRPC client library itself balances across the subchannels. This is the pattern gRPC was designed for, and it is what Google uses internally. Third, use a purpose-built L7 load balancer like Google Cloud's gRPC-aware load balancing or AWS's ALB (with HTTP/2 support) — but ALB terminates HTTP/2 and re-encodes, which loses end-to-end streaming benefits unless you enable end-to-end HTTP/2.

The second major trade-off is browser support. Browsers do not expose HTTP/2 framing APIs to JavaScript, so a browser cannot speak gRPC natively. The workaround is gRPC-Web — a translation layer that runs as a proxy (Envoy, or a purpose-built gateway) and converts gRPC-Web (browser-friendly HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 with a different framing) to native gRPC on the backend. This adds a hop and a proxy to maintain. If a service must be callable from browsers, you either accept gRPC-Web + proxy or expose a REST/JSON gateway alongside it (grpc-gateway generates the REST endpoints from the .proto). Either way, gRPC-only is a server-to-server decision.

The third trade-off is debugging and observability. A gRPC error is a status code in HTTP/2 trailers, not the HTTP status line — so curl and browser devtools do not show it. grpcurl is the standard CLI (grpcurl -d '{"orderId": 42}' server:50051 order.OrderService/GetOrder), and reflection must be enabled on the server. Tracing works the same as REST (propagate trace IDs in metadata), but distributed tracing tools need to be configured for gRPC interceptors. Metrics come from interceptors — request count, latency histogram by method, error codes — the same categories as REST but keyed by full method name (/order.OrderService/GetOrder) rather than URI.

The fourth trade-off is schema evolution and deployment coupling. Protobuf allows adding fields with new tag numbers, but removing fields or changing types is breaking. Two services that share a .proto file must be deployed with compatible versions, and the contract is harder to see than JSON (a .proto file is not curl-able). The discipline is: add fields, never remove; reserve removed tag numbers; version the service name (order.v1.OrderService, order.v2.OrderService) for breaking changes; and use buf to lint and detect breaking changes in CI.

The fifth trade-off is resource management. HTTP/2 connections are long-lived, which means graceful shutdown is harder — you must send GOAWAY, drain in-flight streams, then close. gRPC's ServerBuilder exposes this: server.shutdown() sends GOAWAY and waits, but Kubernetes readiness probes must fail before shutdown so the load balancer stops routing new traffic. Misconfigured, this causes 5xx errors on every deploy.

In an interview, name the L4 stickiness problem and the L7 solution (proxy or client-side LB), the browser problem (gRPC-Web + proxy), the debugging problem (grpcurl, reflection, trailers), and the schema-evolution discipline. That demonstrates operational experience, not just syntax.
bullets: gRPC's long-lived HTTP/2 connections break L4 (TCP) load balancers — one client connection sends all RPCs to one backend pod, leaving others idle.
The fix is L7 load balancing: Envoy/NGINX/HAProxy sidecar (service mesh) or client-side load balancing with a subchannel per backend.
Browsers cannot speak gRPC natively — use gRPC-Web + a proxy (Envoy) or generate a REST gateway (grpc-gateway) for browser-facing services.
Debugging is harder: errors live in HTTP/2 trailers, not the HTTP status line — use grpcurl with reflection enabled.
Metrics and tracing need gRPC interceptors — request count, latency histogram by full method name, error code.
Schema evolution discipline: add fields (never remove), reserve removed tags, version the service name for breaking changes, lint with buf.
Graceful shutdown requires GOAWAY + readiness probe failure before shutdown; misconfiguration causes 5xx on every deploy.
cards.code:
Problem: L4 load balancing breaks gRPC

  Client --(one TCP/HTTP2 conn)--> [L4 LB] --> Backend Pod A
                                                  (all RPCs go here)
                                              Backend Pod B (idle)
                                              Backend Pod C (idle)

  L4 LB distributes TCP connections, not RPCs.
  gRPC reuses one connection -> one pod gets 100% of traffic.

Solution 1: L7 proxy (service mesh / Envoy)

  Client --HTTP2--> [Envoy sidecar] --HTTP2--> Backend Pod A
                                    --HTTP2--> Backend Pod B
                                    --HTTP2--> Backend Pod C

  Envoy multiplexes per-stream and load-balances per-RPC.
  Standard pattern in Istio / Linkerd / Kubernetes.

Solution 2: client-side LB (gRPC-native)

  Client is given backend list (DNS SRV, control plane).
  Creates a subchannel per backend, balances across them.
  This is what Google uses internally.

Browser problem

  Browsers cannot speak gRPC (no HTTP/2 framing access).
  Options:
    1. gRPC-Web + Envoy proxy (translates framing)
    2. grpc-gateway (generates REST/JSON from .proto)

Debugging

  grpcurl -d '{"orderId": 42}' \
    -plaintext server:50051 order.OrderService/GetOrder

  Requires reflection enabled on the server:
    ServerBuilder.forPort(50051)
                 .addService(ServerInterceptors.intercept(svc, ...))
                 .addService(ProtoReflectionService.newInstance());

Graceful shutdown

  1. readiness probe fails -> LB stops routing
  2. server.shutdown() sends GOAWAY
  3. in-flight streams complete
  4. server.awaitTermination(timeout)

Schema evolution

  ADD:    field with new tag number (old readers skip unknown tags)
  RESERVE: removed tag numbers (reserved 3, 5 to 10;)
  VERSION: order.v1.OrderService -> order.v2.OrderService for breaking
  LINT:   buf lint / buf breaking in CI

cards.title: ServiceTalk (Netflix): A JVM Networking Framework Built on Netty, Unifying HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and gRPC
cards.summary:
ServiceTalk is Netflix's open-source JVM networking framework, built on top of Netty (the event-driven, non-blocking I/O library that everything from gRPC to Cassandra to Elasticsearch uses). ServiceTalk's thesis is that application servers, clients, and protocol details should not be separate concerns — a single framework should provide HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and gRPC APIs on a shared, reactive, Netty-based foundation. The JD you are interviewing for names ServiceTalk explicitly, so understanding what it is and why it exists is a differentiator.

The problem ServiceTalk solves is protocol proliferation in a microservices fleet. A large company like Netflix uses HTTP/1.1 for legacy services, HTTP/2 for modern internal calls, and gRPC for high-performance service-to-service.
