Without a unified framework, each protocol has its own client libraries, server containers, connection pools, load balancers, and observability integration. A team that wants to add tracing across all three protocols writes the same hook three times, in three different styles, with three subtly different behaviors. ServiceTalk's value proposition is one API style, one connection pool model, one observability story, one server lifecycle — across protocols. You write a ServiceTalk HTTP client or server and get HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 from the same code; you write a gRPC service and get the same lifecycle and observability integration.

The framework's design choices are what make it distinctive in interviews. ServiceTalk is reactive: request and response bodies are Publisher<Buffer> streams, and every operation returns a CompletableFuture-like asynchronous type. Backpressure is built in — a slow consumer does not buffer unboundedly. Serialization is pluggable: JSON (Jackson, Gson), Protobuf, Avro, Thrift, text, bytes — chosen per endpoint or globally. Connection pooling is a first-class concern: ServiceTalk owns the pool, so HTTP/2 multiplexing (many streams per connection) and HTTP/1.1 pipelining (limited) are handled by the framework, not by ad-hoc retry logic. Load balancing is built in as a first-class concept — the framework takes a service address and produces a client that balances across the instances it discovers. These are the same concerns gRPC forces you to solve with interceptors or external proxies; ServiceTalk bundles them.

Netflix's use of ServiceTalk is instructive. Netflix has been migrating from a traditional blocking HTTP stack to ServiceTalk for performance reasons — the reactive model handles high concurrency with fewer threads, and HTTP/2 multiplexing reduces connection overhead across the fleet. Internally, Netflix uses ServiceTalk for everything from API gateways to internal service-to-service calls, and it has become the foundation for much of their Java infrastructure. The framework's HTTP/2 support was a major driver — the fleet gained the multiplexing and header compression benefits without rewriting services.

The trade-off is that ServiceTalk is less famous than Spring MVC or gRPC, so the ecosystem is smaller. It does not have the same volume of tutorials, Stack Overflow answers, or third-party integrations. It is also a lower-level framework than Spring Boot — you write more code to get a working service. The payoff is performance, protocol flexibility, and full control over the networking layer. In an interview, the strongest answer is: 'ServiceTalk is Netflix's reactive networking framework on Netty. It unifies HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and gRPC on one API with first-class connection pooling, load balancing, and backpressure. Netflix uses it heavily for high-performance internal traffic. The trade-off is a smaller ecosystem than Spring or gRPC; it earns its place in fleets where protocol flexibility and reactive performance matter more than developer on-ramp speed.'
bullets: ServiceTalk is Netflix's open-source JVM networking framework built on Netty — a reactive, unified API for HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and gRPC.
Solves protocol proliferation: one connection pool, one load balancer, one observability story across protocols instead of three separate stacks.
Reactive by design: bodies are Publisher<Buffer> streams with backpressure; operations return CompletableFuture-like async results.
First-class connection pooling and load balancing — HTTP/2 multiplexing and instance discovery are framework concerns, not ad-hoc client code.
Pluggable serialization: JSON (Jackson/Gson), Protobuf, Avro, Thrift, text, raw bytes.
Netflix uses ServiceTalk for API gateways and internal service-to-service calls; the HTTP/2 migration was a major motivator.
Trade-off: smaller ecosystem than Spring MVC or gRPC; lower-level than Spring Boot, more code to write, but higher performance and protocol flexibility.

quizzes.question: A developer overrides equals() on a User class to compare by email but forgets to override hashCode(), then adds 100 users to a HashSet and two of them share the same email. What happens at insertion?
options: Both are stored because HashSet compares by reference and sees them as different objects
Only the first is stored because HashSet falls back to equals() when hashes collide
Both are stored because HashSet falls back to identity hashCode() from Object, so 'equal' users hash to different buckets and both get inserted
The second is rejected with an IllegalStateException
quizzes.explanation: HashSet uses a two-stage lookup: hashCode() finds the bucket, equals() finds the entry within it. Without overriding hashCode(), both users inherit Object's identity-based hashCode and hash to different buckets, so equals() is never consulted. Both are inserted, silently violating the Set's 'no duplicates' guarantee. Option B is wrong because with different hashCodes, equals is never even called.

quizzes.question: Given `Thread t = new Thread(() -> process()); t.run();`, what happens?
options: A new OS thread is created and process() runs on it
process() runs synchronously on the caller's thread; no new thread is created
t enters RUNNABLE state and process() runs asynchronously
The JVM throws IllegalThreadStateException
quizzes.explanation: run() is an ordinary method — calling it directly executes the task body on the calling thread, synchronously. Only start() asks the JVM to allocate a new OS thread and then invoke run() on it. The code compiles and runs without error, which is why this bug reaches production.

quizzes.question: You create a ThreadPoolExecutor with corePoolSize=10, maximumPoolSize=100, and a default LinkedBlockingQueue<>(). Under sustained load, active threads stay at 10 and the queue grows without limit. Why?
options: The pool forgot to set keepAliveTime, so extra threads time out
LinkedBlockingQueue's default constructor uses Integer.MAX_VALUE capacity, so the queue is never 'full' and maximumPoolSize is never triggered
ThreadPoolExecutor always caps at corePoolSize regardless of configuration
The rejection handler silently discards tasks, masking thread creation
quizzes.explanation: The task flow is: core threads → enqueue → only if queue is full and active < max, spawn more. With an unbounded queue, the enqueue step never fails, so max is never reached. This is why Executors.newFixedThreadPool (which uses exactly this unbounded queue) is unsafe for production — memory grows until OOM.

quizzes.question: A user-facing HTTP service submits jobs to Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10) with an unbounded queue. During a spike, 500k jobs queue up and the service runs out of memory. What is the correct fix?
options: Increase the pool size to 500,000 so all jobs run immediately
Replace with Executors.newCachedThreadPool so threads scale with load
Construct a ThreadPoolExecutor with a bounded ArrayBlockingQueue and an explicit CallerRunsPolicy for backpressure, plus timeouts on submission
Use ForkJoinPool.commonPool() for the jobs
quizzes.explanation: The root cause is the unbounded queue absorbing load until memory dies. A bounded queue plus CallerRunsPolicy gives natural backpressure — the submitting thread executes the task itself, slowing submission. Increasing pool size just delays the same failure; newCachedThreadPool replaces an unbounded queue with unbounded thread creation (thread-explosion OOM); ForkJoinPool.commonPool is shared and CPU-sized, which is even worse for IO jobs.

quizzes.question: A CompletableFuture pipeline has multiple thenApplyAsync stages, no exceptionally/handle/whenComplete attached anywhere, and one of the async stages throws a RuntimeException. What does the caller (who never calls get or join on the result) observe?
options: The exception propagates to the main thread and crashes the JVM
The exception is logged automatically by the JVM
Nothing — the CompletableFuture completes exceptionally and, without a handler attached downstream, the exception is silently swallowed
The pipeline automatically retries the failed stage
quizzes.explanation: CompletableFuture does not print or propagate exceptions. If no exceptionally, handle, or whenComplete is attached and the caller never inspects the future via get/join, the exception is lost — a classic production bug. Always attach a handler or ensure the result is awaited somewhere.

quizzes.question: A User class implements compareTo to sort by email, but equals() compares by id. You add two users with the same email but different ids to a TreeSet. What is the result?
options: Both are stored because equals() determines uniqueness
Only the first is stored — TreeSet uses compareTo (returns 0) to detect duplicates, silently dropping the second
TreeSet throws a ClassCastException at insertion
TreeSet falls back to hashCode() and stores both
quizzes.explanation: TreeSet is a red-black tree that uses compareTo/compare to place elements and to detect duplicates. When compareTo returns 0, the element is treated as a duplicate and not added — even though equals() would return false. This is why the contract requires compareTo/compare to be consistent with equals.

quizzes.question: What is the result of `String a = "hello"; String b = new String("hello"); System.out.println(a == b);`?
options: true — the compiler interns both strings to the same pool object
false — a is interned in the pool, b is a fresh heap object; == compares references
true — String overrides == to compare content
Compile error — you cannot compare Strings with ==
quizzes.explanation: String literals like "hello" are interned into the JVM's string pool at compile/class-load time and reference the same instance across the codebase. new String("hello") explicitly allocates a new object outside the pool. == compares references, so they are not equal. a.equals(b) returns true because content matches. You cannot override ==, so option C is wrong.

quizzes.question: A developer builds a 10,000-character log line with `String s = ""; for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) s += "x";` and it takes seconds. Why?
options: String concatenation always uses the String pool, which is slow under load
Each += allocates a new immutable String and copies all previous characters — O(n²) total work
The JIT compiler does not optimize String operations, so the loop runs in the interpreter
Concatenation triggers a Full GC on every iteration
quizzes.explanation: String is immutable: s += "x" is equivalent to s = new StringBuilder().append(s).append("x").toString() (roughly). Each iteration creates a new String of growing length and copies the entire previous content, so total work is 1+2+3+...+n = O(n²). Use StringBuilder to accumulate in a mutable buffer.

quizzes.question: A developer says 'Spring is a library that I call to create objects.' Why is this an inaccurate description of Spring's IoC container?
options: Spring is a compiler plugin, not a library or container
IoC inverts control — the container owns creation, wiring, and lifecycle of your beans; your code declares what it needs rather than calling a factory
Spring is only a collection of utility classes and has no container
Spring only works with databases, not with general objects
quizzes.explanation: The defining principle of IoC is that control is inverted: instead of your code calling constructors and wiring dependencies, a container manages object creation, dependency resolution, lifecycle callbacks, and proxying. Spring's ApplicationContext is that container. Spring does ship utility libraries, but its core value is the container that owns your beans.

quizzes.question: Two beans of type PaymentClient exist — StripePaymentClient and PaypalPaymentClient — and OrderService has @Autowired PaymentClient client with no @Qualifier or @Primary. What does Spring do at startup?
options: Picks the bean whose name is alphabetically first
Picks the bean whose name matches the field name 'client' if -parameters is enabled; otherwise throws NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException
Silently injects null and continues
Always picks the bean declared last in the container
quizzes.explanation: The resolution chain is: unique type → @Qualifier → @Primary → bean-name fallback (requires -parameters to preserve parameter names; enabled by default in Spring Boot) → error. If the field name 'client' does not match either bean name and no qualifier/primary exists, Spring throws NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException at startup. It never silently injects null for a required dependency.

quizzes.question: A class has @Transactional on a public method, but when it calls another @Transactional method on itself (this.otherMethod()), no transaction is started. Why?
options: Spring does not support transactions on public methods
The AOP proxy is bypassed on self-invocation — the internal call goes directly to the target instance, not through the proxy
The @Transactional annotation must be repeated on every method call site
Spring Boot disables @Transactional by default
quizzes.explanation: Spring's @Transactional is implemented via a BeanPostProcessor that wraps the bean in a proxy during postProcessAfterInitialization. External callers hit the proxy, which starts the transaction, then invokes the target. Self-invocation (this.otherMethod()) bypasses the proxy entirely and calls the raw method — no transaction is started. The fix is to extract the second method into another bean, use @Transactional on the outer method only, or use TransactionTemplate.

quizzes.question: Which statement about @Service and @Component is most accurate?
options: They register beans with different lifetimes — @Service is always singleton, @Component can be prototype
@Service is functionally identical to @Component at runtime; the difference is semantic, signaling business logic to readers and tools
@Service is required for @Transactional to work
@Component is only for controllers, @Service is for repositories
quizzes.explanation: @Service is meta-annotated with @Component and produces identical bean registration behavior. Its value is documentation and tooling. Only @Repository has additional runtime behavior (persistence exception translation). Only @Controller affects MVC handler mapping. @Transactional works on any Spring bean, not just @Service-annotated classes.

quizzes.question: A service class uses field injection (@Autowired PaymentClient client). In a unit test that does new OrderService(), the client field is null and calls throw NullPointerException. Why?
options: Field injection is deprecated and does not work in production
Field injection is performed by Spring via reflection after construction; without a Spring context, the field is never set
PaymentClient must be annotated with @Primary
Field injection requires the field to be static
quizzes.explanation: Field injection is a container feature — Spring uses reflection to set the field during bean population. A plain new OrderService() creates the object but never populates fields, so the field stays null. Constructor injection avoids this because the test passes dependencies explicitly. This is one of the standard arguments for preferring constructor injection.

quizzes.question: Bean A has a constructor that takes Bean B, and Bean B has a constructor that takes Bean A. Both are @Service. What happens at startup, and why?
options: Spring resolves it via the three-level cache — the cycle is broken automatically
Spring throws BeanCurrentlyInCreationException because constructor injection cannot satisfy a cycle; the three-level cache only works for field/setter injection
Spring injects null for one of the parameters and warns in logs
Spring retries construction until the cycle resolves
quizzes.explanation: To construct A you need a fully constructed B; to construct B you need a fully constructed A. Neither can be created first, so Spring fails fast with BeanCurrentlyInCreationException. The three-level singleton cache only works when a bean can be instantiated without its dependencies (no-arg constructor) and have them populated afterward via field or setter — that is exactly what constructor injection forbids.

quizzes.question: Why does Spring's singleton cache have three levels (singletonObjects, earlySingletonObjects, singletonFactories) instead of just two?
options: Three levels are required by the Java Memory Model for visibility of shared state
The singletonFactories level can decide at exposure time whether to hand out the raw bean or an AOP proxy, so cyclic beans still see the proxied version (e.g. @Transactional works)
Three levels improve cache lookup performance by a factor of three
The third level exists only for backwards compatibility with Spring 2.x
quizzes.explanation: During a cycle, an early reference to a partially constructed bean must be exposed so other beans can hold it. If that bean is proxied (due to @Transactional, @Async, etc.), the early reference must be the proxy — otherwise the other bean holds the raw instance and AOP silently bypasses. singletonFactories holds an ObjectFactory that can produce the proxy on demand, giving Spring the ability to wrap the reference before exposure. earlySingletonObjects caches the exposed result so repeated lookups are consistent.

quizzes.question: A service has @Transactional on a public method, and a call to that method from outside the class correctly starts a transaction. But when the same method calls another @Transactional method on the same class (this.other()), no new transaction is started. Why?
options: Spring requires @Transactional to be on a final method to open a new transaction
Self-invocation goes directly to the raw target instance, bypassing the proxy that would otherwise start the transaction
Spring disables transactions on methods called internally for safety
Constructor injection prevents self-invocation transactions
quizzes.explanation: Spring's @Transactional is installed via an AOP proxy that external callers hit. A self-call (this.other()) executes on the target instance directly, never touching the proxy, so the interceptor that would start the transaction is never invoked. The fixes are: extract the second method into another bean, use TransactionTemplate, or AspectJ load-time weaving. Option A is the opposite of the truth — final methods cannot be proxied and their @Transactional is silently ignored.

quizzes.question: A @Service class has no interfaces and a @Transactional method marked final. External calls reach the method without errors, but no transaction appears in the logs. What is the most likely cause?
options: Spring does not support transactions on classes without interfaces
CGLIB cannot override final methods, so the proxy does not intercept the call — @Transactional is silently ignored
The class needs a @Repository annotation to enable transactions
Final methods require @Transactional(propagation = MANDATORY)
quizzes.explanation: Without an interface, Spring uses CGLIB, which generates a subclass and overrides methods. Final methods cannot be overridden, so the interception point does not exist and @Transactional has no effect. Spring does not warn you — the annotation is a no-op on a final method. Transactions work fine without interfaces when methods are non-final. Neither @Repository nor propagation affects this.

quizzes.question: Inside @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false), method jdbc() calls ds() directly to build a JdbcTemplate. Compared to the default proxyBeanMethods=true, what happens?
options: Nothing changes — @Bean methods always return the same singleton
ds() is called as a plain Java method with the proxy disabled, so a new DataSource is created every time jdbc() runs, causing duplicate connection pools
Spring throws a compile error because @Bean methods cannot call each other in lite mode
The DataSource bean is registered twice with different names
quizzes.explanation: With proxyBeanMethods=false, Spring does not create the CGLIB subclass that intercepts @Bean method calls, so ds() runs as ordinary Java code and builds a fresh DataSource each time. Only the DataSource returned by Spring's own invocation is registered as a bean; the one created inside jdbc() is a duplicate that lives outside the container. The fix is to inject DataSource as a parameter instead of calling ds().

quizzes.question: Which BeanPostProcessor actually installs @Transactional proxies around beans?
options: AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor
CommonAnnotationBeanPostProcessor
AbstractAutoProxyCreator (and its subclasses like InfrastructureAdvisorAutoProxyCreator)
ConfigurationClassPostProcessor
quizzes.explanation: AbstractAutoProxyCreator and its infrastructure variants are BeanPostProcessors whose postProcessAfterInitialization checks each bean for matching advisors (from @Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async, @PreAuthorize, etc.) and returns an AOP proxy wrapping the original. AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor handles @Autowired/@Value injection; CommonAnnotationBeanPostProcessor invokes @PostConstruct/@PreDestroy; ConfigurationClassPostProcessor is a BeanFactoryPostProcessor that parses @Configuration classes — it runs before any bean is instantiated.

quizzes.question: During startup you see 'Bean myService is not eligible for getting processed by all BeanPostProcessors (for example: not eligible for auto-proxying)'. What is the practical consequence?
options: The bean will not be created and startup will fail
myService was created too early — before the auto-proxy-creator BPP was ready — so @Transactional/@Async on its methods will silently not apply
The bean is automatically switched to prototype scope
The bean is registered twice in the container
quizzes.explanation: BPPs themselves (and their dependencies) are instantiated before the rest of the beans. If myService is created during that early phase — because a BPP depends on it, or a BFPP instantiates it — the auto-proxy BPP has not yet been registered and myService never gets wrapped. Startup does not fail; the bug is silent. The fix is to remove the early dependency (usually use ObjectProvider<MyService> inside the BPP instead of direct injection).

quizzes.title: What Is Spring Boot and Why Does It Exist on Top of Spring?
quizzes.summary:
Spring Framework, for all its power, is painful to start a project with. Setting up a web app in vanilla Spring requires: an XML file or a @Configuration class for the DispatcherServlet, a servlet container (Tomcat) downloaded and configured separately, a Jackson ObjectMapper configured correctly, a DataSource bean wired to a database driver, a transaction manager, a connection pool, plus manually curated dependency versions in Maven or Gradle. The problem is not that any one step is hard — it is that every new Spring project requires all of them, and every version mismatch between Spring 5.3.x, Jackson 2.13.x, Hibernate 5.6.x, and Tomcat 9 is a debugging session waiting to happen.

Spring Boot's core thesis is Convention over Configuration: pick sensible defaults for common choices, let the developer override only what they care about, and make the whole thing runnable as a single jar. Concretely, Spring Boot contributes four things on top of Spring: (1) Starters — curated dependency bundles (spring-boot-starter-web pulls Spring MVC, Jackson, Tomcat, and validation, all version-compatible); (2) Auto-configuration — Spring Boot inspects what is on the classpath and configures beans automatically (if H2 is on the classpath and no DataSource bean exists, Boot creates an in-memory one); (3) An embedded server — Tomcat, Jetty, or Undertow is packaged inside the jar, so `java -jar app.jar` is a runnable web server with no external install; (4) Actuator — production features like health checks, metrics, and environment inspection out of the box.

The distinction people get wrong: Spring Boot is NOT a replacement for Spring. It is Spring — the same ApplicationContext, the same @Service, @Autowired, @Transactional, the same AOP, the same bean lifecycle. Spring Boot adds a launcher (@SpringBootApplication), a dependency management layer, a classpath-driven auto-configuration mechanism, and production defaults. If you are debugging a @Transactional issue in a Spring Boot app, you are using Spring's @Transactional — Boot does not change how it works. If you are debugging circular dependencies, you are using Spring's bean lifecycle — Boot only sets allow-circular-references=false by default.

A good analogy: vanilla Spring is a fully stocked professional kitchen where you must organize every utensil yourself; Spring Boot is the same kitchen pre-arranged with a default layout, common ingredients stocked, and a recipe book open on the counter — you can rearrange anything, but the default setup gets you cooking in five minutes. The kitchen is the same; the arrangement is different.

The interview-relevant mental model: @SpringBootApplication on a main class is a composed annotation of @SpringBootConfiguration (a @Configuration class), @EnableAutoConfiguration (turn on classpath-driven bean provisioning), and @ComponentScan (scan the current package and below). When main() calls SpringApplication.run(...), Boot builds an ApplicationContext, runs auto-configuration, starts the embedded server, and fires ApplicationReadyEvent. Everything else — starters, actuators, embedded Tomcat — is a layer on that context. If you understand the context, you understand the app; if you understand only the annotations, you are memorizing.
bullets: Spring Boot is Spring + convention over configuration; same IoC container, same annotations, same AOP.
Four contributions on top of Spring: starters (curated deps), auto-configuration (classpath-driven beans), embedded server, Actuator.
@SpringBootApplication = @SpringBootConfiguration + @EnableAutoConfiguration + @ComponentScan.
The embedded server means java -jar app.jar is a fully self-contained web application — no external Tomcat.
If you are debugging a bean or a transaction in Spring Boot, you are debugging Spring — Boot does not change that behavior.

quizzes.title: What Happens Inside Spring Boot During Startup: Step-by-Step Sequence
quizzes.summary:
When you call SpringApplication.run(Application.class, args), Spring Boot executes a well-defined sequence that lasts from 'JVM started main' to 'ApplicationReadyEvent fired and the port is listening'. Understanding this sequence is what lets you debug slow startups, order-of-initialization bugs, and 'why did my bean get created before that other bean?' problems.

The sequence, in order: (1) SpringApplication constructs — it inspects the classpath to guess the application type (SERVLET, REACTIVE, or NONE), discovers listeners via spring.factories / META-INF/spring.factories, and detects the main class. (2) The application starts an Environment — property sources (system properties, environment variables, application.yml, application-{profile}.yml, command-line args) are loaded in priority order. (3) The banner is printed. (4) ApplicationContext is created — AnnotationConfigServletWebServerApplicationContext for a typical Spring MVC app. (5) ApplicationContextInitializers run — user-supplied hooks that can modify the context before beans are loaded. (6) Environment-prepared listeners fire. (7) The context is refreshed: this is the big one. It triggers ConfigurationClassPostProcessor (parses @Configuration classes, discovers @ComponentScan targets, evaluates @Conditional, registers @Bean definitions from auto-configuration), then instantiates all singletons in dependency order, runs BeanPostProcessors (which install @Autowired, @PostConstruct, AOP proxies), and finally starts the embedded web server. (8) ContextRefreshedEvent fires. (9) ApplicationRunner and CommandLineRunner beans run — with @Order determining sequence. (10) ApplicationReadyEvent fires; the app is now serving traffic.

The most common startup failure modes map to these phases. Missing bean errors (NoSuchBeanDefinitionException) happen during step 7 when bean instantiation runs. Port-in-use errors (WebServerException: Unable to start embedded Tomcat) happen during the server-start sub-phase of step 7 — after all beans have been created. Configuration exceptions (invalid properties, failed @ConfigurationProperties binding) surface during step 7's bean instantiation, especially for beans that fail-fast. ApplicationRunner exceptions run AFTER the web server is up — if one throws, the app has already started listening and will only begin shutting down because of the error.

The banner is a nice diagnostic marker: if you see the banner but no 'Tomcat started on port 8080', you know you failed during context refresh. If you see 'Tomcat started' but nothing serving, the issue is probably downstream (ApplicationRunner throwing, then triggering shutdown) or a filter chain misconfiguration.

Two startup-tuning facts matter in production. First, lazy initialization (spring.main.lazy-initialization=true, or @Lazy per bean) defers non-critical bean creation until first use — startups go from 30s to 3s in large apps, at the cost of first-request latency spikes and delayed failure detection. Second, startup failures are much easier to diagnose with debug logging (logging.level.root=DEBUG or --debug on the command line): Boot prints an auto-configuration report ('Positive matches', 'Negative matches', 'Exclusions') that lists exactly which conditions failed and why.

An interview answer that names the phases in order, knows the difference between 'context refresh' and 'web server start', and explains why ApplicationRunner runs after the port is open, is a stronger answer than any list of annotations.
bullets: Order: construct SpringApplication → load Environment → create context → refresh context (parse @Configuration, run BPPs, instantiate beans) → start embedded server → ApplicationRunner → ApplicationReadyEvent.
Environment is built from property sources in priority order: command-line > env vars > application-{profile} > application.yml > defaults.
Context refresh is where most failures happen: bean instantiation, auto-configuration, AOP wrapping, and the web server start all occur here.
ApplicationRunner/CommandLineRunner run AFTER the server is listening — exceptions here trigger shutdown of an already-started app.
spring.main.lazy-initialization=true trades startup speed for first-request latency and delayed failure detection.
--debug prints an auto-configuration report listing positive and negative condition matches — best tool for 'why was this bean not created?'
quizzes.code:
SpringApplication.run(Application.class, args)

1. SpringApplication construct
   - guess application type (SERVLET / REACTIVE / NONE)
   - load listeners from META-INF/spring.factories
   - dedupe and reorder listeners

2. Environment prepared
   - property sources loaded in priority order
   - active profiles resolved

3. Banner printed

4. ApplicationContext created
   (AnnotationConfigServletWebServerApplicationContext)

5. ApplicationContextInitializers run

6. context refresh() -- THE BIG ONE
   a. ConfigurationClassPostProcessor
      - parse @Configuration classes
      - resolve @ComponentScan
      - evaluate @Conditional on auto-configs
      - register @Bean definitions
   b. BeanFactoryPostProcessors (placeholder resolution, etc.)
   c. Instantiate singletons in dependency order
   d. BeanPostProcessors per bean (@Autowired, @PostConstruct, AOP)
   e. Start embedded web server (Tomcat)

7. ContextRefreshedEvent fired

8. ApplicationRunner / CommandLineRunner run (with @Order)

9. ApplicationReadyEvent fired -> app is live

quizzes.title: Auto-Configuration Internals: @Conditional, spring.factories, and How a DataSource Appears
quizzes.summary:
Auto-configuration is the magic that makes Spring Boot feel instant: add spring-boot-starter-data-jpa to pom.xml, declare a few properties, and a fully configured DataSource, EntityManagerFactory, and transaction manager appear. The mechanism is not magic; it is a set of @Configuration classes that are conditionally loaded based on what is on the classpath, what beans already exist, and what properties are set. Understanding the mechanism is what turns 'why is my custom DataSource ignored?' into a five-minute diagnosis.

@EnableAutoConfiguration (composed into @SpringBootApplication) triggers AutoConfigurationImportSelector, which reads class names from META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports (Spring Boot 2.7+; older versions used META-INF/spring.factories). These are the auto-configuration classes shipped with Boot and any third-party starter. The list is huge (over a hundred for a typical app) but most classes do not produce any beans because their @Conditional checks fail.

Conditions are the gatekeepers. @ConditionalOnClass(DataSource.class) — only applies if the class is on the classpath. @ConditionalOnMissingBean(DataSource.class) — only applies if you have NOT already defined a DataSource. @ConditionalOnProperty(name="spring.datasource.url") — only applies if the property is set. @ConditionalOnBean(DataSource.class) — only applies if a DataSource exists (used for dependent configs, like entityManagerFactory which requires a DataSource). Together these form a boolean expression: 'activate this auto-config only when the environment supports it and the developer has not overridden it.'

Take the DataSource example. DataSourceAutoConfiguration has @ConditionalOnClass({ DataSource.class, EmbeddedDatabaseType.class }) — the JDBC API must be present (because spring-jdbc is on the classpath). Inside, several nested configurations apply conditionally: EmbeddedDataSourceConfiguration activates only if no spring.datasource.url is set and an embedded DB driver (H2, HSQLDB, Derby) is on the classpath; PooledDataSourceConfiguration activates only if spring.datasource.url is set or an embedded DB driver exists. HikariDataSource is the default pool when HikariCP is on the classpath (which spring-boot-starter-jdbc brings). If you define your own DataSource bean, @ConditionalOnMissingBean back-off kicks in and Boot's auto-config steps aside — this is the ordering contract you rely on to override any auto-configured bean.

Ordering matters when one auto-config depends on another. @AutoConfigureAfter(DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class) on JpaAutoConfiguration ensures JPA config is evaluated after the DataSource config is registered. This is how Boot avoids a chicken-and-egg situation where the entity manager is configured before its DataSource exists.

The debugging tool is --debug or logging.level.org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure=DEBUG. Boot prints a ConditionEvaluationReport with 'Positive matches' (which auto-configs ran and why) and 'Negative matches' (which did not and why). If your custom Configuration is being ignored, the report tells you whether the auto-config's @ConditionalOnMissingBean actually saw your bean, or whether your bean was registered too late.

The interview-grade mental model: auto-configuration is a large library of @Configuration classes, each guarded by conditions, loaded from a classpath index (AutoConfiguration.imports), applied in a deterministic order, and designed to back off the moment you define your own bean. Everything else — starters, spring.factories, condition reports — is machinery around that core idea.
bullets: @EnableAutoConfiguration reads AutoConfiguration.imports (formerly spring.factories) to discover candidate auto-config classes.
Conditions decide applicability: @ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnMissingBean, @ConditionalOnProperty, @ConditionalOnBean.
Every auto-config is designed to back off when the developer defines their own bean of the same type — this is why overriding works.
@AutoConfigureAfter / @AutoConfigureBefore enforce ordering between dependent auto-configs (e.g., JPA after DataSource).
--debug prints a ConditionEvaluationReport: 'Positive matches' = ran, 'Negative matches' = skipped and why.
DataSourceAutoConfiguration: activates on DataSource.class + spring-jdbc; EmbeddedDataSourceConfiguration for in-memory, PooledDataSourceConfiguration for real URLs, HikariCP as default pool.

quizzes.title: Starters and BOM: Why You Rarely Specify Versions in a Spring Boot pom.xml
quizzes.summary:
Two mechanisms make dependency management in Spring Boot almost invisible: starters and the Bill of Materials (BOM). A starter is a POM-only dependency (no classes) that aggregates a curated set of libraries. The BOM is a POM that declares <dependencyManagement> entries for dozens of libraries with specific versions, so all children inherit those versions without repeating them. Together, starters give you the right libraries and the BOM gives you the right versions — and they are tested as a set, so you do not hit 'Jackson 2.15 does not work with Spring MVC 6.0.3' surprises.

spring-boot-starter is the base — Spring core, logging (Logback + SLF4J), autoconfigure, and the Spring Boot launcher. spring-boot-starter-web adds Spring MVC, Jackson, Tomcat (embedded), and validation. spring-boot-starter-data-jpa adds Spring Data JPA, Hibernate, HikariCP, and spring-jdbc. spring-boot-starter-security adds Spring Security plus its filter chain. spring-boot-starter-test pulls in JUnit 5, AssertJ, Mockito, Hamcrest, JSONAssert, and Spring Test — with scope test. Each starter is a curated bundle the Spring team has verified to work together.

The parent POM does the version management. Every Spring Boot app has either <parent>spring-boot-starter-parent</parent> (simplest) or imports spring-boot-dependencies via <dependencyManagement><scope>import</scope></dependencyManagement>. Either way, when you declare spring-boot-starter-web without a <version>, Maven consults the BOM's dependencyManagement and inserts the version automatically. If you explicitly specify a version, you override the BOM — usually a mistake.

The <parent> variant does more than the BOM import. spring-boot-starter-parent is itself a parent POM that configures the compiler plugin (Java version defaults), resource filtering for application.properties placeholders, surefire for tests, and repackage for executable jars. If you cannot inherit from the parent (multi-module builds, corporate parents), use <scope>import</scope> to get the BOM but expect to configure plugins yourself.

Starters are not magic — they are just well-designed dependency graphs. Removing a transitive dependency a starter brings in (for example, excluding Tomcat to use Jetty) is normal: <exclusions> on the starter, then add spring-boot-starter-jetty. Overriding a starter's transitive version (say, a newer Jackson) is possible but risky — you lose the version compatibility guarantee the Spring team tested.

Maven or Gradle? Spring Boot works with both. In Gradle, apply the io.spring.dependency-management plugin to get the same BOM behavior, or use Spring Boot's newer convention of a platform BOM (implementation platform(org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-dependencies:3.x.y)). Either way, the principle is the same: declare the starter without a version and let the BOM resolve it.

An interview-worthy summary: starters = curated bundles; BOM = version catalog applied via dependencyManagement; together they eliminate the 'what version of Jackson goes with Spring 6?' question. If you override versions, do it deliberately and re-run the full test suite — you are opting out of the compatibility guarantee the Spring team verified for that release.
bullets: A starter is a POM-only artifact that aggregates curated dependencies (spring-boot-starter-web = Spring MVC + Jackson + Tomcat + validation).
The BOM (spring-boot-dependencies) declares <dependencyManagement> versions so children omit <version> and inherit tested combinations.
<parent>spring-boot-starter-parent</parent> gives both the BOM and plugin configuration (compiler, surefire, repackage).
Without parent inheritance, use <dependencyManagement><scope>import</scope> to bring in the BOM — you must configure plugins yourself.
Overriding a transitive version (e.g., newer Jackson) opts you out of the version-compatibility guarantee — do it only with a full test run.
Excluding a transitive dep (e.g., exclude Tomcat, add spring-boot-starter-jetty) is standard and safe.
quizzes.code:
<!-- Standard: inherit parent -> BOM + plugins configured -->
<parent>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
    <version>3.2.0</version>
</parent>

<dependencies>
    <!-- no version needed -- BOM supplies it -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

<!-- Corporate parent: import the BOM instead -->
<dependencyManagement>
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-dependencies</artifactId>
            <version>3.2.0</version>
            <type>pom</type>
            <scope>import</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

<!-- Swap Tomcat for Jetty -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    <exclusions>
        <exclusion>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-tomcat</artifactId>
        </exclusion>
    </exclusions>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-jetty</artifactId>
</dependency>

quizzes.title: Configuration Precedence and Profiles: Where Does a Property Value Actually Come From?
quizzes.summary:
Spring Boot reads properties from over a dozen sources, and when the same key exists in multiple sources, the one with the highest precedence wins. This is powerful but also the source of 'my change to application.yml had no effect' bugs — someone set an environment variable with the same name, and env vars beat file config.

The precedence order (highest to lowest, simplified but practical): (1) Devtools global settings (~/.config/spring-boot); (2) @TestPropertySource on a test; (3) command-line arguments (--server.port=8081); (4) SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON env var; (5) ServletConfig / ServletContext init parameters; (6) JNDI attributes; (7) System.getProperties() (Java system properties, -Dkey=value); (8) OS environment variables (SERVER_PORT); (9) application-{profile}.yml outside the jar; (10) application-{profile}.yml inside the jar; (11) application.yml outside the jar; (12) application.yml inside the jar; (13) @PropertySource on a @Configuration; (14) SpringApplication.setDefaultProperties. Memorizing the whole list is less important than remembering the two rules: command-line and env vars always beat file config, and {profile} files beat non-profile files at the same location.

The OS environment variable behavior is where most confusion lives. If application.yml has server.port: 8080, but the container also exports SERVER_PORT=9090, then 9090 wins. Boot's relaxed binding maps SERVER_PORT to server.port, so any UPPER_SNAKE_CASE env var overrides the property of the same lowercase.dotted name. This is normally desirable in containers (you set config via env vars, not files), but it becomes a trap when a leftover env var from a CI job silently overrides a recent file change.

Profiles are named sets of configuration you activate via spring.profiles.active. Files named application-{profile}.yml override application.yml for the same location. You can activate multiple profiles at once (comma-separated) and Boot merges them left-to-right — the rightmost profile wins for conflicting keys (after the base). Common patterns: application-dev.yml for local, application-prod.yml for production, and profile-specific beans annotated with @Profile("prod") that only instantiate in that profile. Since Spring Boot 2.4, profile groups let you activate a named group (spring.profiles.group.production=prod-db,prod-metrics) so one flag turns on multiple profiles.

Practical debugging: the Actuator /actuator/env endpoint (when exposed) lists every property with its source and precedence — the fastest way to find 'where is this value coming from?'. If you cannot enable Actuator, an EnvironmentAware bean can print the property source list at startup for the same purpose. For any property you care about, always ask: which of the twelve sources has it, and does anything higher-precedence override it?

An interview-quality answer names the general rule (command line > env vars > profile files > base files) rather than reciting all twelve, gives the SERVER_PORT example, and mentions @Profile / profile groups and Actuator's env endpoint as the practical tools. That shows you understand configuration as a precedence system, not as scattered @Value lookups.
bullets: Command-line args and env vars beat all file config; profile files beat non-profile files at the same location.
SERVER_PORT env var overrides server.port from application.yml — relaxed binding maps UPPER_SNAKE_CASE to dot.case automatically.
spring.profiles.active activates profiles; application-{profile}.yml overrides application.yml; multiple profiles merge left-to-right with the rightmost winning.
Profile groups (spring.profiles.group.production=prod-db,prod-metrics) let one flag activate several profiles.
@Profile("prod") on a @Bean or @Configuration makes it conditional on the active profile.
Actuator /actuator/env shows every property with its source and precedence — the fastest 'where does this value come from?' tool.
quizzes.code:
# Layered config
# application.yml              (base, lowest in-jar priority)
server.port: 8080
spring.datasource.url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/app

# application-prod.yml         (overrides base in prod)
spring.datasource.url: jdbc:postgresql://db.prod:5432/app
spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size: 30

# Run with:
java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod --server.port=9090
# effective server.port: 9090     (command line wins)
# effective datasource.url: prod  (profile file wins over base)

# Container override
#   docker run -e SERVER_PORT=7070 -e SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod app
#   SERVER_PORT overrides server.port from any file

# Profile group -- one switch, multiple profiles
# spring.profiles.group.production=prod-db,prod-metrics
# java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=production

# Inspect everything live
# GET /actuator/env    -> every property + source + precedence

// Conditional bean by profile
@Configuration
@Profile("prod")
class ProdConfig {
    @Bean DataSource dataSource() { ... }
}

quizzes.title: @ConfigurationProperties vs @Value: Type Safety, Relaxed Binding, and When to Use Each
bullets: @Value injects one scalar; @ConfigurationProperties binds an entire prefix tree to a POJO.
@ConfigurationProperties gives relaxed binding (kebab, camel, snake, env-var forms all match the same field), type conversion (Duration, DataSize, enums), JSR-380 validation, and IDE metadata.
@Value does no validation, no relaxed binding, no autocomplete, and fails cryptically when a required property is missing.
@ConfigurationProperties class must become a bean — @Component, @ConfigurationPropertiesScan, or @EnableConfigurationProperties.
Rule of thumb: @Value for one-off scalars, @ConfigurationProperties for anything with 3+ related fields, nesting, or validation.

quizzes.title: @Transactional Internals and the Six Silent Failures
quizzes.summary:
@Transactional is the most misused annotation in the Spring ecosystem. It is a thin, easy-to-write annotation that looks like it 'just works', but its semantics are governed by proxies, propagation rules, and rollback contracts — and it fails silently in six common ways that ship to production and cause data corruption or phantom transactions.

How it actually works. @Transactional is implemented by a BeanPostProcessor (AbstractAutoProxyCreator via InfrastructureAdvisorAutoProxyCreator) that wraps the finished bean in a proxy (JDK dynamic proxy if it implements interfaces, CGLIB otherwise). External callers hit the proxy, which starts a transaction (or joins one), invokes the target method, commits if it returns normally, and rolls back if it throws. This is why self-invocation (this.someMethod()) bypasses @Transactional — the internal call skips the proxy. This is also why final methods break — CGLIB cannot override them.

Propagation controls what happens when a transactional method calls another. REQUIRED (default) joins the existing transaction if one exists, otherwise starts a new one. REQUIRES_NEW always suspends the current transaction and starts a fresh one — useful when you need to persist audit logs even if the outer transaction rolls back. NESTED creates a savepoint inside the current transaction; it rolls back to the savepoint, not the whole transaction. MANDATORY requires an existing transaction or throws. NEVER forbids one. SUPPORTS uses one if present, else runs non-transactionally. NOT_SUPPORTED suspends any existing transaction. Most bugs live in REQUIRES_NEW (people forget it commits independently) and NESTED (savepoints need database support).

Isolation levels map to the database's own: READ_COMMITTED (default), READ_UNCOMMITTED, REPEATABLE_READ, SERIALIZABLE. Setting anything stricter than the database default has real cost — locks, retries, deadlocks — so choose deliberately, not by habit.

The six silent failures:

1. Self-invocation. this.method() bypasses the proxy. Calls inside the same class do not start a new transaction. The fix is to move the inner method to another bean, use TransactionTemplate, or use AspectJ load-time weaving.

2. Checked exceptions do not roll back. @Transactional only rolls back on RuntimeException and Error by default. If your method throws a checked exception (IOException, a custom Exception), the transaction commits. Fix: @Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class), or throw an unchecked exception, or handle and rethrow wrapped.

3. Final methods and final classes cannot be proxied by CGLIB. @Transactional on a final method is silently ignored — no transaction starts, no warning. Fix: remove final, extract into an interface (JDK proxy handles it), or use AspectJ.

4. Private methods are not proxied. Spring's proxy-based AOP only intercepts public methods (and protected for CGLIB, but the common contract is public). @Transactional on a private method does nothing. Fix: make the method public or restructure.

5. Wrong proxy target in injection. If you @Autowired the concrete class but Spring produced a JDK proxy of the interface, injection fails at startup with BeanNotOfRequiredTypeException. Fix: inject the interface, or force proxyTargetClass=true.

6. readOnly=true on a method that writes. readOnly is a hint to Hibernate to skip dirty-checking and to the JDBC driver to mark the connection read-only. If the method writes, the write is either silently ignored or fails when the driver enforces read-only. Fix: remove readOnly on write methods; use it only for genuine reads.

Additional common pitfalls worth knowing: long transactions holding database locks across network calls to downstream services (never do IO inside a transaction); @Transactional on @Async methods (async executes on a different thread with a different transaction context — the transaction often does not propagate as expected); and nested @Transactional where the inner REQUIRES_NEW bean is actually the same bean invoked via self-invocation, so REQUIRES_NEW silently does nothing.

An interview answer that names the proxy model, the six failure modes, and the REQUIRED vs REQUIRES_NEW distinction is far stronger than 'it makes methods transactional'. Bonus points for mentioning TransactionTemplate (imperative, no proxy, no self-invocation risk) as the escape hatch when @Transactional's proxy model gets in the way.
bullets: @Transactional uses a runtime AOP proxy (JDK or CGLIB) — external callers hit the proxy, which manages begin/commit/rollback.
Six silent failures: self-invocation, checked exceptions, final methods/classes, private methods, wrong injection type, readOnly on writes.
Rollback default: only RuntimeException and Error. Use rollbackFor = Exception.class for checked exceptions.
Propagation: REQUIRED (join or create), REQUIRES_NEW (suspend outer, always new), NESTED (savepoint), MANDATORY, NEVER, SUPPORTS, NOT_SUPPORTED.
Never do network IO inside a transaction — long-held locks cause cascading timeouts.
TransactionTemplate is the imperative escape hatch — no proxy, no self-invocation trap.

quizzes.title: Actuator: Health, Metrics, Env, and the Endpoints That Make Spring Boot Production-Ready
quizzes.summary:
Actuator is the module that gives a running Spring Boot app an HTTP interface for introspection and operations. Add spring-boot-starter-actuator and Boot exposes a set of endpoints under /actuator by default: /actuator/health (are you up?), /actuator/info (build and git metadata), /actuator/metrics (JVM and application metrics), and a few others, depending on what is on the classpath. The full set of possible endpoints includes env, beans, configprops, mappings, loggers, threaddump, heapdump, httptrace, scheduledtasks, and prometheus — but most are disabled by default because they can leak sensitive data.

/actuator/health is the endpoint Kubernetes readiness and liveness probes talk to. It aggregates multiple HealthIndicators (database reachable, disk space, Redis ping, Kafka broker reachable) into an overall status: UP, DOWN, OUT_OF_SERVICE, UNKNOWN. You can write custom HealthIndicators by implementing the interface and registering them as beans, and you can control what is shown to unauthenticated users with management.endpoint.health.show-details (default never; use when_authorized to reveal DB details only to authenticated callers).

/actuator/metrics exposes Micrometer meters — JVM memory, GC pauses, HTTP request timings, thread pool stats, DataSource pool utilization, and any custom counters or timers you register. Meter names follow Micrometer conventions (http.server.requests, jvm.memory.used, hikaricp.connections.active). The /actuator/prometheus endpoint (when the micrometer-registry-prometheus dependency is present) exports these in Prometheus text format, ready to be scraped.

/actuator/env lists every property with its source and precedence — the single best tool for 'where is this value coming from?' debugging. /actuator/configprops shows the bound @ConfigurationProperties beans. /actuator/beans shows every bean in the context with its type and dependencies. /actuator/mappings shows all HTTP routes. /actuator/threaddump dumps thread stacks (great for hanging requests). /actuator/heapdump produces a .hprof file you can open in a profiler — be careful with this in production, it can be hundreds of MB.

Security is critical. By default, most endpoints are disabled. Even health and info should generally not be exposed on the public internet — Kubernetes probes work fine on an internal port. The recommended production setup: management.server.port=8081 puts Actuator on a separate internal port, unreachable from the outside; secure it with Spring Security on that port; enable only the endpoints you need (management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,prometheus); and put health behind authentication with management.endpoint.health.show-details=when_authorized.

Custom endpoints are easy: annotate a class with @Endpoint(id = "features") and @ReadOperation methods for GET-like reads, @WriteOperation for POST-like writes. Custom health indicators: implement HealthIndicator and register the bean — Boot's aggregate picks it up automatically.

An interview answer that names health, metrics, env, and loggers specifically (with the security warning) shows real production experience. An answer that only says 'it exposes endpoints' is superficial.
bullets: Actuator exposes operational endpoints under /actuator: health, info, metrics, env, beans, configprops, loggers, threaddump, heapdump.
/actuator/health aggregates multiple HealthIndicators (DB, disk, Redis, custom) into UP/DOWN — used by Kubernetes probes.
/actuator/metrics exposes Micrometer meters; /actuator/prometheus exports them for scraping.
/actuator/env shows property sources and precedence — best tool for config debugging.
Security: most endpoints disabled by default; put Actuator on a separate port (management.server.port) and expose only what you need (exposure.include).
Custom: @Endpoint for operations, HealthIndicator for health checks.

quizzes.title: Embedded Server and Graceful Shutdown: How java -jar Actually Serves HTTP
quizzes.summary:
In classic Java web deployments, your application was a WAR file dropped into a pre-installed Tomcat, and the server lived outside your build. Spring Boot flips this: the application IS the server. spring-boot-starter-web brings spring-boot-starter-tomcat, which brings the Tomcat embed jar, and Spring Boot creates a Tomcat instance programmatically inside the JVM. When you run java -jar app.jar, your main method runs, the context refreshes, and around step 7e of the startup sequence Boot instantiates Tomcat, binds the port, deploys the DispatcherServlet, and starts accepting requests. There is no external install, no war file, no container — one JVM, one jar, one server.

The default is Tomcat, but Jetty and Undertow are drop-in swaps: exclude spring-boot-starter-tomcat, add spring-boot-starter-jetty or spring-boot-starter-undertow. Jetty is often chosen for lower memory and better support of long-lived connections like WebSockets; Undertow has the smallest footprint and is optimized for very high concurrency. Configuration is uniform via server.* properties regardless of choice: server.port, server.servlet.context-path, server.tomcat.max-threads, server.undertow.io-threads.

server.tomcat.max-threads (default 200) is the maximum number of worker threads — if it saturates, new requests queue in the OS accept backlog or are rejected depending on the OS. This is different from the HikariCP connection pool size; if max-threads is 200 but the DB pool is 10, 190 threads will block on connection acquisition, which is where many production latency incidents originate. Sizing those two together (threads ≈ pool × expectedIOwaitRatio) is a real engineering decision, not a checkbox.

Graceful shutdown is the property that separates a toy app from a production app. When a pod receives SIGTERM (Kubernetes rolling update, deploy), the default behavior in Spring Boot pre-2.3 was to kill the JVM immediately — in-flight requests get 500 errors and clients see broken responses. With server.shutdown=graceful (since Boot 2.3, default in 3.x is still immediate unless enabled), Boot stops accepting new requests on the connector, waits up to spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase (default 30s) for in-flight requests to finish, then proceeds to close the context and run @PreDestroy / DisposableBean / custom destroy-method on beans. Kubernetes should set terminationGracePeriodSeconds greater than the timeout so the pod does not get SIGKILLed mid-drain.

Graceful shutdown is a chain: stop accept connector → wait for in-flight requests → stop the servlet container → publish ContextClosedEvent → run @PreDestroy on beans → run DisposableBean.destroy → run custom destroy-method → close the JVM. If you have background executors or message listeners (Kafka, Rabbit, SQS pollers), they must be stopped during shutdown too — that is what @PreDestroy and SmartLifecycle implementations are for. Kafka consumers should stop their pollers, commit offsets cleanly, and leave the consumer group so partitions reassign without a rebalance storm. Getting this right is the difference between a deploy that loses zero in-flight requests and one that drops a small percentage on every rollout.

An interview answer that explains (1) the server is inside the JVM, not external, (2) Tomcat is the default but Jetty/Undertow are drop-in swaps, (3) graceful shutdown is opt-in and needs Kubernetes terminationGracePeriodSeconds coordination, and (4) background processors must be stopped in @PreDestroy, is a complete answer.
bullets: Spring Boot embeds the server (Tomcat default) inside the JVM; the app jar is the web server, no external Tomcat install.
Jetty and Undertow are drop-in alternatives via starter swap; same server.* properties apply.
server.tomcat.max-threads (default 200) is worker-thread limit; mismatch with DB pool size causes connection-acquire latency spikes.
server.shutdown=graceful stops accepting new requests, drains in-flight up to spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase, then destroys beans.
Kubernetes terminationGracePeriodSeconds must exceed the shutdown timeout, or the pod is SIGKILLed mid-drain.
Background processors (Kafka, Rabbit, executors) must be stopped in @PreDestroy / SmartLifecycle for clean shutdown.

quizzes.question: A team migrates from RabbitMQ to Kafka but keeps designing topics with a single partition 'to guarantee ordering' and sets retention to 1 hour 'to clean up after ourselves'. What is the core mistake?
options: Kafka cannot support single-partition topics

They are applying queue habits to a log — Kafka ordering is per-partition, and retention is a storage policy independent of consumption; single-partition topics cap parallelism and short retention destroys replay
Kafka requires at least three partitions per topic
Retention must always be infinite in Kafka
quizzes.explanation: A single partition gives total order but caps consumer-group parallelism at one consumer and is a capacity bottleneck. Kafka retention is about how much history remains on disk, not about deleting after consumption — short retention eliminates replay, which is Kafka's core differentiator from a queue. The correct design uses key-based partitioning (per-key order, parallel across keys) and retention sized to replay requirements.

quizzes.question: A topic has 4 partitions and a consumer group has 6 consumers. What happens to the extra 2 consumers?
options: They share partitions with the existing consumers, splitting the load
They sit idle — within a consumer group, each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer, so only 4 consumers can be active
Kafka automatically increases the partition count to match the consumer count
The group rebalances and evicts the extra consumers
quizzes.explanation: Kafka's consumer-group assignment guarantees that each partition is owned by exactly one consumer at a time. With 4 partitions, at most 4 consumers in the group can be active; the remaining 2 are assigned no partitions and sit idle until a partition is freed (consumer leaves, crashes, or the topic is expanded). Adding consumers beyond the partition count does not increase parallelism.

quizzes.question: A developer says 'the producer writes to the Kafka cluster and the consumer reads from the cluster.' Why is this imprecise in a way that matters for debugging?
options: Producers write to ZooKeeper and consumers read from brokers

Both producers and consumers talk to specific partition leaders on specific brokers; followers replicate but do not serve client requests, so a 'leader not available' error is a broker-specific failure, not a cluster-wide one
Consumers write to the cluster and producers read from it
Kafka clients always connect to every broker simultaneously
quizzes.explanation: Kafka clients communicate with partition leaders, not with the cluster as an abstract entity. Each partition has one leader broker; producers send to that leader, and consumers fetch from that leader. Followers replicate in the background and are not read from under normal conditions. This matters for debugging: a leader election, a broker that is overloaded, or a network partition between a client and a specific broker produces errors scoped to those partitions, not to the whole topic.

quizzes.question: Three downstream services — analytics, fraud detection, and billing — all need to react to the same 'order_placed' events. Which approach best fits Kafka's model?
options: Create three separate queues and have the order service publish three copies
Use one topic with three independent consumer groups — each group reads the full stream at its own pace with its own offsets
Use a single consumer group with three consumers, one per service
Kafka cannot fan out one event to multiple services
quizzes.explanation: Kafka fan-out is natively achieved with multiple consumer groups on the same topic. Each group maintains independent committed offsets, so analytics, fraud, and billing each read the entire stream without interfering. A single consumer group with three consumers would divide partitions among them, meaning each event goes to only one service — that is queue semantics, not fan-out. Publishing three copies creates coupling and duplication.

quizzes.question: A high-throughput pipeline uses acks=all and idempotence, but throughput is lower than expected. Which producer tuning change is most likely to improve throughput without sacrificing durability?
options: Switch acks to 0
Increase linger.ms (e.g., to 10–20 ms) and batch.size (e.g., to 64 KB), and enable compression (lz4 or zstd)
Disable idempotence
Reduce max.in.flight.requests.per.connection to 1
quizzes.explanation: With acks=all and idempotence, durability is fixed; the remaining throughput levers are batching and compression. A larger linger.ms lets batches fill, a larger batch.size allows more records per request, and compression reduces network I/O and broker disk usage. acks=0 and disabling idempotence sacrifice durability. Reducing max.in.flight to 1 serializes requests and hurts throughput further.

quizzes.question: What exactly does the idempotent producer protect against, and what does it NOT protect against?
options: It protects against duplicate records caused by producer retries within one producer session; it does not protect against duplicates across producer restarts or consumer-side reprocessing
It guarantees exactly-once end-to-end across producers and consumers
It protects against message loss but not duplication
It requires ZooKeeper to track producer sequence numbers
quizzes.explanation: The idempotent producer assigns a Producer ID and per-partition sequence numbers; the broker deduplicates retries within that session. A producer restart gets a new PID, so cross-session deduplication requires transactions (exactly-once semantics). Consumer-side duplicates from at-least-once processing are a separate problem solved by idempotent consumers, not by the producer.

quizzes.question: A consumer uses auto-commit, polls records 100–199, auto-commit fires and commits offset 200, then the consumer crashes while processing record 150. What happens on restart?
options: The consumer resumes from offset 150 and reprocesses 150–199
The consumer resumes from offset 200, and records 150–199 are lost — this is at-most-once behavior
The broker replays 150–199 automatically because the crash was detected
The consumer enters a rebalance loop until the missing records are recovered
quizzes.explanation: Auto-commit commits the latest offset returned by poll(), not the last processed offset. Once offset 200 is committed, restarting seeks to 200, skipping any records between 150 and 199 that were polled but not processed. This is the classic auto-commit data-loss scenario. Manual commit after processing is required for at-least-once semantics.

quizzes.question: A consumer processing a batch of 500 records takes 7 minutes, exceeding max.poll.interval.ms (default 5 minutes). What is the consequence?
options: Kafka buffers the extra time and no action is taken
The consumer is considered dead, a rebalance fires, its partitions are reassigned, and another consumer reprocesses the same records — causing duplicates
The consumer commits offsets automatically and continues
The broker increases max.poll.interval.ms dynamically
quizzes.explanation: max.poll.interval.ms is the maximum allowed time between poll() calls. If processing exceeds it, the group coordinator removes the consumer from the group, triggering a rebalance and reassigning its partitions. The new owner starts from the last committed offset, which may be behind the slow consumer's actual position — so the same records are processed again. The fixes are to reduce max.poll.records, process asynchronously while polling, or increase the interval if long processing is legitimate.

quizzes.question: A topic has 3 partitions and a consumer group has 5 consumers. Two consumers sit idle. A developer proposes increasing the partition count to 5 to use all consumers. What is the consequence for messages already in the topic?
options: No consequence — existing messages are automatically redistributed
The key-to-partition mapping changes for keys whose murmur2 hash maps to the new partitions, so messages with the same key may no longer land in the same partition, breaking per-key ordering
Kafka refuses to add partitions to a topic that already has data
All existing offsets are invalidated and consumers must start from offset 0
quizzes.explanation: Increasing partition count changes the modulo divisor in murmur2(key) % numPartitions. Keys that previously mapped to partition 0 may now map to partition 3 or 4. Existing messages stay where they are, but future messages with the same key may go to a different partition — so per-key order across the repartitioning boundary is no longer guaranteed. Adding partitions is safe for throughput but not for key-based ordering unless the partitioner is designed to be stable across count changes.

quizzes.question: A consumer receives a higher generation ID than it expected in a heartbeat response. What should it do, and why?
options: Ignore it and keep processing — generation IDs are informational only
Stop fetching, commit its current offsets (with the old generation, which the coordinator may reject), and send a JoinGroupRequest to rejoin the group
Immediately shut down the JVM to avoid committing stale offsets
Increase session.timeout.ms and continue
quizzes.explanation: A higher generation ID means a rebalance has been triggered and this consumer's membership is stale. It must stop fetching, attempt to commit what it has processed, and rejoin via JoinGroupRequest. The coordinator rejects commits from an older generation to prevent a zombie consumer from overwriting offsets that a new owner is already advancing. Shutting down the JVM is excessive; ignoring the generation leads to rejected commits and duplicate or lost work.

quizzes.question: A topic has replication.factor=3, min.insync.replicas=2, acks=all, and unclean.leader.election.enable=false. Two brokers become unreachable, leaving one replica. What happens to producer writes?
options: Writes succeed with acks=1 behavior because one replica is still alive
Writes fail — the ISR is below min.insync.replicas, so the leader rejects acks=all writes rather than accept non-durable data
Kafka automatically lowers min.insync.replicas to 1
The remaining broker becomes leader and writes succeed with acks=all
quizzes.explanation: With min.insync.replicas=2, acks=all writes require at least two replicas to acknowledge. When only one replica remains, the ISR is below the minimum and the leader rejects the write — Kafka prefers to fail rather than silently degrade to acks=1 and risk data loss. Kafka does not auto-lower min.insync.replicas; that would defeat the durability guarantee.

quizzes.question: Consumers cannot read records beyond the high watermark even though the leader's log end offset is higher. Why?
options: The high watermark is a performance optimization that limits read bandwidth
Records beyond the high watermark have not been replicated to all ISR members; reading them could expose data that would be lost if the leader failed before replication
The high watermark is the retention boundary — older records are deleted past it
Consumers can read past the high watermark if they set isolation.level=read_uncommitted
quizzes.explanation: The high watermark is the highest offset replicated to every in-sync replica. Records between the high watermark and the leader's log end offset exist only on the leader (and possibly some followers), so if the leader failed, those records could disappear. Kafka hides them from consumers to preserve the durability guarantee. isolation.level=read_uncommitted controls visibility of aborted transactional records, not the high watermark boundary.

quizzes.question: A team wants exactly-once processing from a Kafka topic to an external PostgreSQL database. They enable Kafka transactions on the producer. What is still missing?
options: Nothing — Kafka transactions guarantee exactly-once to any downstream system

Kafka's exactly-once guarantee is internal to Kafka; writes to PostgreSQL are outside the transaction, so the database write must be made idempotent (e.g., upsert or inbox table) to prevent duplicates on retry
They must set isolation.level=read_uncommitted on the consumer
They must increase max.in.flight.requests.per.connection to 10
quizzes.explanation: Kafka transactions make the Kafka-side writes and offset commits atomic, but PostgreSQL is a separate system that is not part of the Kafka transaction. If the consumer commits the Kafka transaction and then the PostgreSQL write fails, or vice versa, the two systems diverge. The external write must be idempotent (upsert, unique constraint, inbox table) to close the gap. read_uncommitted would make things worse (it exposes aborted records); increasing in-flight requests does not address the boundary.

quizzes.question: A consumer uses manual commit. It processes a payment record (charging the customer via an external API), then crashes before commitSync() succeeds. On restart, the record is redelivered and the customer is charged twice. What is the correct fix?
options: Switch to auto-commit so the offset is committed before the external call
Use an idempotency key with the payment provider so the retry returns the original result instead of charging again, and store the key in a dedup table alongside the local state
Increase session.timeout.ms so the crash is not detected
Disable retries on the producer
quizzes.explanation: The crash happened after the side effect but before the offset commit — the classic dual-write gap. Auto-commit would commit before processing and lose payments instead of duplicating them, which is worse. Increasing session timeout does not prevent the crash or the redelivery. The correct fix is idempotency at the external system (Stripe-style Idempotency-Key) plus a local dedup record so retries are safe.

quizzes.question: A consumer uses enable.auto.commit=true. It polls records 100–199, auto-commit fires and commits 200, then crashes while processing record 150. What happens on restart, and what is the failure class?
options: It resumes from 150 and reprocesses — at-least-once
It resumes from 200 and records 150–199 are lost — at-most-once
It resumes from 100 and reprocesses everything — at-least-once
The broker automatically replays 150–199
quizzes.explanation: Auto-commit commits the latest offset returned by poll(), not the last processed offset. Once offset 200 is committed, restarting seeks to 200 and skips records 150–199 that were polled but never processed. This is at-most-once behavior — data loss. The fix is enable.auto.commit=false and commit only after processing succeeds.

quizzes.question: An order service publishes events with key=orderId to a 6-partition topic. A new order-123 event is produced and then a second order-123 event follows. Which statement is guaranteed?
options: Both events land on the same partition and are consumed in production order by any consumer group
The events may land on different partitions because the partitioner is not deterministic
Both land on the same partition only if they are produced by the same producer instance
Ordering is guaranteed globally across all partitions
quizzes.explanation: Key-based partitioning (murmur2(key) % partitions) is deterministic, so both events land on the same partition as long as the partition count does not change. However, Kafka's ordering guarantee for same-key messages is stated for a single producer: if two different producer instances send order-123 events, the broker may interleave them depending on timing. With a single producer, order is preserved. Global ordering across partitions is never guaranteed.

quizzes.question: A producer sends null-key records to a topic with 6 partitions. A consumer expects to see the records in the same order they were sent. What is wrong with this expectation?
options: Null-key records are rejected by Kafka
Null-key records use a sticky partitioner and have no ordering guarantee — consecutive records can land on different partitions and be processed out of order
Null-key records always go to partition 0, so order is guaranteed
Null-key records are replicated more slowly, causing reordering
quizzes.explanation: With a null key, the producer uses the sticky partitioner: it fills one partition's batch before switching to another. There is no deterministic mapping, and records can be distributed across partitions with no cross-partition order. If ordering matters, the producer must supply a key (e.g., entity ID) so all related records land in the same partition.

quizzes.question: A developer uses topic-partition-offset as the idempotency key for a consumer that writes to an external database. After a cluster failover and replay, duplicate records appear despite the dedup logic. Why?
options: Kafka does not support idempotency keys in record headers
Topic-partition-offset is not stable across replays and cluster moves — the same logical message gets a new offset after failover, so the dedup key changes and the duplicate is not recognized
The external database does not support unique constraints
Consumer idempotency requires enable.idempotence=true on the producer
quizzes.explanation: Offsets are positional and change when data is replayed, retained/compacted, or mirrored to another cluster. The same logical event can have a different topic-partition-offset after failover, so using that triple as the dedup key fails to recognize the redelivered copy. The key must be generated at the origin (eventId UUID or business key) and carried in the record so it survives redelivery.

quizzes.question: What exactly does the idempotent producer (enable.idempotence=true) protect against, and where does its guarantee stop?
options: It guarantees exactly-once end-to-end from producer to consumer and external databases
It deduplicates producer retries within a single producer session using PID + per-partition sequence numbers; it does not survive producer restarts and does not make consumers idempotent
It prevents duplicate messages across all producers in the cluster
It requires ZooKeeper to track producer sequence numbers
quizzes.explanation: The idempotent producer assigns a Producer ID (PID) per producer session and a sequence number per partition. The broker drops duplicate (PID, partition, sequence) batches within that session. A producer restart gets a new PID, so cross-session exactly-once requires transactions. Consumer-side duplicates from at-least-once processing require application-level idempotency (dedup table or idempotency keys) — enable.idempotence does nothing for that.
